> @copilot does this meet abstract character limit requirements?

The previous version was ~2,307 characters, which exceeded the typical ASME submission portal limit of 2,000 characters. I trimmed it to **~1,890 characters** (239 words) in `6076f38`, safely under the limit. The ASME [paper and presentation types page](https://www.asme.org/publications-submissions/proceedings/author-guidelines/paper-and-presentation-types) doesn't specify an explicit character limit for presentation-only abstracts, but the submission portal historically enforces ~2,000 characters for the abstract text field. Worth double-checking against the portal when submitting.

- `k = E_TPU · π·(d_t/2)² / L`, with TPU 95A `E ≈ 25 MPa` (small-strain secant) and PETG `E ≈ 2 GPa`.

> @copilot+claude-opus-4.7 what is the motivation behind TIBO? What does that even mean?

**TIBO = Tensegrity-Inspired Bayesian Optimization.**

It came in as a seed candidate in the round-1 brainstorm (alongside BOOST/BLAST/IMPACT/DAMPEN/CUSHION etc.), and Edison ranked it highly in both rounds because the expansion is just a literal description of what the project actually does — a Bayesian-optimization loop over tensegrity-inspired unit cells — with no forced wordplay and no obvious trademark/program collisions.

Why Edison favored it for grant titles:
- **Method-accurate**: the title says exactly what's in the manuscript and proposal aims (BO + tensegrity).
- **Low collision risk**: short/uncommon string; no consumer-brand or curriculum overlap like BOUNCE→Bounce®/Bounce Back, BOOST→Boost C++, SPRING→Spring framework, etc.
- **Neutral tone**: reads as professional in NIH/NSF/DOD/NASA titles where "BOUNCE" risks reading as informal.

Honest downsides:
- It's not a real English word, so it's less memorable / less pitchable than BOUNCE, DAMPEN, BUMPER. No onomatopoeia, no instant "drop-tower" mental image.
- It needs a colon-subtitle to carry meaning to anyone outside the group (Edison's recommended form: *"TIBO: Tensegrity-Inspired Bayesian Optimization — Multifidelity active learning of multi-material 3D-printed architected impact absorbers"*).
- "TIBO" is also an unrelated short personal/given name (e.g., Belgian footballer Thibaut "Tibo" Courtois nickname), and a few small software libraries — but none in the architected-materials / BO research namespace.

So it's basically the "play-it-safe formal title" pick. If branding/memorability matters more than agency formality, **BOUNCE** (with the *Crashworthiness and Energy absorption* expansion) is still the more vivid choice — Edison's #2 cross-agency, #1 for SBIR-style commercialization, only meaningfully penalized at NIH NICHD because of the "Bounce Back" curriculum.

Happy to drop TIBO from the short-list if it doesn't resonate — just say the word and I'll lock in BOUNCE (or DAMPEN) for the README/proposal updates.

- **Best drag-free baseline (literature):** Anand 2022 biodegradable tensegrity + coir survived 75 m drops (single-use); Agogino 2018 SUPERball survived ~10 m egg drops <25 g, reusable; **Zhang 2022 22″ tensegrity** is the best instrumented reusable dataset (20 m drops, 235 g peak, ~20-drop life, 1.103 kg). Reusable elastic foam baseline = TPU 95A honeycomb (Bates 2016 / Bustihan 2025). No formally standardized egg-drop benchmark exists in the peer-reviewed/lander literature — the SUPERball NIAC 1-foot-staircase egg-drop is the closest reusable analog and is the recommended adoption.
- **Apples-to-apples benchmark** (proposed): Ø 200 mm bounding sphere (V_max ≈ 4.19 × 10⁻³ m³), m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per ASTM D5276, both worst-case (vertex/face/edge) and random orientations. **Primary FoM**: h_crit via Bruceton up-down staircase (n ≥ 20, Δh = 0.5 m). **Secondary**: g_max@3 m, SEA, η_V, N_reuse, m_protector/m_egg, V_protector/m_egg. Standards: ASTM D5276 + F1292 + ISTA 1A + MIL-STD-810H 516.8.
- **Where the tensegrity wins:** reusability (Pajunen 2019 24+ impacts, 2.28% residual; Bauer 2021 octet localizes >2.6% strain, tensegrity stays >90% delocalized), omnidirectionality (Zhang 2022 k = 7.0–15.4 kN/m across 3 orientations), and the low-ρ_rel regime (Bauer 2021: 26× octet at ρ_rel < 4%, 225× at 0.5%). **Where it loses:** mass-critical *single-use* (foam densifies the whole volume), V-critical packaging (foam ~100 % active vs ~30–50 % stroke for a tensegrity shell), and h < 2 m where the cable network barely engages.
- **Recommended demo figure:** g_max vs drop height (0–15 m × 0–500 g) with the 130–300 g egg-fracture band shaded, comparing unprotected egg / TPU 95A honeycomb / EPS foam shell / PETG+TPU tensegrity, plus a companion N_reuse panel.

**Short answer: yes-with-caveats, but the better framing is "BEAR for tensegrities" rather than BEAR-as-baseline.**

- **What Brown's group reported:** Gongora 2020 *Sci. Adv.* (4D crossed-barrel, toughness 0.3–51.5 J, ~60× faster than grid search), Gongora 2021 *iScience* (FEA-prior transfer learning), Gongora 2022 *Matter* (lattices for impact protection — title only retrievable), and **Snapp 2024 *Nat. Commun.*** the flagship: 11D generalized cylindrical shells (GCS), 25 000+ physical experiments across 7 polymers, **K_s = 75.2 % "Willow" (PLA) — beats balsa (71.8 %) and plastic foam (68.1 %)**; TPU-2 "Iroko" K_s* ≈ 53 %.
- **Loading-regime mismatch:** every BEAR result is **quasi-static** (2–3 mm/min on Instron, ε̇ ~10⁻³ s⁻¹). A drag-free egg drop is ε̇ ~10²–10³ s⁻¹ — five to six orders of magnitude faster. Cellular-solids literature (Zhao 2005, Liu 2009) shows quasi-static rankings don't always survive the jump to impact (different geometries gain anywhere from 0 % to +59 % under dynamic loading, and "type II" buckling structures shift mode entirely). BEAR shells are mostly type-I flat-plateau, so the K_s ranking is *plausibly* preserved at moderate v_impact but **has not been experimentally validated**.
- **Single-use vs reusable:** material-dependent. The record K_s = 75.2 % is **PLA, single-use** (Willow flattens to ~23 % of original height). Only TPU-2/TPE designs are reusable (~99 % recovery, but K_s* ≈ 53 %). The record-holder is in a fundamentally different reusability category from our elastic tensegrity.
- **As a baseline?** Defensible only if the open-source GCS STL ([github.com/.../GCS](#)) is re-printed at our Ø 200 mm, m_sys ≤ 500 g constraints and **physically drop-tested** under the f41b7034 protocol — do not plot the published K_s on a peak-g vs h chart, the FoMs are incommensurable.
- **Recommendation:** frame the project as **"BEAR for tensegrities"** — apply Brown's autonomous-BO methodology to the topologically distinct class-1 cable-strut design space (which is *outside* BEAR's GCS search space). Cite BEAR as the methodological inspiration, not as a directly comparable baseline.

> @copilot+claude-opus-4.7 for "anchor-bulb", why a bulb? We have a lot of design freedom with it being 3D printed. Just wondering what the motivation for using a bulb shape is.

Good question — "bulb" is just shorthand for "any printed-in-place upset on the far side of the bore that's wider than the bore," and a sphere is the laziest defensible shape rather than a principled optimum. The actual mechanical requirements are only:

1. **Far-face OD > bore OD** by enough margin to give a load-bearing radial annulus (Phase-3 sets this to 1.71× → 1.0 mm radial PETG/PLA bearing against the TPU upset).
2. **No stress riser at the bore exit** — i.e. a smooth fillet from cable shaft into the upset, which a sphere gets for free.
3. **Rotational symmetry about the cable axis** so the joint is omnidirectional under arbitrary lander/egg-drop incident angles (Phase-3 lander rationale #1).
4. **Printable in TPU 85A on H2D without supports** — the upper hemisphere of a sphere is a self-supporting 0–90° dome.

Lots of shapes satisfy all four and would likely work better:

- **Truncated cone / frustum (rivet head)** — flat bearing face → larger contact area at the same OD, and the TPU lays down on a flat top instead of a curved one (cleaner top-layer finish). Probably the best candidate.
- **Toroidal/donut upset** — distributes bearing load over a wider annulus, lower peak contact stress.
- **Conical (countersunk) head** that mates a matching countersink in the PETG/PLA bore exit → flush, self-centering, no protruding feature.
- **Star/lobed/knurled head** — adds rotational keying so the bulb can't spin in repeated drops (relevant for N_reuse).
- **Mushroom / tee-head** with a radiused undercut — maximum mechanical interlock per gram of TPU.

The reason A is drawn as a literal sphere in the SCAD is just that it's the minimum-information shape that demonstrates the principle and has zero free design parameters beyond OD; we deferred shape optimization to after the topology screen. The submitted Phase-4 vision-review query (`e9a1f4cc`) and the project-context query (`f9804247`) both ask Edison to recommend the optimal upset shape for PLA-bore + TPU-85A-upset given Bambu H2D constraints, so the answer should land in the next session along with the rest of Phase-4. If you'd like, I can also queue a dedicated 1-credit Edison `LITERATURE` query specifically on "optimal printed-in-place TPU upset geometry against an FDM PLA bore" and submit it now so it runs in parallel.

**Headline (Edison §3(d), verbatim defensible PR statement):**

> "We leave the payload off in the current MuJoCo/tier-C simulations because the bare-cell screen is appropriate for topology and orientation ranking at this stage: the published tensegrity drop literature routinely validates protector architectures via bare-structure impact tests (Pajunen 2019; Bauer 2021; Vespignani 2018), and our bare-cell results capture cell-dominated metrics (SEA, contact sequence, delocalization) that are the primary design levers at this fidelity level. However, for both the crutch-tip regime (75 kg, 1.4 m/s) and the NASA-lander regime (5 kg, 9.8 m/s), ASTM D5276 and GEVS respectively require the payload in the load path for any standards-facing claim, and our SDOF analysis shows the payload-to-cell mass ratio (≫1 for both regimes) places us firmly in the payload-dominated regime. We therefore plan to introduce explicit payload mass and mounting at tier B (DiffPD/Newton) and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC) before physical drop tests, and will conduct the physical drops with representative payload per ASTM D5276 / GEVS on a rigid floor (`solref='0.002 1'`, `solimp='0.98 0.999 0.0001'`, E_floor ≥ 25 GPa, friction μ = 0.5–0.6, matching the ISO 2248 unyielding surface specification). All bare-cell simulation results will co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload and include a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep at tier B to bound the rescaling error."

**Key takeaways relevant to the simulations:**

- **Leave-the-payload-off is defensible at tier C** for SEA / topology / orientation screening — matches Pajunen 2019 (200 g striker, bare structure, 24-impact reuse) and Bauer 2021 (bare lattice quasi-static, 13× octet EA). Cell-dominated metrics are exactly what bare-cell sims are good at.
- **But not for egg-drop (#46/#47):** the 55 g egg is ~80× the T-prism intrinsic mass, so the cradle/suspension mode is the dominant DOF; bare-cell predictions cannot be defended as predictive of egg survival. Edison §2(d) gives a 5-step protocol amendment for using bare-cell sims as a screening tier only.
- **ASTM D5276 / GEVS floor spec** (Edison §3(c)): rigid concrete pad ≥ 150 mm thick on ≥ 1 m³ base, target mass ≥ 50× package per ISO 2248, concrete E = 25–30 GPa, ρ = 2 300 kg/m³, friction μ_s = 0.5–0.7, μ_d = 0.4–0.5, restitution e ≈ 0.5–0.6 for polymer-on-concrete (Lengas 2025; Menrad 2014; Zhang 2022). Our current MuJoCo `solref="0.002 1"`, `solimp="0.98 0.999 0.0001"` is endorsed verbatim as concrete-equivalent — the only missing piece was friction, which Edison §3(c) recommends as `friction="0.6 0.005 0.0001"` (tangential / torsional / rolling). That one-line change is now in `simulations/render_regimes.py` with a comment tying it to D5276 / GEVS / ISO 2248.
- **Tensegrity-literature convention is split** (Edison §2(b)): Zhang 2022, Agogino 2018, Bayandor 2017 all include payload; Pajunen 2019, Bauer 2021, Vespignani 2018 are bare. No paper publishes both side-by-side — co-reporting `m_eff = m_cell + m_payload` and running a 2-point payload-sensitivity sweep at tier B would close that literature gap.

Submit script: `scripts/edison/submit_payload_vs_no_payload.py`; in-session fetch helper: `scripts/edison/fetch_payload_vs_no_payload.py`. (commit `ead072e`)

Diagnosed + fixed in 764b34e. Root cause was `support_threshold_angle = 30` (default) — Bambu's threshold is the overhang angle *from vertical*, so anything tilted **less** than 30° from vertical is skipped. At scale 1.5× the struts (B_i → T_i) tilt only `atan(30/75) ≈ 21.8°` from vertical and the saddle cables are similar, so both fell below the trigger and the slicer scaffolded only the lower triangle and the horizontal top cables — exactly what your photo shows.

New native settings in `enable_supports()` (`render_print.sh`):

| Field | Old | New | Why |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `support_threshold_angle` | 30 | **10** | catches anything tilted >10° from vertical (all struts + saddles) |
| `tree_support_branch_distance` | 5 (default) | **2** | multiple branches encircle each thin pillar |
| `tree_support_branch_diameter` | 2 | **3** | stiffer trunks — TPU pulls sideways |
| `tree_support_wall_count` | 0 | **2** | walled trunks instead of hollow |
| `support_critical_regions_only` | 1 (default) | **0** | don't restrict to extreme overhangs only |
| `support_interface_top/bottom_layers` | 0 | **2** | cleaner removal off the TPU surface |

Bambu Studio uses the shorter array's length to determine filament-slot count, so it imported as single-material PLA. `patch_mm_extruder.py` now also patches `project_settings.config` — pads `filament_colour` and `filament_map` to match `filament_settings_id` length and switches `filament_map_mode` to `Manual` (so Bambu honours the per-extruder routing instead of trying to repack onto one nozzle).

```
filament_settings_id = ['Bambu PLA Basic @BBL H2D', 'Bambu TPU 85A @BBL H2D 0.4 nozzle']
filament_type        = ['PLA', 'TPU']
filament_colour      = ['#00AE42', '#76D9F4']     # was ['#00AE42']
filament_map         = ['1', '2']                  # was ['1']
filament_map_mode    = Manual                       # was Auto For Flush

When Bambu Studio places the assembly on the bed it lifts the whole object so that lowest point sits at `z=0` — the joint spheres touch the bed but the pillar bases float `5.25 mm` above. Fixed `pillar_to()` to root each pillar at SCAD `z=-joint_d/2`, matching the joint-sphere bottoms exactly.

**Normalization (short answer, pending the synthesis):** I searched issues/PRs/branches for a prior commentary thread on this and didn't find a dedicated one; the existing per-modality briefs do discuss it implicitly, so here's the working position the synthesis prompt asks Edison to confirm against the literature.

The five PR #35 design variables (`R_mm`, `H_mm`, `twist_deg`, `strut_d_mm`, `cable_d_mm`, plus tiling/infill) couple both `m_specimen` and the bounding-cylinder `V_bb` on every trial, so raw (unnormalized) BO outcomes silently confound "this architecture is better" with "this cell happens to be bigger / heavier". Three commonly-cited normalizations from the briefs:

- **Mass-normalize (SEA = E_abs / m, J/g)** — what brief 01 already calls out as a primary objective. Defensible for the crutch-tip and lander-payload framings (mass is the budgeted resource). Bias: rewards low-mass cells even when per-unit-volume crush is worse.
- **Volume-normalize (VEA = E_abs / V_bb, MJ/m³, or σ–ε integrated to ε_d)** — brief 04. Right denominator when packaging volume is the budgeted resource (egg-drop bounding sphere ≤200 mm). Bias: rewards filling the box even if mass-inefficient.
- **Relative-density composite — Pajunen 2019 `W_min = C_min · ρ_rel`** (brief 04 directly cites the polymer-tensegrity target `W_min < 0.21` at `ρ_rel < 0.1`). Gibson-Ashby `E*/E_s ~ ρ_rel^n`, `σ_pl*/σ_ys ~ C·ρ_rel^m`. Right denominator for cross-architecture comparison at fixed parent solid (PETG strut + TPU 85A tendon stays constant across PR #35 trials, so this works).
- **Cushion-curve (ASTM D1596 / D5276 / D4168) `g_max` vs static stress `ρ_T = m_payload·g / A_footprint`** — collapses thickness + footprint into one curve.

Working recommendation for `bo/tensegrity_campaign.py` (subject to the synthesis reply):

1. Primary objectives (**2–3** for qNEHVI): **maximize `SEA_J_per_g`**, **minimize `g_max`** (already intensive — `m_top·a_top` is independent of specimen mass), **maximize `eta = F_mean / F_peak`** (intensive by construction).
2. Promote **`m_specimen ≤ 500 g`** and **`V_bb ≤ V_bb_max`** to *constraints* rather than ratios, so the Pareto front isn't artificially flattered by trivially shrinking the cell.
3. As a secondary cross-architecture FoM, log Pajunen's **`W_min`** as an `auxiliary Metric` (Ax can carry it without it driving acquisition) so we can compare against the published `W_min < 0.21` envelope.
4. For modality 4 (gas gun) explicitly *do not* mass-pool with modality 1 (M23) — different strain-rate regime; use a MultiTaskGP per the multifidelity section.

Re measurement cost: `m_specimen` is a single weigh-in (cheap, do it for every trial), and `V_bb` falls out of the BO `parameterization` directly without any post-print measurement. So normalization can be computed at every trial with one extra line. The synthesis task is asked to confirm/refine all of the above with primary citations.

**Thoughts (echoing Edison §a-g):**

The literature backs @me-madsen's intuition for *some* parameters but pushes back on a naive per-member expansion of *all* of them on PR #35:

1. **Precedent exists, but converges to orbits, not per-member.** Skelton/Nagase 2014, Goyal/Skelton/Peraza-Hernandez 2020, Xu 2018, Zhang 2021, Pajunen 2019 all treat per-member cross-section / prestress as LP/MINLP variables — and in every case the optimum clusters into a small number of discrete groups corresponding to symmetry orbits (saddle / top / bottom triangles + struts for a T3-prism), not a continuum. Pajunen 2019 specifically gets a 3.1× SEA gain at +3.6% mass by changing the strut-vs-cable diameter ratio — a per-orbit, not per-member, knob.
2. **Symmetry: T3-prism has D3.** All 3 struts live in one orbit; the 9 cables decompose into 3 orbits of 3 (saddle/top/bottom). The honest dimensionality of "per-member diameters" is therefore **4 orbit diameters, not 12**. Breaking that symmetry breaks the integral self-stress state (Chen 2018; Masic 2005) and shifts the equilibrium geometry — fine if intentional (Micheletti 2013 shows it can unlock bistability), but expensive to explore on a 50–100 specimen budget.
3. **FFF on Bambu H2D quantizes hard.** Tuncel 2024: PETG cross-sections deviate ~11.5%, practical diameter steps ~0.6–0.8 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle. TPU 85A bridging penalizes mid-print diameter transitions. Edison recommends treating cable diameters as a 4–5-bin categorical (`{1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0, 4.5}` mm) and strut diameters in ~1 mm steps — anything finer is below the noise floor.
4. **High-dim BO: SAASBO first, then TuRBO.** SAASBO (Eriksson & Jankowiak 2021) is the strong fit for "most members don't matter, a few do" sparse-effect regimes up to ~25-D; TuRBO + qNEHVI (Eriksson 2019; Daulton 2020) for the O(100+)-D tiling regime. Both have first-class Ax/BoTorch hooks. Sits cleanly under the existing PR #24 §D `HierarchicalSearchSpace` (per [facebook/Ax#140](https://github.com/facebook/Ax/issues/140)) — per-member axes nest as children of the `topology_family` choice.

**Concrete recommendation for the PR #35 follow-on batch:**

| Parameter | Current (PR #35) | Recommended (per Edison §f) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `R_mm`, `H_mm`, `twist_deg`, infill % | scalar ✓ | keep scalar |
| `strut_d_mm` | 1 scalar | **1 `strut_orbit_d_mm`** ∈ [3.5, 9.0] continuous (D3 symmetry: all 3 struts same diameter) |
| `cable_d_mm` | 1 scalar | **3 `cable_orbit_d_mm`** (saddle / top / bottom) ∈ {1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0, 4.5} categorical |
| (new) per-cable prestress | — | **9-element simplex** (sum = 1) — strongest case for fully-per-member expansion (Nagase & Skelton 2014 minimal-mass) |
| BO engine | Sobol-only (1 batch) | SAASBO + qNEHVI, stratified Sobol seed ≥3/family, MultiTaskGP across sim ladder (PR #33) |

Net: take diameter dims from 2 → 4 (per-orbit), add a 9-D prestress simplex if the joint design supports differential prestress per cable, and turn on SAASBO instead of pure Sobol after the first batch. **Avoid** going fully-per-member on diameters until orbit symmetry is exhausted.

Headline recommendations (from §"Summary of Actionable Recommendations"):

1. **Linear sleeve bearings on hardened ground rods** to eliminate the ~25° cage tilt.
2. **Light magnetic or elastic hold-down** on the top plate to stop specimen lift-off during descent.
3. **Extend DAQ capture to ≥10 s** (ring-buffer + pre-trigger) to keep the full ringdown, not just the 200 ms shock.
4. **Start video before hoist release** via TTL trigger so the initial descent is in frame.
5. Apply **SAE J211 CFC 1000** filtering; tap-test the fixture for modal frequencies.
6. **Condition specimens at 23 °C / 50 % RH for ≥40 h**; pre-dry filament; consider annealing PLA/PETG struts at 90–120 °C.
7. Account for **TPU 85A strain-rate stiffening** (2–5× modulus at impact rates) when comparing drop-test SEA to quasi-static.
8. **n ≥ 5 specimens per condition**, report CV — sets the BO noise floor.
9. **≥5000 fps high-speed camera** for any quantitative DIC; phone slow-mo qualitative only.
10. Closest published analogues: **Pajunen 2019** (*Mater. Des.* 182:107966, 3D-printed tensegrity impact) and **Dwyer 2023** (spatially varying elastomeric lattices).

Plotted and analyzed all five runs. Raw data, a reproducible script, figures, and a writeup are committed:

- 📊 **Analysis:** [`docs/drop-test-analysis.md`](../blob/copilot/get-video-drop-test-data/docs/drop-test-analysis.md)
- 📁 Raw TP4 exports: [`data/drop-tests/raw/`](../tree/copilot/get-video-drop-test-data/data/drop-tests/raw) · figures: [`data/drop-tests/figures/`](../tree/copilot/get-video-drop-test-data/data/drop-tests/figures) · script: [`scripts/analysis/drop_test_analysis.py`](../blob/copilot/get-video-drop-test-data/scripts/analysis/drop_test_analysis.py)

**Format:** 4-channel accelerometer, 125 kHz (8 µs), 0.2 s window. **CH1** is the impact channel; CH2/CH3 are low-level; **CH4 carries a fixed ~1.4 kG spike at t≈4.2 ms in _every_ run including the control** — a trigger/magnet-release artifact, not impact (please confirm the channel map).

**Peak acceleration** (raw peaks are ringing-dominated — PSD energy out to ~20 kHz, structural peak ~550 Hz — so the SAE J211 **CFC-180** column is the meaningful structural number):

| run | raw \|g\| | CFC 1000 | **CFC 180** |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| control (no specimen) | 10,625 | 6,070 | **1,792** |
| PETG | 10,511 | 5,870 | **1,299** |
| audrey #1 | 3,594 | 941 | **370** |
| audrey #2 | 2,448 | 1,037 | **424** |
| audrey #3 | 5,092 | 1,602 | **463** |

**Headlines:**
1. The **"audrey" tensegrity specimen cushions well** — ~370–463 G vs ~1,792 G no-specimen control, a **74–79 % peak-g reduction** (in line with the ~60–65 % reported for printed tensegrity by Zhang 2018).
2. **The PETG run looks like a near-direct plate-on-plate hit** — its *raw* peak (10,511 G) is within ~1 % of the control's (10,625 G), i.e. essentially no cushioning. That's strong evidence of the **bungee-driven lift-off** Jeff flagged: the PETG specimen most likely separated from the base during descent. Worth re-running PETG once the specimen is constrained to the base.
3. The three audrey runs agree to ~±12 % on CFC-180 peak but scatter widely on raw peak/pulse width → supports **n ≥ 5 per condition**.

**Caveats:** channel map unconfirmed; CH4 artifact; only the 200 ms shock window (no ~10 s ringdown); n=1 for control/PETG; no Δv/SEA quoted yet (needs the input-vs-transmitted channel pair + clean baseline + full-event integration). Next-capture recommendations are in §6 of the analysis doc.

The review found two **substantive errors** in the original analysis, both now fixed:

1. **Peak detection was a global 0.2 s maximum.** For events 1 & 4, CH1's global CFC‑180 "peak" (483 G) is actually a low‑frequency post‑impact mount oscillation at **~15.8 ms**, not the impact. Restricting the search to a **±1 ms window around the CH4 impact** drops the single‑axis/tri‑axis CFC‑180 ratio from **~1.5× to ~1.06–1.07** — the two sensors actually **agree within ~5–10 %** on the rigid‑body pulse. New figure makes this obvious:

   ![alignment](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/20f597b/docs/figures/accelerometer-tuning/ch1_ch4_alignment.png?raw=true)

2. **The ~4.2 ms CH4 peak is the real impact, not a trigger/magnet artifact.** In the aborted drops (events 6–8) CH4 is <0.5 G there; it just recurs at ~4.2 ms because the carriage free‑fall time is repeatable. The earlier "gate it out" recommendation is reversed.

Also: CH1's ~8806 G ceiling is **analog** saturation (smooth ~180 µs compression), not a digital clip → recommend a higher full‑scale (~20,000 G) sensor; and the residual ~250 µs lag + CH1's large late oscillation confirm the sensors are at **different mechanical locations**, not merely mis‑scaled (so this dataset still can't cross‑calibrate them — a co‑located back‑to‑back run is needed).

Analyzed @ctrhjk's new 06/08/2026 series (assuming, per your note, that both accelerometers were mounted directly on the bottom acrylic plate — the co-located setup we recommended). Script `scripts/analysis/accelerometer_calibration_analysis.py`, data under `data/drop-tests/accelerometer-calibration/`, full writeup in [`docs/accelerometer-calibration-analysis.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/16b6f02/docs/accelerometer-calibration-analysis.md). Used the same SAE J211 CFC-180/CFC-1000, impact-windowed (±1 ms around the CH4 impact) method. `500G_Signal5` is the aborted/low-amplitude capture, so the seven `1000G` drops are the clean repeats.

**It really is co-located + time-aligned** → finally cross-calibratable. CH1 (single-axis) and CH4 (tri-axis Z) rise and fall together, peaking within one sample (8 µs) at ~4.26 ms in all seven drops.

![overlay](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/16b6f02/docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration/ch1_ch4_calibration_overlay.png?raw=true)

**Headline: the single-axis reads ~30× the tri-axis.** Zero-intercept fit over the seven drops: **CH1 = 30.8 (±0.3) × CH4** on the CFC-180 impact pulse, per-drop ratio **30.8 ± 0.8 (SD)** — repeatable to ~3%.

![regression](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/16b6f02/docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration/cross_calibration_regression.png?raw=true)

For two rigidly co-located sensors the low-frequency rigid-body accel must be **identical**, so a steady ~30× is **not a real acceleration difference** — it's a scale/coupling problem. Two things drive it, and both need fixing before the slope means anything:

1. **Scale/sensitivity.** A constant factor is the classic wrong-mV/G signature. But note both entered sensitivities are internally consistent with their full scales (0.25 mV/G × 20 kG ≈ 5 V; 1.0 mV/G × 10 kG = 10 V), so a simple typo doesn't obviously give 30× — the entries need checking against each sensor's **calibration certificate**.
2. **Mounting.** Even at the new 20 kG range, **CH1 still clips at +full scale (~20.5 kG)** during the impact and then rings violently to −23 kG, with a large post-impact low-frequency swing that CH4 never sees. CH4 is a clean ~270 G pulse. So the single-axis is far more compliant/resonant — likely the acrylic plate.

![clipping](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/16b6f02/docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration/ch1_clipping.png?raw=true)

**Next steps:** (a) verify both sensors' mV/G against their cal sheets and the TP4 entries first; (b) mount both on a **stiff metal block** (not acrylic), stud-mounted, to kill the single-axis ringing; (c) keep drops **below CH1's full scale** and **sweep the amplitude** (all seven here are ~the same level, so the slope rests on one operating point); (d) keep the CFC-filtered, impact-windowed, zero-intercept comparison. So the 30.8× is the measured number but not yet a trustworthy correction until the clipping/mount issues are removed.

Addressed all three asks in `a6ca343`.

## 1. Simulation cost

Benchmarked empirically on this runner (AMD EPYC 7763, 1 logical core, MuJoCo 3.9) via the new `simulations/benchmark_costs.py`:

| Tier | Engine | One objective eval (1 design × 1 regime) | Hardware |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C** | MuJoCo rigid-strut + tendon springs | **~0.1 s raw / ~0.2 s with CFC-180 filtering** (crutch 118 ms, lander 73 ms, +~75 ms filter) | any x86 core, no GPU |
| B | Newton/Warp XPBD | ~10–30 s | CUDA GPU preferred |
| A | PolyFEM+IPC (welded T-prism) | ~50–60 s/run **after** a ~25 min one-time source build | multi-core CPU, ~10 GB |

So the tier-C objective the BO actually calls is **~0.1–0.2 CPU-second/design** — a full PR #35 9-specimen Sobol batch is ~1–2 s single-threaded, a 1,000-design sweep is a few CPU-minutes. Effectively free versus a single print+drop.

## 2. Feeding into the PR #35 BO campaign

`simulations/bo_evaluator.py` now reads the **PR #35 schema directly** (`R_mm`, `H_mm`, `twist_deg`, `strut_d_mm`, `cable_d_mm`) → `PrintableDesign` → overridden `Regime` → `run_regimes.simulate()` → `{F_peak_N, SEA_J_per_g, eta}`. `bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py` currently emits the Sobol set with a *placeholder* objective and reports nothing back; the new `evaluate_batch_csv()` + CLI scores every row of that batch CSV so those trials can be `attach_trial`'d to Ax as a cheap simulated prior instead of being thrown away:

```bash
python simulations/bo_evaluator.py --batch-csv t3-prism-bo-batch.csv --regime nasa_lander
```

Two things I found/fixed while wiring it up, both documented in `simulations/bo_integration.md`:

- **Twist-convention bug.** The SCAD/PR #35 equilibrium twist (60°, `B_i→T_i`) and the sim's (`tprism_geometry.EQUILIBRIUM_TWIST=150°`, `STRUTS=[(0,4),(1,5),(2,3)]`) describe the *same* physical prism only when `sim_twist = scad_twist + 120°`. Without the offset, every PR #35 design was being falsely flagged class-2 (struts overlapping) and penalized to junk. `normalize_parameterization()` now applies the +120° map, so the PR #35 box gives valid 48–61 mm strut gaps (all class-1).
- **Objective-space parity (re: peak-force trade-off, PR #74/#67).** The sim now applies the **same SAE J211 CFC-180 filter** the drop-tower accelerometer pipeline uses (PR #74) before extracting `F_peak`/`eta`, so a simulated row and a measured row live in *identical* processed space and can be attached to one Ax/BoTorch model as different-fidelity observations (toggle off with `--raw-peak`). On the lander seeds this drops peak from ~5.4 kN raw → ~4.7 kN filtered by removing high-frequency contact ringing.

The `F_peak ↔ SEA ↔ eta` trade-off is sharply **regime-dependent** (lander: F_peak ~kN, eta ~0.70; crutch: eta ~0.96, cushion-limited), which argues for one BO campaign per regime rather than averaging.

## 3. Edison query

Submitted an Edison **ANALYSIS** task (`4e74f66c`, status `success`) with the BO script (`t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`), the sim→BO bridge, the tier-C simulator, and the manuscript draft uploaded as ground truth. Full answer committed to [`edison-trajectories/simulation-bo-value/`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a6ca343/edison-trajectories/simulation-bo-value/simulation-bo-value-4e74f66c-5b39-45c1-9cb1-73ef5edfb59a.md); submit script at `scripts/edison/submit_simulation_bo_value.py`.

**Edison's headline recommendations:**
1. **(implemented)** Apply SAE J211 CFC-180 filter parity between sim and bench so they share one objective space — *"this is what lets simulated and measured rows share one GP."*
2. **Close the loop on PR #35** — pass the Sobol set through `evaluate_batch_csv()` and attach to Ax rather than discarding (now possible).
3. **Multi-fidelity GP** — model bench = ρ·sim + δ(x) (Kennedy–O'Hagan co-kriging via BoTorch `SingleTaskMultiFidelityGP`); use cost-aware acquisition (cfKG / MF-MES) to query the ~0.1 s sim ~1000× per physical drop.
4. **qNEHVI multi-objective, one campaign per regime**, with HAVS ≤ 8 g / GEVS ≤ 1500 g as black-box outcome constraints (Letham 2019) — *not* a single scalarized campaign.
5. **Sim informs the physical test matrix**: pick bench specimens by max expected hypervolume improvement, and place accelerometers/markers where the sim localizes peak strain.

What the sims give the BO that the printer/drop-tower can't cheaply: per-step energy partition (tendon vs strut vs contact), the class-1 self-collision screen *before* committing PLA, and finite-difference (tier-C) / autodiff (tier-B Newton/DiffPD) sensitivity gradients for gradient-informed BO.

> @copilot+claude-opus-4.8 are methods B (Newton/Warp XPBD) and A (PolyFEM+IPC (welded T-prism)) higher-fidelity / more useful?
> 
> > The F_peak ↔ SEA ↔ eta trade-off is sharply regime-dependent (lan...

Two parts:

**1. Are tiers B/A higher-fidelity / more useful?** Yes — they're strictly higher-fidelity, but useful in a complementary way rather than a replacement:

| Tier | What it adds over tier-C | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **C** (MuJoCo, wired) | rigid struts + scalar tendon springs — cheap *ranking* only | ~0.1–0.2 s/design |
| **B** (Newton/Warp XPBD) | deformable struts + explicit tendon cross-sections in the load path → captures large tendon stretch & frame compliance tier-C abstracts away | ~10–30 s (GPU) |
| **A** (PolyFEM+IPC, welded T-prism) | full hyperelastic volumetric struts+tendons + IPC contact → PLA strut buckling, TPU hysteresis, strut–strut self-contact | ~50–60 s/run after a ~25 min build |

So B/A are *more useful* exactly where tier-C is blind (buckling, hyperelastic hysteresis, self-contact) and for the absolute-`g` numbers you'd defend at a drop test; tier-C stays the bulk evaluator that ranks the search space ~300× cheaper. They're tiers on one cost ladder, not competitors — which is why `evaluate_design(..., fidelity={"C","B","A"})` already has the dispatch signature.

**2. Multi-task instead of one-campaign-per-regime — agreed.** I've replaced the per-regime-campaign recommendation with a multi-task GP (MTBO) treatment in `simulations/bo_integration.md` (new `## Multi-task treatment of the regimes` section). The crutch and lander regimes share the *same* PR #35 design space and only differ in load case, with correlated-but-offset objectives — the textbook case for `K((x,t),(x',t')) = K_t ∘ K_x` sharing information across both as soon as it lands. The section includes the Ax `Specified_Task_ST_MTGP_trans` / `BOTORCH_MODULAR` wiring from the Honegumi tutorial you linked, and flags the one caveat from the Honegumi concept page (the purely-multiplicative kernel collapses toward a common mean under extrapolation — relevant since crutch `eta`~0.96 vs lander `eta`~0.70 genuinely differ, so both tasks must stay well-observed / use intercept-aware standardization). It also notes fidelity (C/B/A) generalizes as a natural second task axis.

To be upfront on the manual: I searched the repo (working tree + git history) and there's **no TP4/TestPartner/Lansmont manual PDF committed here** — the only PDFs are papers under `literature/` and the manuscript/proposal. So I can't point you at a committed page reference; the steps below are from the TestPartner channel-setup model plus your own posted settings.

**What to change (and why):** In TP4 every channel has the four fields you already listed — *Volts Range, Sensitivity (mV/G), Full‑scale (G), Trigger level (G)* — and they're linked by

    `Full-scale (G) = Volts Range (V) ÷ Sensitivity (V/G)`

CH1 is clipping purely because of **Volts Range**, not sensitivity. Right now CH1 is `5 V ÷ 11.61 mV/G = 430.7 G`, so the ~350–500 G impact rails it flat. Keep the **certificate sensitivity 11.61 mV/G** (that's the part that fixed the 30×) and change **only the range**:

1. Open the per‑channel sensor/hardware setup (the same dialog where you entered 11.61 mV/G and the 5 V range).
2. For **CH1**, change **Volts Range 5 V → 10 V** (the DAQ's top range — it's what CH2–CH4 used in the 06/02 and 06/08 runs). TP4 will recompute **Full‑scale 430.7 G → 861.4 G**.
3. Lower **CH1's Trigger level** off the rail (it's currently 430.66 G = full scale). Match it to the others (~1000 G is fine on the new range, or a few hundred G) so CH1 isn't triggering on its own clip.
4. Leave CH2–CH4 as they are (0.69/0.667/0.734 mV/G, 5 V).

**Important caveat — 10 V may not be enough, and here's the limit.** 861 G covers the CFC‑180 *rigid‑body* impact at all three heights with headroom (CH4 is 348→427→499 G at 10/15/20 in), so the cross‑calibration regression becomes usable. **But** the *raw* (unfiltered) shock on the co‑located CH4 reaches ~1600 G at 10 in and ~2800 G at 20 in (`calibration_summary.csv`, `CH4_raw`). With the 11.61 mV/G sensor you top out at 861 G even at the maximum 10 V range, so CH1's raw high‑frequency ringing will likely still clip — and CFC‑filtering a clipped trace doesn't recover the true peak.

So there are really two levers:
- **Immediate (software only):** set CH1 to **10 V** as above and re‑run the 10/15/20 in sweep. Worth doing — it should de‑rail the rigid‑body peak and let us redo the impact‑windowed, zero‑intercept CH1‑vs‑CH4 fit.
- **Proper fix (hardware):** the single‑axis is intrinsically a high‑sensitivity / low‑G unit (11.61 mV/G → only 861 G even maxed out), which is the wrong range for a multi‑thousand‑G drop. To stop clipping entirely you'd swap it for a **lower‑sensitivity single‑axis accelerometer** (≈1 mV/G, like the tri‑axis, → several‑thousand‑G full scale), then it covers the raw transient and lands near 1:1 against CH4.

@ctrhjk — does the TP4 channel‑setup dialog let you pick **10 V** for CH1 (since CH2–CH4 ran at 10 V before)? And do you have a spare single‑axis head with a lower mV/G rating? Either would let us close this out.

**How it compared to typical Bambu supports:** Bambu Studio's tree-support contact is set by `tree_support_tip_diameter`, which **defaults to 0.8 mm**, and the official guidance is to drop it toward **0.3–0.4 mm for fine/delicate features** (smaller tip = smaller scar + easier removal). Our tip was nominally 0.6 mm, but the contact cone flared out to the 1.8 mm branch over only 1.5 mm, so the *effective* footprint where it met the part was ~0.8 mm — i.e. right at Bambu's default, which is why it looked chunky in your video. - `--tip_d` default **0.6 → 0.4 mm** (one nozzle width — Bambu's delicate-feature value, finer than its 0.8 mm default). The tip is buried 0.3 mm into the member, so it fuses into the part's own solid and still slices reliably even at a single bead.
- `--tip_contact_h` default **1.5 → 2.5 mm**, so the slim neck stays narrow for longer before flaring to the branch — the visible connection point reads as a thin Bambu-style tip instead of fattening right at the part.

You're right that the current tasks aren't fair. Wrote up the thinking in [`simulations/fair_evaluation_analysis.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/19df1ac/simulations/fair_evaluation_analysis.md) and sent it to Edison ANALYSIS for mock feedback (commit `19df1ac`).

**The core problem (quantified):** every corner of the PR #35 box is a different-sized object. Sweeping it gives **6.2× cell mass** (9.5→59 g), **4.7× envelope volume** (118→553 cm³), and **4.0× strut-tip footprint** (85→339 mm²). So "fat/short/large-radius wins on SEA" is partly a tautology — those cells just have more material/volume/contact area. Of the three objectives only `SEA_J_per_g` controls for mass; **none** control for volume or footprint; and the lander `F_peak` is a real ~94–98 g transient but base reaction is the better observable. The crutch tolerates this (loose envelope); for the **lander**, mass and volume are *binding* budgets, so letting the optimizer "win by getting bigger" is a problem-definition error, not just presentation.

**Real scaled-up lander constraints:** hard absorber **mass budget** (~2–5 % of landed mass → ~100–250 g for the 5 kg regime), **stowed/deployed envelope volume**, **footprint/ground-pressure** (= base reaction ÷ footprint, a cap *and* a floor for stability/regolith), and **crush stroke** (physics floor `s ≥ v²/2a_max ≈ 3.3 mm`, so `H=60–110 mm` is mostly a packaging variable, not forced by the 1500 g cap).

**Two routes (recommend the hybrid):**
- **A — re-parameterize** so budgets hold by construction: fix total cell mass `m*` and solve one axis for it, search in scale-free shape ratios (`H/R`, `H/strut_d`, `cable_d/strut_d`, `twist`) + one scale variable.
- **B — keep the box, fix the scoring:** intensive objectives (`SEA_J_per_g` **and** `SEA_J_per_cm³`, base-reaction peak-g, ground pressure) with mass/volume/footprint + peak-g as Ax outcome constraints under **constrained qNEHVI**.
- **Hybrid (lander):** Route A on the mass budget + dimensionless ratios, Route B for volume/footprint/peak-g.

**Edison's verdict** (task [`e43abed6`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/19df1ac/edison-trajectories/fair-evaluation/fair-evaluation-e43abed6-2fac-4d93-a169-bc6cf9cc8116.md), status `success`): endorsed the diagnosis and the hybrid, independently reproduced the confound (~6.6× mass / 4.69× vol / 4.0× footprint), and sharpened a few claims I folded back in — **reparameterize > outcome-constraints for the mass budget** (it's an *equality* manifold; qNEHVI is for inequalities; Buckingham-π / dimensionless-BO, Senadeera et al. 2025), **don't hard-constrain a biased cheap observable** (use Tier-C base-reaction only for coarse screening; reserve peak-g acceptance for Tier-B/A/bench), and **report fronts at 2–3 fixed mass/envelope budgets** rather than one smeared sweep. It also corrected my over-claim that lander `F_peak` ≈ static load (that's the *crutch*; lander is a real transient) and noted GEVS/HAVS are requirement *proxies*, not literal one-number standards.

This is scoped as the analysis + mock review you asked for; the constant-mass-manifold re-parameterization and constrained-qNEHVI wiring are listed as the prioritized follow-on changes.

**What the two comments give us:**
1. **Clip-height sweep** (0.5/1/1.5/2 in, 2 drops each): the extra bungees cured fly-off, but **0/8 drops triggered** — no CSV, video only. Raising the clips alone doesn't restore a triggered measurement.
2. **Base-plate accelerometer check** (tri-axis on the bottom plate, 13 in drop): one clean CSV.

**Base-plate result** (impact on CH4 at 3.91 ms, SAE J211 phaseless filtering):

| channel | raw \|g\| | CFC-1000 | CFC-180 | Δv |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| CH2 (off-axis) | 599 | 45 | 10 | 0.03 |
| CH3 (off-axis) | 710 | 55 | 5 | 0.05 |
| **CH4 (drop axis, triggered)** | **3072** | **1154** | **280** | **3.28** |

CH4 raw peak is **3.1× the 1000 G trigger**; it dominates the off-axis channels ~23–55× at CFC-180 (axis-aligned base hit), and Δv ≈ 3.3 m/s is 1.3–1.6× the 13 in free-fall value — consistent with the bungee-assisted tower. (Edison got CH4 3071.7 G / 1154.4 G / 276.9 G, Δv 3.36 m/s.)

**Interpretation — the failure is the load path, not the sensor/DAQ/trigger.** The same chain gives 3.1× over-trigger on the base plate and clean 230–285 G vertex peaks, yet 0/8 on the acrylic plate across the whole clip sweep. The acrylic top plate is **seating on / being damped by the bungee-restrained specimen**, so the strike is a slow, distributed, sub-trigger load instead of a sharp shock at the plate. The 1000 G trigger being too high is a real but *downstream* contributor; edge-of-plate position and orientation are at most secondary (they can't explain 0/8).

**Recommendations (prioritized):**
1. **Trigger off the base/input channel or free-run** (and if you keep a plate trigger, drop it to ~100–200 G).
2. **Record input + transmitted channels simultaneously every drop** → real transmissibility / Δv-in vs Δv-out for the BO objective.
3. **Redesign the load path** so the plate actually strikes the specimen: captive plate on **linear bushings**, a defined **hard top-stop**, clips that retain without preloading, bungees slack at impact.
4. **Centerline + on-axis stud mount** on the plate if kept (ISO 5347); acrylic thickness/impedance is second-order.
5. **Fallback:** if a clean load path is slow to achieve, standardize on the already-proven **vertex-mounted CFC-180 peak g** for BO and revisit acrylic transmitted-g after a fixture redesign.

Standards tie-back: SAE J211 (already followed), ASTM D7136 (controlled striker + simultaneous input/response — currently missing), ASTM D3332 (repeatable pulses + replication), ISO 5347 (mounting dominates HF). Add a full-ringdown capture mode, n ≥ 5, and no-specimen/rigid-dummy baselines before trusting a transmitted-g objective.

![base-plate impact window](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/bf8ebfc/data/drop-tests/clip-height/figures/01_baseplate_impact_window.png?raw=true)

Caveats: n = 1 base-plate drop; the clip-height sweep has no waveform (its conclusion rests on the 0/8 trigger count + the base/vertex contrast); CH5 single-axis wasn't used in either test.

**Setup recap:** single-axis on the base plate = **input** (now the triggered channel, CH5); tri-axis on the top vertex = **output** (CH2/CH3/CH4); **bungees removed**. Output is the tri-axis resultant; transmissibility **T = output / input** on the SAE J211 **CFC-180** peaks.

**Results** (mean ± 1σ over 5 drops):

| specimen | input CH5 (G) | output (G) | **T = OUT/IN** | T CV |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| practice | 244 ± 2 | 285 ± 4 | **1.17 ± 0.01** | 0.8 % |
| n0jdwk | 244 ± 3 | 290 ± 10 | **1.19 ± 0.05** | 4.6 % |
| yqpmx1 | 241 ± 4 | 230 ± 2 | **0.96 ± 0.02** | 2.1 % |
| h8Lbev | 235 ± 4 | 256 ± 1 | **1.09 ± 0.02** | 2.0 % |

**Headlines:**
1. **The input-output design works.** All **20/20 drops triggered cleanly** (vs 3/4 failures in the acrylic series and 0/8 in the clip sweep), and with the bungees gone the **input is nearly constant across every specimen and drop** (235–248 G, ≤1.7 % CV) — a controlled, reproducible strike at last.
2. **Transmissibility discriminates geometry.** Where the prior vertex-only peaks were indistinguishable (229–284 G), `T` separates the specimens: **`yqpmx1` is the only attenuator (T ≈ 0.96)**, `h8Lbev` ≈ 1.09, `practice`/`n0jdwk` ≈ 1.17–1.19. Because the input is held fixed, that spread is a real structural-response difference → `T` (or output-peak-at-fixed-input) is a usable BO objective.
3. **A mild drift across the 5 cyclic drops** (output creeps up at constant input; n0jdwk T 1.11→1.24).

![transmissibility](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/555d199/data/drop-tests/input-output/figures/02_transmissibility_bars.png?raw=true)

**Edison's feedback** (task `fe044079`) reproduced our T values *exactly to two decimals* and added:
- The drift is **statistically real and most likely mount-driven** — T-vs-drop regression is positive for all four specimens (pooled +0.015/drop, p = 0.0001); output rising at constant input fits hot-glue seating/creep over 5 cycles better than material softening. **Don't start 20-drop / to-failure campaigns on hot glue and call the trend fatigue** — switch to a rigid z-aligned keyed seat (ISO 5347) first.
- `T` is a sound **first-pass screening** objective but it's a peak ratio, not a transfer function; T > 1 for 3/4 specimens (stiff vertex-to-vertex path → amplifies) rules out "cushioning" claims. Once we exploit the simultaneous input+output pair, an **FRF / SRS-band reduction** is more physical; **output peak at fixed input** is the easy near-equivalent for BO now. Feed within-specimen SD as heteroscedastic BO noise.
- **n ≥ 5 distinct prints per geometry** (not just 5 drops of one), randomized order, extend capture past 200 ms for ringdown, anchor SOP in SAE J211 / ISO 5347 / ASTM D3332.

@copilot+claude-opus-4.8 does the recent igloo design in #35 meet the intent of the key seat described in https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/67#issuecomment-4805044500 ?

On the igloo vs. the "keyed seat": mostly yes — it's the right move and hits the core of the intent, with two gaps to close before trusting cyclic/to-failure data.

**What the "key seat" was asking for.** The recommendation in [#67 (comment)](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/67#issuecomment-4805044500) was Edison's, prompted by the mild T-drift across the 5 cyclic drops: *"Don't start 20-drop / to-failure campaigns on hot glue and call the trend fatigue — switch to a rigid z-aligned keyed seat (ISO 5347) first."* The drift was almost certainly hot-glue seating/creep, so the ask is a **rigid, repeatable, z-aligned mechanical mount** that registers the sensor identically every drop, so mount creep can't masquerade as material fatigue.

**Where the igloo (`accel_mount()` in `cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad`, branch `copilot/get-bambu-sliced-print-t3-prism`) meets it:**
- **Rigid & reproducible** — a printed PLA pocket fused into the joint shell (sinks 2 mm in) replaces the hand-applied hot-glue blob on a rounded vertex. It's identical on every print and removes the operator-to-operator variation, which is the "keying" Edison wanted.
- **Keyed** — the rectangular pocket (3 walls + floor) registers the cubic 6×6×5.94 mm Dytran 3133A4 in XY position and yaw, and the floor sets a fixed z datum.
- **Z-aligned** — placement only rotates about global Z (`rotate([0,0,ang])`), so the pocket floor stays horizontal and the sensor's sensitive axis sits parallel to the vertical drop axis repeatably, instead of being glued onto a round vertex at a hand-set angle.

**Where it falls short of the full ISO-5347 intent:**
1. **It's still adhesive-in-a-clearance-pocket, not a gap-free seat.** `accel_clear = 0.4 mm`/side leaves a compliant adhesive + PLA layer, so some seating/creep can remain (less than hot glue, not zero). For a to-failure run I'd either tighten toward a press/clip/set-screw fit or, at minimum, re-run the T-vs-drop regression on the first few drops to confirm the drift is actually gone rather than assume it.
2. **Only the top (output) vertices get the seat.** The base-plate **input** single-axis sensor — the now-triggered channel — is still loosely/hot-glue mounted; it needs an equivalent keyed seat for a clean, drift-free input too.

Minor: the PLA block adds mass at the very node whose response we measure, so keep it constant across all specimens (it's a fine control variable, just don't vary it). And it keys the sensor flat-to-plate — for vertex-down impacts confirm that's the axis you want as the QoI.

Net: directionally correct and it satisfies the rigid/keyed/z-aligned/reproducible core. Close gaps (1) and (2) before reading cyclic data as fatigue.

Pressed onto a flat, rigid plate it gives a stiff, well-aligned, repeatable seat — far better than glue on a round vertex — and the data back that up: the **input was the most reproducible channel in the whole series (235–248 G, ≤1.7 % CV across all 20 drops)**. Two caveats specific to wax, mostly for the future to-failure / higher-G runs rather than now:
- Wax has a usable amplitude/frequency ceiling (it can shear/decouple at high g and softens when warm). At ~240 G input it's fine; if input g climbs or the lab warms up, watch for a quiet downward creep in the input peak, and switch to a stud/cement or the printed pocket.
- It's flat-plate-only — it doesn't solve the **output**-vertex mount, which is what the igloo seat in #35 addresses.

Net: the input mount is in good shape as-is; the remaining keyed-seat work is the output vertex (the #35 igloo), exactly where the cyclic T-drift showed up.

### The actual bug: the committed support STL was stale
Re-casting the underside rays against the real PR #35 mesh produces **188** contact points (z ≈ 1.6–126.1 mm), but the committed `t3-prism-pr35-pillars.stl` only had **181**, reaching just z ≈ 112 mm — the **7 top-cap/joint undersides were missing**, so the highest members printed unsupported. Regenerated it: **188 tips / 31 feet / 23,520 tris** (combined mesh 50,336 tris). That's exactly the "supports weren't touching the vertical members" symptom you circled earlier, now closed by automated checks rather than eyeballing.

### New geometric verification — `verify_support_geometry.py` (gates CI, all PASS)
Uses trimesh's exact ray/proximity engine, exits non-zero on any failure:
- **CONTACT** — every tip lands on the part underside, max gap **0.0000 mm** (they go all the way to contact).
- **REALISED** — every intended tip is present in the committed STL (this is the check that caught the stale artefact).
- **ON-PLATE** — no geometry below z=0; **662** foot vertices on the build plate ("touching the floor").
- **COVERAGE** — re-samples undersides at 2× density: **99.3 %** of flat overhangs within 5 mm of a support, worst **6.3 mm** (within PLA's bridge), 0 beyond 8 mm.

### Layer-by-layer FEA — `fea_support_stability.py` (CalculiX `ccx`)
Reconstructs the emitted branch network, extracts the worst-case column (longest continuous run = **108.5 mm**, 1.2° from vertical, Ø1.8–3.1 mm) and grows it from the plate:
- **Self-weight buckling** — min safety factor **61×** at full height (and thousands× when shorter). It can't collapse under its own weight as it prints. ✅
- **Tip-over** — COM sits **27.8 mm** inside the convex hull of the 1148 plate contacts (79 mm base span). Can't topple. ✅
- **Lateral compliance** — reported as a worst-case bound: a *fully free-standing* 108 mm Ø1.8 mm column is floppy, but it never stands free in practice (neighbouring struts + the rest of the tree print in lockstep, in-print forces are ~hundredths of a N, 5 mm brim anchors the feet). Surfaced so it's on record; bump `--trunk_d` (stiffness ∝ d⁴) or `--merge_radius` if a future geometry yields a taller lone column.

@copilot by hybrid, do you mean implement two separate campaigns or do you mean incorporate both into the same campaign?

> @copilot by hybrid, do you mean implement two separate campaigns or do you mean incorporate both into the same campaign?

Same campaign — not two separate ones. The "hybrid" combines **Route A and Route B inside one `AxClient` campaign per regime**, not a second campaign. Route A and Route B are just two mechanisms for removing the size confound, and a single campaign can apply both at once:

- **Route A (structural)** fixes the *binding* budget — for the lander that's **mass**: re-parameterize onto a constant-mass manifold (search scale-free shape ratios `H/R`, `H/strut_d`, `cable_d/strut_d`, `twist` + drop one axis to hold `m*`), so the GP never sees a heavier-than-budget design and SEA's denominator is constant.
- **Route B (scoring)** handles the *remaining* budgets in that same campaign — envelope volume and footprint as Ax **outcome constraints** under constrained qNEHVI, plus intensive objectives (`SEA_J_per_g`, `SEA_J_per_cm³`, base-reaction peak g instead of the payload-accel proxy).

So the structure stays one-campaign-per-regime, exactly like `sim_bo_campaign.py` / `pareto_render_campaign.py` run today; the hybrid only changes *that* campaign's coordinates, objectives, and constraints. Crutch and lander stay separate campaigns from each other because they're different regimes (and the crutch can get by with Route B alone), not because of the hybrid. Clarified this in `simulations/fair_evaluation_analysis.md` (commit be9 — see the new paragraph under "Recommended hybrid").

### Key-seat mount validation — analysis of `prc1kn` (5 drops)

Analyzed Jinkwan's new run from [#67 (comment)](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/67#issuecomment-4837240958). Data, a reproducible script, figures, and a writeup are committed (`3deccb1`):

- 📊 **Analysis:** [`docs/drop-test-key-mounted-analysis.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/3deccb1/docs/drop-test-key-mounted-analysis.md)
- 📁 Data + README: [`data/drop-tests/key-mounted/`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/tree/3deccb1/data/drop-tests/key-mounted) · script: [`drop_test_key_mounted_analysis.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/3deccb1/scripts/analysis/drop_test_key_mounted_analysis.py)

**Setup recap.** Same input-output pair as before — single-axis **input** wax-mounted on the base plate (CH5, the triggered channel); tri-axis **output** on the top vertex (CH2/CH3/CH4); bungees removed. The **one** change under test is the **output mount**: the printed **key-seat** ("igloo" from #35) instead of a hot-glue blob. `prc1kn` is a deliberately-failed print (TPU bubbles) used to exercise the *mount/DAQ*, not to compare geometry. (File-name note: `Signal4` was discarded, so drops 1–5 = `Signal{1,2,3,5,6}`.)

**Per-drop (CFC-180):**

| drop | input CH5 (G) | output tri-axis (G) | **T = OUT/IN** |
|---:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 223 | 232 | **1.04** |
| 2 | 223 | 232 | **1.04** |
| 3 | 220 | 239 | **1.08** |
| 4 | 212 | 233 | **1.10** |
| 5 | 218 | 233 | **1.07** |
| **mean ± 1σ** | **219 ± 4** (CV 2.0 %) | **234 ± 3** (CV 1.3 %) | **1.07 ± 0.03** (CV 2.4 %) |

**Headlines:**

1. **The key-seat fixes the output-mount drift — this is the result you were after.** In the prior hot-glue series the *output* crept up at constant input and the T-vs-drop slope was significant (+0.015/drop, p = 1e-4). With the key-seat the **output is flat: slope +0.39 G/drop, p = 0.74, CV 1.3 %** — no significant trend. That confirms the earlier drift was **mount creep** (exactly as Edison concluded), and the printed seat removes it. So cyclic / to-failure campaigns can now go ahead without mistaking mount creep for fatigue.
2. **Whatever residual trend remains has moved to the input (wax) side, and it's not significant.** T drifts +0.012/drop (p = 0.17, n.s.), and the contribution is the *input* sliding **down** (−2.04 G/drop, p = 0.15), not the output rising. Worth watching, but far below the hot-glue effect — this is the input-side gap you and I flagged earlier, and Sterling's "3rd accelerometer in a bottom-vertex key-seat" idea is the natural fix if it grows.
3. **The system is reproducible and triggered 5/5** — input 219 ± 4 G, output 234 ± 3 G, Δv ≈ 2.6 m/s, all consistent with the bungees-removed controlled strike.

**On the sensor falling off:** the key-seat *seat* is doing its job (rigid, z-aligned, drift-free), but the **press-fit alone didn't retain the sensor**. Adding wax inside the housing (your suggestion) is the right call — it keeps the rigid keyed seat while preventing fall-off, and a thin wax film sits in the ISO-5347 couplant hierarchy without reintroducing hot-glue-scale creep. Recommend re-running this same OLS drift check on the first few drops after the wax fix to confirm the seat stays drift-free with the retainer in.

> `prc1kn`'s `T ≈ 1.07` is **not** a geometry result (single failed print) — it just shows `T` is well-defined and tight (CV 2.4 %) under the new mount. Geometry discrimination still needs n ≥ 5 distinct intact prints per geometry, randomized order, capture > 200 ms.

| drop | impact frame | descent (s, playback) | descent slope (px/fr) | rebound fraction |
|---:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 251 | 3.10 | 2.312 | 0.50 |
| 2 | 277 | 3.07 | 2.302 | 0.50 |
| 4 | 340 | 3.07 | 2.300 | 0.51 |
| 5 | 271 | 3.10 | 2.299 | 0.51 |
| **mean ± 1σ** | — | **3.09 ± 0.02** | **2.303 ± 0.006 (CV 0.26 %)** | **0.505 ± 0.006 (CV 1.1 %)** |

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/899cfc2/data/drop-tests/key-mounted/video-figures/01_centroid_descent_overlay.png?raw=true)

**Headlines:**

1. **Independent corroboration of the rig repeatability.** Aligned at impact, the four descents fall almost exactly on top of each other — descent slope matches to **CV ≈ 0.3 %** and rebound to **≈ 1 %**, same ballpark as the accelerometer's input 219 ± 4 G (2.0 %) / output 234 ± 3 G (1.3 %). An optical channel and a contact accelerometer agreeing the strike is this reproducible is a solid "the rig is controlled now" signal.
2. **The descent really is free-fall → confirms bungees removed.** Every drop shows a consistent *downward* curvature (≈ 0.022 px/fr²) — the structure accelerating under gravity, the opposite of the bungee-assisted lift-off from the first drops.
3. **Big, repeatable elastic rebound (~50 % of the drop depth).** The centroid springs back to ~half the fall height, then settles — the tensegrity acting as a spring, and **identical across all four drops**, so the spring-back you said we don't care about isn't adding scatter and sits cleanly *after* the impact event.
4. **Fall-off clip pins the failure on the output seat, not the input.** The silver **input** sensor (wax on the plate) stays perfectly stationary frame-to-frame, while the **tri-axis output** sensor detaches from the vertex key-seat — exactly the press-fit-not-enough failure @ctrhjk saw. **Caveats:** uncalibrated slow-mo factor + pixel scale (frames/px only); `prc1kn` is one failed print (mount/rig validation, not geometry); the orange-centroid proxy mixes translation with cage tilt — a fixed fiducial or ≥5000 fps DIC (per the Edison synthesis) would give calibrated displacement + strut strain. ### Key-seat + wax-retainer retest — analysis of `prc1kn` (5 drops)

Analyzed Jinkwan's wax-retainer follow-up from [#67 (comment 4838901017)](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/67#issuecomment-4838901017). Data, a reproducible script, figures, and a writeup are committed (`9fe3082`):

- 📊 **Analysis:** [`docs/drop-test-key-mounted-wax-analysis.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/9fe3082/docs/drop-test-key-mounted-wax-analysis.md)
- 📁 Data + README: [`data/drop-tests/key-mounted-wax/`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/tree/9fe3082/data/drop-tests/key-mounted-wax) · script: [`drop_test_key_mounted_wax_analysis.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/9fe3082/scripts/analysis/drop_test_key_mounted_wax_analysis.py)

**The one change under test:** wax added **inside** the key-seat housing to retain the tri-axis output sensor (which fell off on press-fit alone last run). Same input-output pair otherwise — single-axis **input** wax-mounted on the base plate (CH5, triggered); tri-axis **output** in the vertex key-seat (CH2/CH3/CH4); bungees removed. Captures are contiguous this run: `Signal{7..11}` = drops 1–5.

**Per-drop (CFC-180):**

| drop | input CH5 (G) | output tri-axis (G) | **T = OUT/IN** |
|---:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 230 | 226 | **0.98** |
| 2 | 229 | 228 | **0.99** |
| 3 | 228 | 228 | **1.00** |
| 4 | 227 | 229 | **1.01** |
| 5 | 228 | 230 | **1.01** |
| **mean ± 1σ** | **228.5 ± 1.2** (CV 0.5 %) | **228.2 ± 1.5** (CV 0.6 %) | **0.999 ± 0.011** (CV 1.1 %) |

**Wax vs no-wax (same specimen, same key-seat):**

| metric | bare press-fit (prior) | **+ wax retainer** |
|---|--:|--:|
| input CV | 2.0 % | **0.5 %** |
| output CV | 1.3 % | **0.6 %** |
| T CV | 2.4 % | **1.1 %** |
| output slope (p) | +0.39 G/drop (0.74, n.s.) | **+0.90 G/drop (0.005, sig.)** |
| T slope (p) | +0.012/drop (0.17, n.s.) | **+0.0064/drop (0.011, sig.)** |
| sensor retained? | **no** (fell off) | **yes** |

**Headlines:**

1. **The wax retainer works — and gives the cleanest run in the series.** 5/5 captured, sensor stayed put, and the CVs roughly **halved** (input 2.0→0.5 %, output 1.3→0.6 %, T 2.4→1.1 %). Input and output are both flat and tight, T ≈ 1.00 ± 0.01. This is the low noise floor a BO objective wants.
2. **A small output creep is now "statistically significant" — but that's a side-effect of how tight the data got, not a big effect.** Output rises +0.90 G/drop (p = 0.005), T +0.0064/drop (p = 0.011), yet the *magnitude* is tiny: output 226→230 G over 5 drops (~1.8 %), T 0.98→1.01 (~3 %). Because residual scatter collapsed to CV ≈ 0.6 %, even a whisper of a trend clears p < 0.05 — whereas the noisier bare run's larger wobble didn't. The slope direction (output up at near-constant input) is the classic **mount-seating** signature — here ~half the T-slope of the original hot-glue creep — so it reads as **wax progressively seating over the first few impacts**, not material softening.
3. **The input (wax-on-plate) side is now rock-stable** — the −2.04 G/drop drift I flagged in the bare run shrank to −0.58 G/drop (p = 0.13, n.s.), best input CV in the whole series (0.5 %).

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/9fe3082/data/drop-tests/key-mounted-wax/figures/04_wax_vs_nowax.png?raw=true)

**Recommendations:**
- **Adopt the wax-retained key-seat** as the standard output mount — it fixes retention and is the most repeatable setup yet.
- **Burn in the wax before a long campaign:** take a few unrecorded settling drops (or discard the first 1–2) so the ~0.9 G/drop wax-seating creep isn't mistaken for early fatigue in 20-drop / to-failure runs; re-run this OLS drift check on the first few recorded drops to confirm.
- **Report effect sizes, not just p-values**, for drift now that CV ≈ 0.5–0.6 % makes the test sensitive to sub-percent trends (quote slope as %/drop of the mean).
- Sterling's **3rd accelerometer in a bottom-vertex key-seat** (or a stud/cement input mount) is the clean fix if even this residual matters later.

<sub>Caveats: n = 1 specimen (failed print `prc1kn`), 5 cyclic drops — validates the *mount/DAQ*, not geometry (T ≈ 1.00 is not a geometry result). 200 ms window only; Δv is a partial-pulse integral; tri-axis output-axis orientation unverified; the wax-seating reading of the residual creep is inferred from slope direction, not yet confirmed against a longer burn-in.</sub>

Bottom surface area is the load-path‑sensitive one.** For a drop from height `h`, impact velocity `v=√(2gh)`; for a roughly linear contact `g_peak ≈ (v/g)·√(k_eff/m)`. A **larger, flatter bottom pad raises contact stiffness `k_eff` → higher g_peak and a shorter, sharper pulse** — the opposite of what we want, and it partly short-circuits the tensegrity network we're trying to characterize (the rigid pad, not the struts/cables, takes first load). A big flat bottom also **grips the acrylic (high friction) → tip-over / non-repeatable orientation**, whereas the top **dome** was specifically chosen to *slide* (low friction). So my caution: **a large flat under-vertex pad (current A) is the riskiest choice for both g_peak bias and repeatability.** **2. Added mass hits SEA twice** (adds to the denominator *and* absorbs ~no energy). If the fixture is **identical on every specimen** it's a constant offset that mostly cancels in *relative* BO comparisons — but it distorts *absolute* SEA and, critically, **interacts with the swept vars**: a fixed seat is a larger fraction of a small‑`R`/small‑`strut_d` design than a large one, which **can confound the GP**. Neither is "wrong" — pick to match the objective. Since the igloo already instruments the **top**, that's a clean "payload" reference; adding a **bottom** sensor gives you contact-side g_peak too. ### Abstract

**Title:** Bayesian-Optimized Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity Crutch Tips for Impact and Vibration Attenuation

**Authors:** Marcus Madsen\*, Audrey Christiansen\*, Jinkwan Han\*, Jeffrey R. Hill† (presenting), Sterling G. Baird† — Department of Mechanical Engineering, Brigham Young University *(\*, † = equal contribution, carried over from #73)*

> Long-term crutch users bear repeated ground-reaction forces of roughly 0.5 body weights per crutch and experience high rates of upper-extremity overuse injury, including crutch palsy, shoulder impingement, and carpal tunnel syndrome, yet commercial crutch tips still rely on simple rubber ferrules or bulky springs. We present a shock-absorbing crutch-tip insert built from multi-material fused-filament-fabrication tensegrity-inspired lattices that pair rigid PETG struts with elastomeric TPU tension elements, exploiting load-limiting buckling and rate-dependent damping. Because the standard 19 to 25 mm ferrule envelope severely limits stroke, we co-optimize unit-cell topology, strut diameter, relative density, and prestress using closed-loop multi-objective Bayesian optimization, maximizing specific energy absorption while minimizing peak transmitted force across quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact tests. A prior-art survey confirms that no existing crutch tip applies tensegrity architectures, and an FDA Class I, ISO 11334-1 regulatory pathway is clear. This demonstrator advances miniaturized, patient-tunable energy absorbers for assistive and protective devices.

Here is a critical peer review of the 150-word abstract, drawn entirely from the evidence already captured in `edison-trajectories/01`–`05`. Overall verdict: **strong, submittable concept, but two claims should be corrected before submission and one number tightened.** The most acceptance-relevant issues are the title's *vibration* promise and the *"regulatory pathway is clear"* wording — both are stronger than trajectories 01/03 support.

---

### 1. Claim-by-claim fact-check

| Claim in abstract | Verdict | Evidence (trajectory) |
|---|---|---|
| ~0.5 BW GRF per crutch | ✅ **Supported** — but qualify | Forearm-crutch swing-through peaks at **51.7–52.4 %BW per crutch** (MacGillivray 2016, `01`). Caveat: able-bodied users, short lab trials, self-selected speed — worth "up to ~0.5 BW." |
| High rates of overuse injury (crutch palsy, impingement, CTS) | ⚠️ **Supported but overstated** | Manocha 2021 (60 studies / 622 people) documents the spectrum, and CTS prevalence in cane/crutch users runs 22–50% (`03`). **But** Manocha's evidence is "mostly case reports and small series, not epidemiological cohort data," and likely *underestimates* prevalence — so "high rates" is defensible only if softened (see §2). |
| Commercial tips "still rely on simple rubber ferrules or bulky springs" | ⚠️ **Partly inaccurate** | Prior art is richer than this: **US 11,712,394 B1 (Spatorico 2023) — a spring+viscoelastic shock-absorbing ferrule**, US 20120260958 (elastomeric-core ferrule), the SideStix polymer damper (MacGillivray 2016), and articulated elastomeric commercial tips (`01`, `03`). The claim reads as if the field is static when a 2023 shock-absorbing-ferrule patent exists. |
| Buckling tensegrity → load-limiting plateau + rate-dependent damping | ✅ **Supported** | Pajunen 2019 (load-limiting plateau, <0.2% residual strain/impact); Santos 2023 (10–23% equiv. viscous damping) (`01`). |
| 19–25 mm ferrule envelope "severely limits stroke" | ✅ **Supported** | Standard ferrule IDs ≈19/22/25 mm; published tensegrity cells are ~48 mm tall → substantial miniaturization needed; small stroke caps absorbable energy (`01`). |
| No existing crutch tip applies tensegrity (novelty) | ✅ **Strongly supported** | Two independent searches (`01`, `03`) found **no patent or publication** applying tensegrity/lattice/metamaterial architectures to a crutch tip. This is the abstract's strongest claim — keep it. |
| FDA Class I + ISO 11334-1, pathway "clear" | ⚠️ **Overstated** | Class I / ISO 11334-1 is the *likely* pathway, but `01` explicitly says the "exact U.S. product code/regulatory pathway … still needs formal verification." "Clear" is stronger than the evidence. |

### 2. Overstatements to soften

- **"vibration attenuation" (title) → the single biggest issue.** The title promises vibration attenuation, but trajectory `03` is unambiguous: **no study has ever measured vibration spectra transmitted through a crutch tip**, and there are *no* transmissibility curves even for anti-shock trekking-pole springs. The body itself only tests *impact* (quasi-static + drop-weight). Promising vibration attenuation you don't measure invites a reviewer to ask for HAVS/accelerometer data you don't have. **Fix:** either drop "vibration" from the title (→ "…for Impact Attenuation") or reframe it as future work.
- **"confirms"** → "a prior-art survey **identified no** existing tensegrity crutch tip" (absence of evidence, not proof).
- **"is clear"** → "a **likely** FDA Class I, ISO 11334-1 pathway."
- **"high rates"** → "**elevated rates**" or "a documented burden of," matching the case-report-level evidence.
- **"severely"** is fine — `01` uses "severely constraining" verbatim.

### 3. Top missing context, ranked by effect on acceptance

1. **Simulated vs. experimental + actual numbers.** The abstract never says whether results exist yet. A materials/biomedical reviewer will look first for a headline result — **specific energy absorption (J/g) and % peak-force reduction vs. a rubber-ferrule control.** Right now there are zero quantitative outcomes. Add one even-preliminary number, or state clearly it's a design/demonstrator study.
2. **PETG–TPU interface durability under cycling.** `01`/`04` flag interfacial delamination as *the* weak link, and **no cyclic/fatigue data for the PETG–TPU (or PLA–TPU) interface exist.** For a device seeing 10⁵–10⁶ gait cycles this is the dominant technical risk — one clause acknowledging it strengthens credibility.
3. **Fatigue life over gait cycles.** Not mentioned; crutch use is inherently repetitive and `01` sets a 10⁵–10⁶-cycle bar.
4. **Slip resistance / ground contact.** `01` and `03` both conclude a printed lattice alone won't meet traction needs (rubber outsole likely required); `03` found *no* crutch-tip-specific COF data. A safety reviewer will ask.
5. **Baseline/control + sample size.** "across quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact tests" implies data — say against what baseline and how many samples.

### 4. The "PETG" vs. "PLA" evidence gap

The abstract commits to **PETG + TPU**, but almost all quantitative material evidence in `01` (fatigue, interface toughness σ≈1.0 MPa / mode-I ≈48 J/m²) is for **PLA + TPU**; PETG-specific data live in `04`. That's fine, but be ready for "why PETG?" — the honest answer (PLA is brittle/creep-prone; PETG's toughness suits cyclic loading) isn't yet in the abstract's evidence trail. Not a blocker, just a Q&A landmine.

### 5. "Laboratory to Market" framing (target TMS symposium)

The chosen symposium rewards a translational arc, and the abstract's regulatory sentence gestures at it — but the actual **market/commercialization** evidence from `05` (DME OEM landscape) and `03` (device-abandonment 31.4% for crutches; CTS burden $2.7–4.8B/yr in Medicare; ~250k rotator-cuff repairs/yr) is absent. **One sentence** citing the abandonment rate or the economic burden would materially strengthen the lab-to-market pitch for this venue.

### 6. Concrete edits (fit within 150 words)

1. **Title:** "…Tensegrity Crutch Tips for **Impact Attenuation**" (remove "and Vibration"), or add "…with a Path Toward Vibration Control."
2. **Sentence 1:** "…experience **elevated rates** of upper-extremity overuse injury…" (was "high rates").
3. **Sentence 1 (prior art):** "…yet commercial crutch tips remain **largely limited to** rubber ferrules and spring dampers" — softer than "still rely on … bulky springs," and it survives the Spatorico-2023 counterexample.
4. **Add a result or scope clause:** e.g., "…**achieving X % lower peak transmitted force than a standard rubber ferrule in drop-weight tests**…" — or, if no data yet, "**In this design study, we…**" so no one assumes unshown experiments.
5. **Novelty + regulatory:** "A prior-art survey **found no** crutch tip using tensegrity architectures, and a **likely** FDA Class I, ISO 11334-1 pathway **applies**." (was "confirms … is clear").
6. **Optional lab-to-market clause** (if room): "…addressing a device with **~31 % user-abandonment** and a multi-billion-dollar downstream upper-limb injury burden." (`03`, `05`)

### Bottom line
Concept, novelty claim, and biomechanical motivation are well-supported by `01`–`05`. Before submitting: (a) **remove/qualify "vibration"** in the title, (b) **downgrade "confirms"/"is clear"** to evidence-matched wording, (c) **add one quantitative result or an explicit design-study scope**, and (d) **name the PETG–TPU interface fatigue risk**. Those four changes close the gap between the abstract's confidence and what the trajectories actually establish.

### What Edison found (and where it goes *beyond* the earlier internal review)

Its overall verdict matches the internal read — **strong, submittable concept, but several claims need hedging before submission** — and it independently surfaced **three sharper, newly-cited critiques**:

2. **"Rate-dependent damping" is mis-attributed.** The tensegrity literature (Pajunen 2019) credits dissipation to *material hysteresis*, and notes damping is *minimal* in stiff polymers — so the rate-dependence comes from the **TPU viscoelasticity**, not the tensegrity architecture. → "buckling-induced load-limiting plateau **and TPU viscoelastic hysteresis**."
3. **The 19–25 mm number conflates shaft bore with the ferrule envelope.** That range is the crutch *shaft OD*; documented ferrule *outer* diameters are 32–47 mm, and no source substantiates "severely limits stroke." → "constrains" stroke.

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| ~0.5 BW GRF per crutch | ⚠️ Partially supported (gait-dependent) |

### 2. But it's **not camera-native** — that's the real catch.

The file's encoder tag is **`https://clipchamp.com`** (Microsoft's editor) and it carries a **48 kHz stereo AAC audio track**. A Sony RX100 IV 960 fps HFR clip is **silent** and tags Sony's encoder. So this clip was exported through **Clipchamp**, which re-containerized it to **30 fps** — whereas @ctrhjk's stated camera setting was **24p / 960 fps**.

### 3. What that does to my `frame ÷ 960` in [comment 4849969620](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/67#issuecomment-4849969620) — it was ~25 % off.

The physical slow-motion factor is set by the **camera-native record rate**, not the export container:

- **Native 24p / 960 fps** → slow factor = 960 / 24 = **40×**. For that native 24 fps file, `real_time = frame ÷ (24 × 40) = frame ÷ 960` — so `÷ 960` would have been *exactly right on the camera file*.
- **This file is a 30 fps Clipchamp re-encode** of that 40×-slow timeline (duration-preserving: 26.93 s → 646 native frames resampled up to 808). For a 30 fps container the correct mapping is `real_time = frame ÷ (30 × 40) = frame ÷ 1200`.

So `÷ 960` **overstated the absolute in-frame descent by 1200/960 = 25 %** → the reported **94.6 ms becomes ≈ 75.7 ms**. I can't nail this from the video alone (the structure enters the top of frame already falling, so there's no clean in-frame free-fall to fit, and there's no scale bar — my scale-free free-fall fit returned garbage/negative curvature, confirming the entry contamination). Treat any absolute video time as **± 25 %** and use the **accelerometer** (Δv ≈ 2.6 m/s, free-fall) as the calibrated clock.

**Crucially, nothing scientific changes.** Every conclusion in the video passes is *relative or dimensionless* — descent-slope CV (0.32 %), rebound fraction (0.47), drift in %/drop, transmissibility — none of which ever used the absolute time base. Only the single absolute "descent ms" figure shifts.
