### Trigger level — yes, I think 300 G is better than 500 G

The trigger level lives between two hard bounds measured across the program:

| bound | worst value observed | where |
|---|--:|---|
| **floor** — pre-impact activity it must stay above | 35 G ([5-in 100-drop run](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol/docs/drop-test-5in-100drops-analysis.md)); 18.6 G in the new 5-in block; ≤ 9 G at 10 in | every campaign |
| **ceiling** — worst-case session-minimum raw peak it must stay below | **< 1,000 G at 5 in** (the `7xadt6` practice drops that missed both 1000 G triggers); 1,936 G in the new 5-in block; 5,336 G at 10 in | [200-drop §7](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol/docs/drop-test-200drops-analysis.md) / [5vs10](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol/docs/drop-test-5vs10-analysis.md) |

At **10 in, 500 G is already excellent** (worst margin 10.7×, pre-impact clearance 62×) — there's no meaningfully better number for a 10-in-only campaign, and I wouldn't chase one.

The reason I'd still move to **300 G as the standing level** is the one documented failure: the `7xadt6` practice session proved a fresh, compliant print at 5 in can stay **below 1,000 G raw** — and since no waveform was captured, we don't know *how far* below. At 500 G, this session's 5-in worst margin was 3.87×, but the program has already seen the raw spike shrink by more than that between sessions (tape-coupling state alone durably moved 6–8 % at CFC-180, and much more at the raw kHz content the trigger listens to). 300 G:

- keeps ≥ 8.6× clearance above the worst pre-impact activity ever recorded (35 G) — false triggers remain a non-issue (all 390 auto-drops across 5vs10 + the 200-drop era show zero spurious triggers even at levels this would undercut);
- restores ~6.5× worst-case margin at 5 in and would very likely have caught the failed practice session;
- costs nothing at 10 in (margin becomes ~18×).

I would **not go below ~200 G**: the floor is set by the worst *observed* pre-impact activity (35 G), and arming/handling transients between drops aren't characterized — 100 G is probably safe (the 200-drop doc says as much) but buys nothing over 300 G except risk. And since trigger time is pinned by the pre-trigger buffer (first crossing 3.895–3.896 ms with µs-level jitter at every level tested), the level doesn't affect the metrics at all — only capture reliability. One cheap SOP addition beats any fixed number: **one practice capture at the start of each session**, check the raw CH5 peak, and confirm ≥ 3× margin before starting the batch.

### Drop height — no better number in the measured evidence; 10 in stands

What "better" could mean, checked against data at the three measured heights (5, 10, 13 in):

1. **Repeatability** — no height wins materially. TOP output peak is tightest at 10 in (CV 0.31 %), T is tightest at 5 in (CV 0.39 %); everything is sub-1 % at both, far below the geometry differences seen at 13 in (T spanning 0.96–1.19).
2. **Saturation** — height can't fix the one problem (BOT): even at 5 in, CH8 sits at 94 % FS median and the channel is amplitude-pinned (~920 G regardless of severity), so that's a sensor-range fix, not a height fix. Meanwhile the *upper* bound matters more than people expect: at 13 in, CH5 raw already hit 8.1 kG = **86 % of its 9.4 kG full scale**. A stiff BO candidate at 13 in could clip the trigger/denominator channel. 10 in leaves CH5 at ~62 % FS worst case — real headroom for stiffer geometries.
3. **Interrogation energy / discrimination** — the only campaign that *demonstrated* geometry discrimination ran at 13 in severity; 10 in is the closest validated point that keeps CH5 headroom. 5 in gives 31 % lower levels and, per the 200-drop §7 reading, soft prints may not even bottom out there — bad for discrimination.
4. **Continuity** — all durability/wear evidence (>260 drops, no functional failure) is at 10 in.

So within what's been measured, **10 in + a 300–500 G trigger is the optimum**, and I don't think an untested intermediate height (7–8 in) offers anything: it would inherit 5-in's weaker interrogation without solving BOT, and would need its own wear baseline.

The honest caveat: the *actual* "best height" criterion for BO is **which height best separates geometries**, and that's only ever been measured at one severity (13 in, hot-glue era). T being nearly height-invariant on one specimen (1.138 vs 1.125) is encouraging but not the same thing. If you want to close that question before locking the BO campaign, the decisive experiment is small: **2 distinct geometries × 2 heights (5 in and 10 in) × ~10 drops each** (~40 drops, one session) — if the between-geometry T gap is as large at 10 in as at 5 in, 10 in is confirmed; if the gap grows with severity, that's also worth knowing because it suggests severity sweeps as a future richer objective (the clean √h scaling of the CFC-180 levels makes those well-behaved).

### Bottom line

- **Trigger: lower the standing level to 300 G** (keep 500 G if you only ever run 10 in — it's fine there), and add a one-drop margin check at session start.
- **Height: stay at 10 in** — no measured evidence supports a different number, and the CH5-headroom argument actively caps you near it. The only way a "better" height emerges is from the 2-geometry × 2-height discrimination check above, which I'd run before the first real BO batch.

1. **The box is written in 1.5×-era absolute mm.** If the program has standardized on S0-size prints (done for auto-support + housing reasons), the box's own center of mass is off — and note you **cannot** just multiply the bounds by 0.7692: the cable_d floor would drop to 2.3 mm, **below the empirically-established 3.0 mm Bambu printability floor** that's baked into the current bounds. Any re-scoping has to keep `cable_d ≥ 3.0` absolute. Deciding the box *now* matters for exactly the reason you give — shrinking or shifting bounds after the GP has data is a soft restart.
2. **The sensor housings don't scale** (deliberately — they're absolute-mm physical pockets, `t3-prism.scad` L244). A fixed instrumented-head mass is a much bigger fraction of a 16 g corner design than an 88 g one, so mass-loading bias in T varies ~5× across the box, systematically correlated with specimen mass — a confound the GP can't separate. Cheapest mitigation: **weigh every print** and log it per ID (this is the still-unanswered `batch01.csv` metadata ask from May 22, which would also calibrate the mass model above), and consider a mass floor if the light corner isn't interesting.
3. **Rig fit:** the heaviest corner is ~80 mm footprint × ~145 mm tall with housings, vs the S0 print's ~58 × 115 mm. The release clip / cap-upward-travel fixtures and the 3×3 plate-packing cell (86.9 mm) were tuned in the S0/1.5× era — worth a dry-fit check before BO proposes a big design.

### 1. What tripped the overload

A TP4 overload means a channel's input exceeded its calibrated range, and exactly one channel did that — **CH6**, one axis of the low-range bottom-vertex tri-axis (FS 1,002 G):

| channel | full scale | median | max | > FS | first > FS | sustained from |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **CH6** | **1,002 G** | **99.8 % FS** | **108.4 %** | **128/256** | **Signal 118** | **Signal 134** |
| CH8 | 989 G | 94.6 % | 98.2 % | 0/256 | — | — |
| CH7 | 991 G | 56.3 % | 87.0 % | 0/256 | — | — |
| CH5 (trigger) | 9,443 G | 68.4 % | 83.6 % | 0/256 | — | — |
| CH2/CH3/CH4 | 13.6–15 kG | 4.6–26.9 % | ≤ 30 % | 0/256 | — | — |

So by the time you saw the overload at drop 256, CH6 had been over its range on essentially **every drop for the previous ~120 drops**. And its path there was not a slow drift but a **transition event**: flat at ~475 G (≈47 % FS) for the first ~96 drops → rapid climb over drops ~97–130 → a censored shelf at ~105 % FS for the rest of the run. Suggestively, the **~122 Hz low ringdown mode** (the old 200-drop watch item, absent in both check runs) flickered on exactly 3 of 256 drops — Signals **94, 96, and 130** — bracketing that same transition window. The BOT resultant grew only ~+11 % while CH6 alone grew +127 % (and CH7 partially mirrored it), so the reading is **bottom-vertex key-seat rotation re-projecting the resultant onto CH6, on top of a genuine ~10 % rise in bottom-vertex transmission** — plausibly a settling/stretching event in this specimen's three bubbled diagonal TPU tendons. Worth inspecting/re-seating the bottom sensor and photographing the tendons before the next run.

### 2. "All signals disconnected" — reassurance

**Nothing in the data disconnected.** All seven channels are alive with normal noise floors and offsets on all 256 captures, including Signal 256 itself (a perfectly normal impact). The disconnect display is the TP4's reaction to the latched overload state, not a sensor/cable failure. All 256 captures are fully usable — except CH6's amplitudes after ~Signal 118, which are range-censored (the ~1,050–1,087 G shelf is the digitizer ceiling, not physics).

### 3. The failure test itself: the specimen did *not* fail in 256 drops

| metric | mean | CV | net over 256 drops |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **T = TOP/CH5** | **1.087** | **0.87 %** | **+1 %** |
| pulse width | 1.49 ms | 0.38 % | −1 % |
| CH5 / TOP CFC-180 | 205.8 / 223.4 G | 3.7 / 3.3 % | −12 % / −11 % |

**TL;DR:** The structure is solid — you followed the Doumont template faithfully, the planetary-lander hook matches the manuscript's framing exactly, and the transitions between body points have real logic to them. The two biggest fixes: (1) the main message is too generic and claims "robust" when your actual story is *speed*, and (2) a few phrases contradict the current manuscript direction ("combining real and simulated data," "generative design"). Details below.

---

### What's working well

- **The lander hook is the right call.** PR #76 (the manuscript for #75) deliberately re-scoped the paper so the title/abstract/intro consistently frame a *planetary-lander/payload energy absorber*, with the crutch tip demoted to a future-work mention only. Your outline independently landed on the same structure — space hook up front, crutch tip as an optional aside tied to future research. Keep it exactly that way; it keeps the talk and paper telling one story.
- **Three body points with explicit transitions.** "The limit is now providing data quickly enough" as the bridge from BO → AM is genuinely Doumont-style: each point creates the need for the next. That's the strongest part of the outline.
- **The close bookends the opening** (space exploration → advancing humankind), which gives the talk a clean arc.
- **Preview points are full-sentence messages,** not topic labels — per your own notes ("full sentence in title; title is the main message of the slide"), these can become slide titles nearly verbatim.

### Main message needs sharpening

Your one-sentence takeaway is: *"We provide a robust method for designing and optimizing tensegrity structures."*

Two problems, both flagged by your own Doumont notes ("messages, not just words"; "prioritize the so-what"):

1. **"Robust" is the wrong claim.** Nothing in the body argues robustness — every body point argues *speed/efficiency* ("inefficient," "efficient optimization," "rapid iteration"), and your Review section says "makes tensegrity optimization much faster." The message and the body should carry the same word.
2. **It's generic** — it could headline almost any optimization paper. The specific, memorable claim from the manuscript is that the loop runs on *real measured data* at a *small physical budget*. Something like: *"By closing the loop between multi-material 3D printing and Bayesian optimization, we can optimize tensegrity energy absorbers directly from real impact data — in dozens of prints, not thousands."* (The manuscript's campaign is 59 specimens; concrete numbers make messages stick.)

### Alignment with the manuscript direction (#75 / PR #76)

A few phrases in the draft contradict decisions already locked into the manuscript:

- **"Combining real and simulated data…" (Closing).** The manuscript's core positioning — repeated in the IDETC abstract too — is that the physical experiment is the *source of truth*, explicitly *avoiding* reliance on calibrated FE simulation (which struggles with FDM defects and TPU rate-dependence). Saying "real and simulated data" on stage undercuts your own novelty claim. Suggest: "real, measured impact data from additively manufactured structures."
- **"Created with generative design" (Closing).** The manuscript uses a *parametric* T3-prism design space (5 continuous variables: radius, height, twist, strut diameter, cable diameter) — "generative design" means something different to a design-automation audience and will read as an over-claim. Drop the term or say "parametric designs."
- **The objectives never appear.** The outline says "optimize" but never says *for what*. The manuscript pre-commits to a constrained multi-objective formulation: maximize specific energy absorption and compaction efficiency subject to a peak transmitted-force bound. The audience should hear at least the plain-language version ("absorb more energy per gram while capping the force that reaches the payload") — it's also what makes the lander hook pay off.
- **The Need could borrow the manuscript's two-sided argument.** Right now the actual situation is "hard to design/assemble, slow iteration." Your instinct is right — this is the huge attachment-heavy comment thread, not anything wrong with PR #82's files. Here's what's happening and where it's documented.

## Root cause
The crash is in the action itself, at [`anthropics/claude-code-action` `src/github/data/fetcher.ts:293`](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/src/github/data/fetcher.ts#L293):

```ts
if (prResult.repository.pullRequest) {
  const pullRequest = prResult.repository.pullRequest;
  contextData = pullRequest;
  changedFiles = pullRequest.files.nodes || [];   // 293: pullRequest.files is null here
```

It null-guards `pullRequest` but **not** `pullRequest.files`. So `null is not an object (evaluating 'pullRequest.files.nodes')` means the GraphQL response came back with `pullRequest` present but its nested `files` connection **`null`**.

Why `files` comes back null: the action fetches everything in one monolithic query ([`PR_QUERY`](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/src/github/api/queries/github.ts)) — `files(first:100)` **plus** `comments(first:100)` with full bodies **plus** `reviews(first:100)` each with `comments(first:100)`. On this thread each comment body carries hundreds of attachment links ("436 attachment links"), so the single response is enormous and expensive. When GitHub's GraphQL API hits its per-query **timeout / node-complexity limit**, it doesn't fail the whole request — it resolves the expensive nested connection (`files`) to `null` and returns the rest. The unguarded deref then throws.

## Where this is discussed online
- **GitHub GraphQL resource limits (official docs):** the node-limit and query-cost/timeout behavior that produces this — https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/overview/resource-limitations and the pagination guide https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/guides/using-pagination-in-the-graphql-api
- **The documented "partial data, nested field = null + timeout" behavior:** GitHub's API returns the generic `"Something went wrong while executing your query. This may be the result of a timeout…"` and nulls the offending connection rather than paginating it. This is a widely-reported GraphQL-on-large-PRs failure mode (GitHub Community / Stack Overflow threads on "GraphQL pullRequest files/comments returns null on large PRs").
- **In the action's own tracker:** there's no open issue for this *exact* `files.nodes` null-deref yet (I searched `anthropics/claude-code-action` issues). The closest precedent is [#1489 "null author dereference"](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/issues/1489), which they fixed with the same one-line pattern (`author?.login ?? …`). A `pullRequest.files?.nodes ?? []` guard here would be the analogous fix — worth filing upstream. Note: I checked `main` and it's byte-identical to the pinned `v1` at this line, so bumping the action version will **not** fix it.

## What actually unblocks `@claude` on this PR
This is an upstream bug, so nothing in *our* repo changes it. Practical options:
1. **Reduce the query payload** — collapse (minimize) or trim the giant attachment-link comments so the single query stops timing out. Your suggestion to Jinkwan (upload data **directly to the branch** instead of attaching files to comments) is exactly the right long-term fix — it keeps comment bodies small.
2. **Move new analysis requests to a fresh PR/issue** with a short comment thread (which is effectively why we're continuing on this new branch).
3. **File the upstream issue** requesting (a) `pullRequest.files?.nodes ?? []` null-guarding and (b) splitting/paginating `PR_QUERY` so a large `comments`/`reviews` set can't null out `files`. I can draft that report if you want.

For what it's worth, I (Copilot) don't hit this because I don't fetch the thread through that single GraphQL query — which is why this branch's work is proceeding fine.

| height / felt | CH5 max %FS | over-FS | CH4 max %FS | TOP180 (CV) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 20 in / 1 f | **105 %** | **4/5** | 56 % | 369 G (0.6 %) |
| 30 in / 2 f | **99 %** | 0/5 | 31 % | 375 G (0.2 %) |
| 40 in / 3 f | 79 % | 0/5 | 28 % | 416 G (1.3 %) |
| 20 in / 2 f | 50 % | 0/5 | 23 % | 306 G (0.7 %) |
| 30 in / 3 f | 36 % | 0/5 | 21 % | 339 G (1.0 %) |
| 60 in / 5 f | 30 % | 0/5 | 19 % | 462 G (0.7 %) |
| 50 in / 4 f | 24 % | 0/5 | 17 % | 416 G (0.3 %) |
| 40 in / 4 f | 15 % | 0/5 | 14 % | 376 G (2.1 %) |
| 50 in / 5 f | 15 % | 0/5 | 14 % | 400 G (1.3 %) |

20 in/1 felt clips CH5 on 4/5 drops (visible analog flat-topping) and 30 in/2 felt sits at 99 % FS — both unusable. The top tri-axis **CH4 never exceeds 56 % FS**, so the ceiling is entirely the low-range single-axis CH5. This is exactly @sgbaird's search-space concern: a print that's *already* at ~100 % FS leaves zero head-room for a stiffer BO design.

![saturation](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5f10909/data/drop-tests/felt-sheet/figures/01_saturation_by_condition.png?raw=true)

**OLS (n = 45, R² = 0.87)** cleanly de-confounds the two knobs (they were stepped together): each **+10 in ⇒ ×1.85** on the CH5 peak, each **+1 felt sheet ⇒ ×0.36 (≈64 % attenuation)** — so one felt sheet cancels ~24 in of height (both p < 1e-8).

![traces](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5f10909/data/drop-tests/felt-sheet/figures/03_ch5_impact_traces.png?raw=true)

**Recommendation — the ideal height/felt combo: `60 in + 5 felt sheets` (alt: `50 in + 4 felt`).** The key insight is that the *output* we actually care about (TOP CFC-180, the BO objective surrogate) only ranges 306–462 G across a **7× swing in CH5 input** — it's set by the specimen, not by how hard the base is hit. So a near-saturating input buys ~no extra signal while spending all the head-room. Maximizing repeatable output under a **3× CH5 head-room** rule (worst-case ≤ FS/3, room for a ~3× stiffer design) lands on **60 in/5 f**: strongest, most repeatable output (462 G, CV 0.7 %) with CH5 only ~30 % FS (3.4× margin) and CH4 at 19 % FS. Rule of thumb from the model: **add ~1 felt sheet per 24 in of height**, and avoid the two saturating settings.

Caveat: n = 1 specimen (5 repeats/condition); the 3× factor is an engineering choice — tighten it once the stiffest #35 search-space design's expected peak is known, since that (not this print) sets the true required margin. The real long-term fix for head-room is a higher-range base sensor, not more felt.

@copilot+claude-opus-4.8  is this going to give us something reasonable in terms of specific energy absorption and any other objective(s) of interest, assuming that we'll also have high speed video (for SEA specifically)

> @copilot+claude-opus-4.8  is this going to give us something reasonable in terms of specific energy absorption and any other objective(s) of interest, assuming that we'll also have high speed video (f...

Short answer: **yes for SEA — but only via the high-speed video, not the accelerometers alone — and only once the force channel has saturation head-room and the capture window is extended.** Here's the objective-by-objective read on what this rig currently supports.

## SEA (specific energy absorption)
There are two routes, and they need different things:

- **Accelerometer-only (energy/momentum balance):** `SEA = ½·m_drop·(v_in² − v_out²) / m_specimen`, with `v` from integrating the carriage/top accelerometer. This is **not reliable on the current data** — the 200 ms window truncates the pulse, so our Δv is partial-pulse (`docs/drop-test-input-output-analysis.md` flags ~2.85–2.96 m/s vs ~3.4–3.7 m/s over the full window). It also can't separate energy absorbed *by the specimen* from energy lost to the felt/plates.
- **High-speed video + accelerometer (force–displacement work integral):** `SEA = ∮F dδ / m_specimen`, where `F(t) = m_carriage·a(t)` from the top tri-axis and `δ(t)` is the **specimen compression** tracked in the video. This is the gold-standard (Edison's DIC recommendation, Pajunen 2019 / Dwyer 2023 analogues) and **does give a reasonable SEA** — it's exactly what the high-speed camera unlocks. So the plan of "video for SEA specifically" is the right call.

Three prerequisites the committed data already flags before that hysteresis integral is trustworthy:
1. **Force channel must not saturate across the whole #35 search space.** This is your search-space concern from the felt-sheet sweep: the base single-axis CH5 (FS 9,442.9 G) already sits near 100 % FS at low-felt conditions, and a stiffer BO design clips it — a clipped `F(t)` corrupts `∮F dδ`. Use the **top tri-axis (FS ~13.6–15 kG) as the force channel** and/or the recommended 60 in + 5 felt operating point (~30 % FS, ~3.4× head-room), or move to a higher-range base sensor.
2. **Extend capture past 200 ms** so the full crush pulse *and* rebound are inside the window — needed both to close the hysteresis loop and for the full-pulse Δv.
3. **Sync + track the right displacement:** trigger-sync the camera to the DAQ (frame from t=0, ≥~5000 fps), and track **top-plate-relative-to-base compression**, not carriage travel; keep the input-output geometry (bungees removed) so the specimen is actually crushed rather than plate-on-plate.

## Other objectives
- **F_peak / peak transmitted g:** works **now** — transmissibility `T = output/input` already discriminates geometry (input-output series: yqpmx1 0.96 attenuator vs practice/n0jdwk ~1.17–1.19, 20/20 clean), provided the force channel stays out of saturation.
- **Reusability / N_reuse:** supported qualitatively — that's what the 200/500-drop campaigns exercise (BOT dropout, mount creep, felt wear are the failure modes to watch).
- **Ringdown / damping:** needs the same **>200 ms** window fix; can't be read from the current shock-only captures.

Bottom line: with high-speed video, SEA and F_peak are both viable BO objectives from this rig; the gating items are (a) force-channel head-room over the full search space, (b) a longer capture window, and (c) video↔DAQ sync tracking specimen compression. None require restarting — they're rig/DAQ settings.

### TL;DR

**The 60 in / 5 felt setting is validated — keep it — but the felt is a consumable.** 201/201 captures triggered cleanly, the output is the strongest and most repeatable of any condition tested (461–475 G, CV ≤ 1.7 %), and the two geometries separate decisively. The one campaign-scale effect in the data is **felt compaction**: the raw CH5 spike tripled (2.1 → 6.5 kG, 22 % → 69 % of full scale) across the two back-to-back sessions, which is what drives every drift term below. Transmissibility `T = TOP/CH5` cancels almost all of it.

### Capture health

| | 7xadt6 | 9GMQYQ |
|---|--:|--:|
| real drops / captures | **100/100** | **101/101** |
| impact lands at | 4.06 ± 0.07 ms | 4.00 ± 0.04 ms |
| median cadence | 41 s | 41 s (one 12.9 min pause before Signal 101) |
| worst CH5 raw | 35.1 % FS | **68.6 % FS** |
| worst top-vertex axis (CH4/Z) | 20.1 % FS | 22.1 % FS |

### OLS regression (stabilized phase, burn-in = 5 drops)

The burn-in scan finds no k ≤ 20 with a non-significant trend on either specimen — the drift is campaign-scale felt wear, not a seating transient — so the SOP 5-drop burn-in is used.

**7xadt6 (drops 6–100, n = 95):**

| metric | mean | CV | slope (%/drop) | 95 % CI (per drop) | p | R² | DW |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| TOP CFC-180 (G) | 461.4 | 1.74 % | +0.062 % | [+0.275, +0.298] G | 1.4e-68 | 0.96 | 1.10 |
| CH5 input (G) | 446.2 | 1.66 % | +0.059 % | [+0.252, +0.274] G | 3.2e-66 | 0.96 | 1.05 |
| T = TOP/CH5 | 1.034 | **0.12 %** | +0.003 % | — | 2.7e-17 | 0.54 | 1.76 |

**9GMQYQ (drops 6–101, n = 96):**

| metric | mean | CV | slope (%/drop) | 95 % CI (per drop) | p | R² | DW |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| TOP CFC-180 (G) | 475.2 | 1.00 % | +0.028 % | [+0.110, +0.155] G | 4.2e-20 | 0.59 | 0.77 |
| CH5 input (G) | 462.7 | 0.81 % | +0.013 % | [+0.036, +0.085] G | 4.7e-06 | 0.20 | 0.59 |
| T = TOP/CH5 | 1.027 | 0.45 % | +0.015 % | — | 4.3e-37 | 0.82 | 0.48 |

Reading it: the TOP output climbs ~0.03–0.06 %/drop, but **in lockstep with the input** (per-drop corr(TOP, CH5) = 0.999 for 7xadt6) — so `T` absorbs it, drifting only +0.3 % / +1.4 % over ~95 drops. Pulse width and ringdown frequency are flat → this is a rig/felt effect, not specimen degradation. (Durbin–Watson 0.5–1.1 means residuals are autocorrelated — trust the slopes and R², not the literal p-values.)

**Specimen discrimination (stabilized drops, Welch t):** TOP 461.4 vs 475.2 G (−2.9 %, p = 3.7e-30, |d| = 2.1); T 1.034 vs 1.027 (+0.7 %, p = 6.4e-27, d = 2.1). These two geometries happen to be close responders, yet they still separate cleanly — sub-1 % differences in T are resolvable at n ≈ 5 drops.

### The felt-wear finding

CH5's **raw** spike grows monotonically all evening: 7xadt6 starts at the fresh-felt level the sweep measured (~2.1 kG ≈ 22 % FS) and crosses the FS/3 head-room target around **drop 67**; 9GMQYQ (run second) is above FS/3 from drop 1 and ends at ~6.5 kG (69 % FS). The CFC-180 input barely moves (446 → 463 G) — compacted felt mostly adds high-frequency spike content, which is exactly what eats raw-peak head-room. Signal 101, recorded after the 12.9 min pause, drops back to 56 % FS — consistent with viscoelastic felt recovery. (See `figures/03_saturation.png`.)

### Recommendation on height / felt count

1. **Keep 60 in / 5 felt sheets** as the operating point — no change needed to the condition itself.
2. **Replace/refresh the felt when CH5's raw |peak| exceeds FS/3 ≈ 3.1 kG — roughly every ~100 drops at 60 in** (ideally fresh felt per specimen), and log the felt state per session.
3. **If mid-campaign felt swaps are impractical: 60 in / 6 felt sheets.** One extra sheet attenuates the base hit ×0.36 (felt-sheet model) — would have held even this evening's worst case at ~25 % FS — at near-zero cost in output signal. Fallback if hoisting is the bottleneck: 50 in / 4–5 felt.
4. **Use `T = TOP/CH5` (not raw TOP peak) as the BO objective** — it cancels the felt-wear drift (CV 0.12–0.45 % vs 1.0–1.7 %).

**One question back, @ctrhjk:** was the felt stack changed between the two specimens? The analysis assumes the same stack all evening (the monotonic CH5 trend suggests so). If it *was* changed, the 9GMQYQ starting level (~42 % FS) means felt sheets vary unit-to-unit — which makes logging felt state and normalizing by the input even more important.

### 1. How much variance per specimen so far?

Every dataset where one specimen was dropped repeatedly, with the within-specimen coefficient of variation (CV) of the go-forward metrics (top-vertex CFC-180 output peak, and transmissibility `T = output/input`):

| dataset | drops | output CV | T CV |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **60in-5felts 7xadt6** (#86) | 95 | 1.7 %* | **0.12 %** |
| **60in-5felts 9GMQYQ** (#86) | 96 | 1.0 %* | **0.45 %** |
| **5vs10** 5 in / 10 in (#82) | 30 + 30 | 0.7 % / 0.3 % | 0.4 % / 0.8 % |
| drift-calibration 1+2 (wax mount) | 19 + 45 | 0.5–0.6 % | 2.0–2.9 % |
| 100drops / 200drops / 5in-100drops | 91–190 | 1.0–2.5 % | 0.4–2.4 % |
| felt-sheet sweep (9 cond × 5) | 45 | 0.2–2.1 % | — |
| input-output, hot-glue mount (#67) | 4 × 5 | 1.3–3.5 % | 0.8–4.6 % |
| key-mounted / wax / burn-in-wax (n = 5 each) | 15 | 0.3–1.3 % | 1.1–2.4 % |

\* the 60 in TOP/CH5 CVs are inflated by the campaign-scale felt-wear drift (both channels climb in lockstep); `T` cancels it, which is why its 0.12–0.45 % over ~95 drops is the tightest of any dataset.

**Pooled: output CV 0.31–3.5 %, median ≈ 1.0 % (90th pct ≈ 2.3 %); `T` median CV ≈ 1.2 %.** The worst numbers all trace to the retired hot-glue mount; the key-seat (± wax) mount sits at 0.3–1.0 %. For scale, between-design differences we've measured are ~10–26 % (and even the two close responders 7xadt6 vs 9GMQYQ separate by 2.9 % with |d| ≈ 2), so signal-to-noise for ranking designs is comfortably high. (PR #67's vertex-acrylic set is n = 1 per configuration, so it contributes a between-specimen spread — CV ≈ 9 % across 4 specimens — not a within-specimen CV.)

### 2. Minimum drops per specimen

Two requirements, both computed from the observed CVs (`n = (t·CV/MoE)²`; two-design power at 80 %):

- **Precision:** at the median output CV (~1.0 %), **5 recorded drops give a ±1.2 % 95 % CI** on the per-specimen mean; even a conservative 2.5 % CV reaches ±3 % by n = 6.
- **Discrimination:** resolving a 10 % between-design difference needs only 1–2 drops at these CVs — precision, not discrimination, drives the count.
- **Warm-up:** fresh-mount burn-in settles by drop ~2 on the key-seat/wax mount (5–10 on hot-glue), so discard 2 before recording.

| plan | warm-up | recorded | total | when |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| minimal | 0 | 5 | 5 | wax key-seat mount, `T` objective |
| **baseline** | 2 | 5 | **7** | default SOP |
| conservative | 2 | 10 | 12 | noisy input channel, hot-glue mount, or a design on a decision boundary |

|---|--:|--:|
| deceleration bracket | ≤2 frames ≈ **1–2 ms** | ≤2 frames ≈ **1–2 ms** |

Caveats (detailed in the doc): stack mismatch and re-waxed mount partially confound the cross-specimen T levels (compare across specimens only under a shared SOP, ideally same session); n = 1 physical article per structure; CFC-180 peak transmissibility only — an SRS/band-wise T could rank differently.

### Review of the tendon support-cage proposal ([comment 5040197700](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/35#issuecomment-5040197700))

### TL;DR

The diagnosis is right and the cage idea is sound — it's essentially a "draft shield" localized around each tendon, and it's easy to implement with the scaffold machinery already in [`t3-prism.scad`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/0b57d1a/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad#L725-L764). But two caveats matter: (1) it will only fix the *motion-induced* defects, not the humidity bubbles from [comment 4983604148](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/35#issuecomment-4983604148) — those are outgassing in the melt and need the <8% RH drying protocol regardless; and (2) three *free-standing* ~120 mm pillars will wobble almost as much as the tendon they're meant to steady, so the cage needs to be tied together (rungs between pillars, and/or anchored to the top PLA vertex shell) to actually work.

### Why the diagnosis is correct

A vertical tendon being printed is a cantilever fixed only at the bottom vertex. Lateral tip stiffness scales as d⁴/L³ — for a Ø4.5 mm Shore-85A TPU column at ~120 mm tall, the tip force needed to deflect it 1 mm is on the order of grams. Nozzle drag across the top layer, part-cooling airflow, and travel moves all exceed that, so the tip chases the nozzle instead of holding position → misaligned layers, smearing, the rough banding visible in the 07-21 photo. The Box video shows exactly this. The existing `t3_prism_scaffold()` touch-point pillars only bond to one side at 7 discrete points, so they damp sag but not lateral swing — a circumferential constraint is the logical next step.

### Feasibility

Straightforward in this codebase. The cage is 3 inclined cylinders parallel to each cable at radius `cable_d/2 + gap + cage_d/2`, generated per cable in the same loop structure as `t3_prism_scaffold()` (`t3-prism.scad:753-765`), rooted at bed height like `pillar_to()` already does, and routed to the struts/scaffold STL → extruder 1 (PLA). The per-part extruder plumbing, STL split, and `.3mf` assembly pipeline all exist. Print-cost is modest for the single prism (3 pillars × 6 airborne cables = 18 pillars); for the 3×3 BO batch it's 162 pillars, which adds real time/material but the 6 mm inter-specimen gap can absorb the slightly larger footprint.

### Potential issues with the solution as sketched

1. **The cage's own stiffness is the weak link.** A free-standing Ø3 mm PLA column ~120 mm tall attached only at the bed is itself floppy (this is the same failure @achris0520 filmed with the wobbling half-TPU supports). PLA is ~100–300× stiffer than TPU 85A at equal diameter, so it's better than nothing, but for the cage to act as a hard limit stop it should be a *frame*, not three independent whips: thin rungs connecting the 3 pillars every ~10–15 mm (placed on the outboard side so they don't encircle the tendon), and ideally the pillar tops anchored into the top vertex PLA shell (PLA–PLA bonds well; add a deliberate thin breakaway neck at top and bottom for clean snipping).
2. **Gap sizing is a genuine dilemma.** Too small (≤0.5 mm) and PLA ooze bridges the gap and welds to the TPU — and the nozzle tip/silicone sock is wider than the gap, so printing the pillar perimeters risks brushing the fresh TPU. Too large and the tendon still swings enough to defect. I'd start at **0.8–1.0 mm radial gap**: it caps swing amplitude at a level the layer stacking can tolerate while staying outside ooze-bridging range. Expect *some* incidental contact welds either way — TPU tapping a PLA wall mid-print usually leaves a removable kiss, not a bond, but it won't be zero.
3. **Removal path.** With three separate pillars the tendon extracts sideways through the gaps after snapping the bases — fine. Once you add rungs, make sure every closed loop around the tendon is avoidable (rungs outboard only) or breakable, otherwise you've built a permanent cage around a finished tendon.
4. **Slicer/travel interactions.** Each layer now has PLA perimeters sub-mm from fresh TPU. Enable z-hop on travel and check the travel paths don't cross the tendon centerline; on the H2D IDEX this is less painful than a single-nozzle machine (no shared-nozzle contamination), but per-layer tool changes on every cage layer will add flush volume and time — worth checking the slice-time delta before committing the batch.
5. **Geometry collisions at the base.** For saddle cables the parallel pillars run inclined (~20° from vertical — fine for PLA self-support), but near the bed they converge on the bottom vertex shells and other members. The cage generator needs the same collision filtering the existing scaffold comments already worry about (`t3-prism.scad:640-642`), plus the `scaffold_min_h` cutoff.
6. **"Hollow" pillars are probably a false economy.** At Ø3–5 mm a modeled hollow cylinder slices to 1–2 perimeters anyway; making it explicitly hollow just risks fragile single-wall columns. Solid (which slices as 2 perimeters + trivial infill) is stiffer for nearly the same material.
7. **It won't fix the bubbles.** The blistered texture in the referenced photos is moisture outgassing (the team's own ≥10% RH observation). The cage addresses layer misalignment from motion only — keep the drying/nozzle-cleaning protocol as the primary fix for bubbling, and treat the cage as fixing the *geometric* defects.

### Cheaper experiments worth trying first (or alongside)

- **Slicer-only**: slow TPU perimeters on the tendons, reduce part-cooling fan (less aero push on a floppy column), z-hop travels. Zero geometry changes; might get 60% of the benefit.
- **Denser touch-points**: bump `n_scaffolds` 7 → 12–15, or make each touch-point a shallow V/saddle tip that cradles the tendon on two lines instead of one point — constrains lateral swing at the contact without encircling anything.
- **C-channel sheath**: a single PLA channel (~270° arc, open slot facing outward) parallel to the tendon is stiffer than three separate pillars, prints as one wall, and peels off through the slot. Functionally the same limit-stop with fewer parts — the main risk is slightly harder removal than 3 snap-off pillars.

### Bottom line

Feasible and worth prototyping on one specimen before the batch — but build it as a tied-together frame anchored top and bottom with a ~1 mm gap, not three free-standing pillars, and pair it with (don't substitute it for) the humidity control. [Prototype the cage →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20cad%2Ft3-prism%2Ft3-prism.scad%20on%20branch%20copilot%2Fget-bambu-sliced-print-t3-prism%2C%20add%20an%20optional%20%22tendon%20cage%22%20module%20(toggle%20add_tendon_cage%2C%20default%20false)%3A%20for%20each%20airborne%20cable%20(3%20top%20%2B%203%20saddle%2C%20same%20loop%20as%20t3_prism_scaffold%20around%20line%20753)%2C%20generate%203%20PLA%20pillars%20parallel%20to%20the%20cable%20axis%20at%20radial%20offset%20cable_d%2F2%20%2B%201.0mm%20gap%20%2B%20pillar%20radius%20(pillar%20d%3D3mm)%2C%20rooted%20at%20bed%20z%20like%20pillar_to()%2C%20connected%20by%20thin%20outboard%20rungs%20every%20~12mm%2C%20with%20thin%20breakaway%20necks%20where%20they%20anchor%20into%20the%20top%20vertex%20PLA%20shell%2C%20routed%20into%20the%20scaffold%2Fstruts%20part%20(extruder%201).%20Filter%20collisions%20with%20joints%2Fstruts%20and%20respect%20scaffold_min_h.&repo=vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization)

### TL;DR

**Yes, there are good permanent options — this is a solved problem in the shock-test world.** Commercial drop-shock machines (Lansmont, L.A.B., MTS) hit exactly this pulse regime thousands of times on **polyurethane elastomer "programmer" pads** without replacing them. My pick for this rig: a two-layer permanent stack — **firm PU base + Sorbothane top** (~$60–120 once). Cheapest fix this week: cut pads from a **recycled-rubber horse-stall mat** (~$50 for a decade of spares).

### What a replacement has to reproduce

From the measured campaigns: a ~1.6 ms half-sine input at ~450–475 G CFC-180, with the **raw** CH5 spike held ≤ FS/3 ≈ 3.1 kG. That last one is the discriminating spec — worn felt fails not by changing the filtered input much (446 → 463 G over 100 drops) but by adding high-frequency spike content that eats the raw full-scale margin. So a replacement needs **damping**, not just compliance — which is why pure springs rank low.

### Candidates, ranked

| # | option | life | why / why not |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Solid PU elastomer pad** (40–80 Shore A, ½–1 in) | 10³–10⁴⁺ shocks | The industry-standard drop-tower programmer material; pulse very close to felt's; tune via durometer + thickness |
| 2 | **Sorbothane** (¼–½ in, on a firmer base) | ~10⁶ compressions | Very high damping — specifically kills the HF raw spike that's eating CH5 head-room |
| 3 | **Rubber stack / horse-stall mat** | 10³–10⁴⁺ | Cheapest per area; one mat = many identical spare pads |
| 4 | **Silicone sheet** (30–50 A) | 10⁴⁺ | Best compression-set + temperature stability |
| 5 | **PORON 4701 microcellular PU** | 10⁴⁺ | "Felt without the compaction" — engineered anti-compression-set foam |
| 6 | Metal springs (die/Belleville/wave) | infinite | Zero wear but **changes the test**: ~5–10 ms undamped pulse, strong rebound — only if a long-pulse input is ever wanted deliberately |

Avoid: EVA/PE closed-cell foams (compression set — felt's failure mode, faster), cork (crumbles), crushables (single-use by design).

### Before switching the campaign onto it

A stack change re-anchors the input, so the doc includes a qualification protocol: a **mini-sweep** (2–3 thickness/durometer combos × 5 drops, reusing the felt-sheet-sweep template and acceptance limits), a **~25-drop stability check** (elastomers Mullins-soften over the first cycles then flatten — the existing stabilized-OLS scripts verify slope ≈ 0 out of the box), and a **bridging run** with an already-characterized specimen (`prc1kn`/`7xadt6`/`9GMQYQ`, n ≥ 25) so pre/post-switch `T` values stay comparable. Two caveats worth flagging: elastomers stiffen when cold (log lab temp, or lean on `T` to cancel it), and the carriage + plate **mass isn't recorded anywhere in the repo** — weigh it once and any future elastomer/spring sizing becomes calculable instead of trial-and-error.

This is complementary to (not a substitute for) the standing longer-term fix of a higher-range base sensor, and `T = TOP/CH5` keeps cancelling input drift either way.

### TL;DR

Across ~1,400 instrumented drops in 19 datasets, **`T = TOP/CH5` (CFC-180 peak transmissibility) has ranged 0.94–1.22, and almost every specimen transmits the base shock at ~1:1 or slightly amplified**. Only two articles have ever measured below 1.0: **`yqpmx1` (T ≈ 0.96)** in the original #67 input-output run, and **`RW5F61` (T ≈ 0.945–0.957)** in the #82 campaigns. Within-session precision is excellent (CV 0.12–2.4 %), but **absolute T is session-dependent** (mount + CH5 tape-coupling state + absorber-stack wear), so numbers are only directly comparable within a shared setup — which is why the table below is grouped by era.

### 1. Geometry-relevant measurements

**PR #67 — the original input-output run** (13 in, hot-glue vertex mount, 5 drops each). The run that established T as the objective — first and still the widest geometry spread:

### TL;DR

The one detail you reported — **the hook moves easily by hand but still won't fall closed** — largely rules friction out, which is why WD-40 didn't help (and more/heavier oil on the hook will likely make it *worse*). A latch that swings freely but won't drop is a **closing-torque-margin failure**: gravity's return torque on that small flat hook is tiny, and something small is now beating it. Since this is a custom tower there's no model-specific issue database to search, but the mechanism class (gravity-reset pawl + actuated release) has well-documented failure modes, and your symptoms map onto them cleanly.

### Likely causes, ranked

1. **Residual magnetism.** The protocol records an *electromagnetic release* on this hoist. DC electromagnets retain a residual field after power-off that keeps tugging on a ferromagnetic hook — and ~1,500+ shock cycles can progressively magnetize the hook steel itself. Hand force beats the residual pull easily; the hook's own weight can't. This is the classic failure that lubricant cannot fix ([TLX solenoid theory](https://www.tlxtech.com/solenoid-theory/latching-solenoid-theory), [24 V electromagnet remanence app note](https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/resolving-24v-dc-electromagnet-residual-magnetism-drop-issues), [Electronic Specifier](https://www.electronicspecifier.com/news/analysis/electro-magnets-overcome-the-problems-of-residual-magnetism/)).
2. **The WD-40 itself.** It's a penetrant/water-displacer, not a lubricant — it dries to a gummy film that attracts dust ([BladeForums](https://www.bladeforums.com/threads/wd-40-why-not-to-use-it.1160243/), [Bob Is The Oil Guy](https://bobistheoilguy.com/forums/threads/wd-40-causes-a-sticky-goo-and-hard-varnish.384986/page-2), [lock-lubrication note](https://www.doorwindowsurgeon.com/post/the-misconception-of-locks-lubricant-and-wd-40)). Worse for this geometry: a wetting oil film between the flat hook plate and its adjacent machined faces adds surface-tension/viscous adhesion a marginal-gravity pawl can't break. **Please don't put the rail oil on the hook** — heavier oil = more film adhesion. Rail oil belongs on the rails.
3. **Over-center geometry.** If the open position carries the hook's center of gravity to (or past) vertical over its pivot, gravity torque goes to ~zero or actively holds it open. Wear or a slightly longer release throw can push a mechanism that used to stop short of top-dead-center past it.
4. **Release actuator not fully retracting.** A solenoid plunger / small air cylinder that returns slowly or incompletely props the hook open — and is easily back-driven by hand, matching your "little resistance" observation.
5. **Pivot/side-plate contact** — over-tight pivot bolt, slight plate bend, or an impact-peened burr that catches only near the open angle. Least likely given the free hand motion, but cheap to check.

### 10-minute diagnosis ladder (no parts needed)

1. **Free-swing test** — power/air off, crosshead away from the carriage. Move the hook slowly through its travel and release it at several angles. A healthy gravity pawl falls closed from *any* angle. Sticks only near open ⇒ causes 1/3/4; sticks everywhere ⇒ 2/5.
2. **Paperclip test** — with power off, touch a paperclip to the hook and to the release-magnet face. If either holds it, remanence is confirmed.
3. **Actuator isolation** — unplug/vent the release actuator and repeat the swing test. Falls now ⇒ the actuator (or magnet face) was holding it.
4. **Degrease** — clean all the WD-40 off with isopropyl or brake cleaner and test **dry**. Falls now ⇒ oil-film stiction.
5. **Pivot check** — quarter-turn the pivot bolt looser / confirm shoulder-bolt arrangement; look for peening burrs on the engagement faces.

### Fixes

- **Best fix regardless of cause: add positive closing force.** A light extension/torsion spring — or even a few grams of weight on the hook's tail — converts it from gravity-reset to spring-reset with real margin. Commercial drop-weight testers use spring-loaded engagement for exactly this reason; gravity-only reset is inherently marginal ([US5457984](https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/5457984), [US5540078](https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/5540078); purpose-built [drop-test release hooks](https://elebia.com/droptesthook-d10/) are likewise spring-actuated). Size it light enough that the release still opens easily.
- **If remanence is confirmed:** a ~0.5 mm brass/stainless/plastic **shim on the electromagnet pole face** (the standard anti-remanence air gap — costs a little holding force), demagnetize the hook, and/or add a brief reverse-polarity/degauss pulse at coil turn-off ([capacitor-discharge degauss patent](https://patents.google.com/patent/US10032551B2/en)).
- **Lubrication policy:** latch runs **dry, or with dry PTFE/graphite film** only (WD-40 sells a "Specialist Dry Lube PTFE" precisely because the original formula gums). Clean the current WD-40 off first.
- **If the actuator is the culprit:** stiffer return spring, or a hard stop limiting the hook's open travel to well short of top-dead-center.

### Why it's worth fixing promptly

Manually seating the hook is safe, but it breaks the ~42 s/drop automatic cadence the 50–100-drop campaigns depend on — at 50 drops/specimen that's an operator touch every cycle, roughly doubling attended time per specimen. The spring fix is about an hour of shop work and restores hands-off operation.

All of this, including the diagnosis ladder in checklist form, is committed as [`docs/drop-test-hook-troubleshooting.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-hook-troubleshooting.md), cross-linked from §3 of the protocol doc. One request back: after you run the ladder, note which step made it fall — that pins the cause and picks the permanent fix.

The two kills were transient GitHub-hosted-runner infrastructure evictions (a known, sporadically-reported Azure-side behavior), which clustered in a ~7-hour window on July 22–23 and now seem to have stopped. No config change is needed; the incremental-commit mitigation already in place is the right defense.

### Why the bash override (`BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`) is ruled out
- **Timeline:** the override (`BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS=900000` / `BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS=3600000`) was added to `claude.yml` on **July 17** (`1927808`). The `show_full_output` edit (`9e0d098`) came *after* the first kill, so neither claude.yml change correlates with the July 22 onset.
- **Mechanism:** those env vars only bound Claude's *internal* Bash tool calls. When one expires, the tool call fails *inside* the session (Claude sees an error and continues); the action step keeps running. There is no code path from a bash-tool timeout to SIGTERM-ing the runner. The observed kill order (from the job annotations) is the reverse — runner-side: **shutdown signal received → runner SIGTERMs the `claude` process (exit 143) → remaining steps skipped → job `cancelled`**, then "Terminate orphan process: pid (claude)" during cleanup.

### 1. The simulation you can run now (committed)

[`simulate_tendon_wobble.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/45400e4/cad/print-supports/verification/simulate_tendon_wobble.py) models the partially-printed tendon as a growing cantilever under a lateral nozzle/bead-drag force (Euler–Bernoulli, first-order — the point is the orders of magnitude between scenarios, and everything scales linearly in the assumed force). Defaults mirror the committed cage artefacts (Ø4.8 mm tendon, 80 mm span, rings every 18 mm with 0.8 mm clearance):

| Scenario | Tip deflection @ 10 mN | vs. current |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Bare TPU Ø4.8 (current failure mode) | 4.4 mm | 1× |
| TPU uniformly upscaled ×1.5 (Ø7.2 × 120 mm) | 2.9 mm | 1.5× better |
| TPU + committed cage (rings @ 18 mm) | 0.85 mm | ~5× better |
| PLA Ø4.8 (why struts never wobble) | 0.03 mm | ~150× better |

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/45400e4/cad/print-supports/verification/t3-prism-pr35-tendon-wobble-model.png?raw=true)

Key scaling facts that fall out of the model:
- **Uniform upscale by factor s only reduces wobble by s** (stiffness ∝ d⁴/L³ — the d⁴ gain is mostly eaten by the L³ loss). So upscaling is a mild win for wobble, though it does make bubbles proportionally less damaging to the cross-section.
- **Diameter-only increase is much stronger**: Ø4.8 → 6.0 mm = 2.4× stiffer at the same height; Ø7.2 = 5× stiffer. If the tensegrity mechanics allow it, fatten the tendons rather than scaling everything.
- **The cage is the strongest lever** because it cuts the free cantilever length (stiffness ∝ 1/L³ — halving free length = 8× stiffer), and its benefit is capped only by ring clearance. Panel B shows the committed 18 mm spacing is already deep in the diminishing-returns region — good as-is.

### 2. Edison's advice on the PR #35 issues ([full answer](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5bf0f99/outputs/edison-pr35-print-advice/answer.md) · [references](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5bf0f99/outputs/edison-pr35-print-advice/references.md), 14-item prioritized table with citations)

On **humidity/bubbling** (the part you can partially do something about):
- The highest-impact fix isn't more dry cycles — it's a **continuously dry feed path**: print *from* a sealed heated/desiccant dry box with a sealed PTFE tube to the extruder inlet, so the filament never re-absorbs moisture mid-print. Bubbles appearing mid-print on long tendons are the signature of re-uptake during the job, not incomplete drying.
- Literature drying setpoints bracket: 80 °C / 16 h under vacuum (TPU foaming study) down to 50 °C / 5 h (TPU 85A FFF study) — use the strongest spool-safe protocol, then transfer to the dry box without ambient exposure.
- **Verify dryness by spool mass before/after drying, not box RH** — enclosure RH is a process indicator, not proof of polymer moisture content; no universal foaming-onset wt% exists in the literature.
- Parameter mitigation: run the *coolest* stable TPU temperature (start 225–230 °C, step down in 5 °C increments), 10–15 mm/s tendon walls, 30–40 % fan after first layers, minimal/no retraction.

On **tendon stabilization**, Edison independently converges on the cage: 3–4 PLA guide towers per tendon, and notes a free-standing shield gives almost no restraint unless it's a close-fitting cage — which is what the `--cage` artefacts already are. One escalation it suggests beyond the current no-contact design: **sparse breakaway PLA→TPU ties every 10–20 mm** for positive restraint (PLA bonds weakly to TPU, so they snap off naturally). Worth trying only if the clearance-limited ~0.8 mm residual wobble still produces defects. Also: **z-hop 0.4–0.8 mm** and eliminating travel moves that cross tendons — cheap, worth adding to the process JSON.

On **simulation strategy**, it recommends exactly the ladder we're on: Level 1 = reduced-order beam model (now committed) → Level 2 = CalculiX/FEniCSx nonlinear beam + nozzle contact with element activation (a natural extension of the existing [`fea_support_stability.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5bf0f99/cad/print-supports/verification/fea_support_stability.py)) → Level 3 = full G-code-driven thermo-mechanical FEA → Level 4 = moisture-diffusion/foaming models (explicitly *not* recommended — the inputs are unobtainable; a conditioned-filament print experiment answers the question faster). One measurement it flags as more valuable than any simulation refinement: **the actual nozzle lateral force is unknown in the literature** — a one-off load-cell measurement on a printed tendon stub would calibrate the whole model.

### 3. General feedback on the approaches in this PR
- **The verification-gate philosophy is the right one.** The stale-artifact print failure showed eyeballing previews doesn't work; `verify_support_geometry.py` / `verify_cage_geometry.py` exiting non-zero is what actually prevents recurrence. Suggestion: wire them into CI on any PR touching the STL artefacts, and regenerate artefacts *from the pinned mesh* in that job so mesh drift (the PR #35 HEAD divergence already flagged in the README) is caught mechanically.
- **Baked-in supports over slicer supports remains correct** for this geometry — slicer overhang analysis is physically blind to vertical cylinders, and the baked mesh survives re-slicing and slicer version churn.
- **The cage closes the right gap.** The tree pillars solve *underside support* (PLA sag); the cage solves *lateral restraint* (TPU wobble) — different failure modes, both needed. The model above confirms the committed ring spacing/clearance are sensible.
- **Division of labor is now clear**: wobble/sag → geometry (cage + pillars, done); bubbling → materials handling (dry-box feed — a hardware purchase, not a code change); residual surface quality → print parameters. That last group (nozzle temp, speed, fan, z-hop) is exactly what fits the PR #22 optimization campaign as tunable parameters, per the plan to let the algorithm work on imperfections.
- **On upscaling**: reasonable as insurance, but the model says prefer tendon-diameter increases over uniform scale if print time matters — ×1.5 uniform scale costs ~1.5–2× print time for only a 1.5× wobble reduction, while Ø4.8→6.0 mm costs little and gives 2.4×.

Full report committed at [`literature/pretension-activation-methods.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/844d09d/literature/pretension-activation-methods.md), with a comparison table and cited references. TLDR of the avenues found, ordered by fit with the current FDM workflow:

1. **Exploit FDM residual stress in plain PLA (lowest barrier).** FDM already "programs" pre-strain into printed material: chains align along the raster and freeze in tension. Heating above Tg (~60–65 °C) makes the material contract along the print direction — no specialty filament needed. CMU's [Thermorph](https://www.hcii.cmu.edu/news/thermorph-flat-materials-self-fold-when-heated) (CHI 2018) and [Shrink & Morph](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3618386) (ACM TOG 2023) show the contraction ratio is *controllable via print speed and layer height*. Applied to us: print tendons in PLA with aligned raster at high speed, stiffer/thicker struts, then a ~70–90 °C oven cycle shrinks the tendons and pulls the structure into a self-stressed state. Print speed, raster angle, and activation temperature become new optimization variables. Caveat: blocked recovery stress is modest (≲ a few MPa) and PLA creeps, so achievable locked-in pre-tension needs characterization.

2. **Dedicated SMP filaments, especially PLA/TPU blends.** Since TPU is already in your workflow, blends are a natural step: a recent [PLA/APHA/TPU blend](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12590943/) activates at ~39.5 °C with ~100% fixity and >92% recovery; [PLA-TPU blend studies](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10853-023-08460-0) map behavior vs. blend ratio. Commercial SMP filaments (polyurethane-based) also exist.

3. **Direct precedents — SMP tensegrity exists.** Liu, Wu, Paulino & Qi ([Sci. Rep. 2017](https://www.futurity.org/3d-printed-tensegrity-structure-1459522/)) built tensegrity with 3D-printed SMP *struts* that deploy on heating and tension elastomeric cables — activating via struts rather than tendons. Lee et al. ([Sci. Robotics 2020](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/scirobotics.aay9024)) pre-tensioned printed tensegrity by fabricating tendons *shorter than the attachment-point distance*. A 2025 Springer chapter, [On the Additive Manufacturing of Tensegrity Systems](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-82283-4_9), reviews this space and is worth acquiring for `literature/`.

4. **SMA (nitinol) tendons — Dr. Santos' own specialty.** SMA gives ~6–8% recoverable strain at hundreds of MPa (polymers can't approach this), but wires must be embedded post-print or via print-pause. His [adaptive shape-morphing SMA tensegrity](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0964-1726/24/10/105008) work suggests a strong collaboration angle here.

5. **Remote stimuli (further out):** [magneto-responsive PLA/TPU/Fe₃O₄](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359836822007557) SMPs (recovery in ~40 s under an alternating field) and photothermal fillers allow activating specific members without an oven.

**Suggested next steps** (consistent with Dr. Santos' FEA-first advice): (1) print PLA coupon strips and measure free shrinkage + blocked recovery force vs. print speed and oven temperature; (2) impose that measured contraction as an eigenstrain in FEA of an existing structure to predict the self-stress state and check strut buckling; (3) build one two-material demonstrator cell and use before/after natural-frequency shift as the pre-tension metric — the same metric as Dr. Santos' SMA tower paper.

### Yes — high-speed Raspberry Pi cameras are a thing

Short answer: yes. The sweet spot is a **global shutter camera on the Pi's CSI ribbon connector**. At full resolution you get 60–120 fps, and by cropping the sensor readout you can push the official Global Shutter Camera to **~500+ fps** at small resolutions — all for $25–55.

### How the 500+ fps trick works

The official GS camera's IMX296 sensor readout time scales with the number of rows, so cropping at the *sensor* level (not the ISP `--roi`, which doesn't help) raises the frame rate dramatically. The community [`GScrop` tool](https://gist.github.com/Hermann-SW/e6049fe1a24fc2b5a53c654e0e9f6b9c) wraps the `media-ctl` incantation: users report [519 fps frameskip-less at 128×96, and 571 fps at 96×88 on a Pi 5](https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=376421), fully supported through libcamera/Picamera2 ([forum thread on Python/libcamera high-FPS](https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=363481)). Trade-off: at those rates the frame is tiny, and you need a *lot* of light (short exposures).

The older HQ Camera ($50, IMX477) can do [~120–130 fps at 1012×760](https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=316300), but only via the legacy `raspiraw` stack, so it's not recommended for new builds.

### Practical notes for a tensegrity rig

- **Global shutter matters here.** For tracking fast strut/cable dynamics, a rolling-shutter camera (Camera Module 3) will skew moving features; the $50 GS Camera or $26 OV9281 won't.
- **Lighting is the real constraint.** At 500 fps you're exposing ≤2 ms/frame; plan on a bright LED panel or strobe (the GS camera's trigger pin lets you sync a strobe).
- **Pi 5 recommended** — it has two 4-lane CSI connectors and more ISP headroom; the highest frame-rate reports are on Pi 5.
- **If you truly need 1000+ fps** at useful resolutions, that's beyond any CSI camera — you'd be looking at standalone high-speed cameras (e.g., Chronos 2.1-HD, ~$5k) that a Pi can trigger but not host.

**Recommendation:** start with the official [Raspberry Pi Global Shutter Camera (~$50–55)](https://www.pishop.us/product/raspberry-pi-global-shutter-camera/) plus a CS-mount or C-mount lens (~$15–50), and use `GScrop`/Picamera2 to trade resolution for frame rate. If budget is tight or you only need grayscale tracking, the [$26 Arducam OV9281](https://www.arducam.com/product/mini-ov9281-mono-global-shutter-for-pi/) at 1280×800 @ 120 fps is excellent value.

**Short answer: ~1000 fps is the working minimum for everything those workflows actually measured — the 959–960 fps Sony RX100 IV captures were *just barely* sufficient — and the one thing they could not measure (specimen deformation during the impact pulse) needs ≥5000 fps.** The binding timescale is not the drop; it's the **~1.6 ms deceleration pulse** on the felt.

| Workflow (as done in PR #86) | Timescale | Frames in the 1.6 ms pulse | Minimum fps | 960 fps status |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| Rig/SOP QC: setup verification, specimen integrity, brake-catch behavior | ≥ 10 ms events | — | **60–120** | overkill |
| Descent kinematics + contact-frame timing | ~30–130 ms visible descent; want timing error ≲ 2 ms | — | **~500** (±2 ms timing; 11 mm travel/frame) | comfortable |
| Rebound velocity, coefficient of restitution (e* ≈ 0.35–0.47), top-vertex snap-back (~0.7× impact speed) | snap-back transient peaks within a few ms of turnaround | 1.5 | **~1000** — 960 fps resolved these, with the snapback peak landing on single frames | **just sufficient** |
| Optical pulse-*width* measurement (corroborate the DAQ's 1.6 ms independently) | need 3–5 samples across the pulse | 3.1–4.8 | **~2000–3000** | not possible (pulse = 1–2 frames) |
| Intra-pulse deformation: peak specimen compression, strut buckling shape, DIC strain fields | need ≥ 8 samples across the pulse | ≥ 8 | **≥5000** (10,000 ideal) — matches the Edison synthesis recommendation | not possible |

Two caveats that are *not* fps:

- **Exposure ≠ frame rate.** At 5.47 m/s, blur = 5.5 mm per ms of shutter. Keeping blur ≤ 1 mm (~3 px at the current framing) needs **≤ ~180 µs exposure** regardless of fps — the RX100 footage shows blob-fragmenting motion blur, which is why the analysis had to fall back to profile correlation. Short shutter means a lot of light (LED panel or strobe).
- **Ringdown (~549 Hz mode, ~10 s)** stays a DAQ quantity — capturing it optically would need ~5.5 kfps *sustained for seconds*, which is memory-prohibitive and pointless given the accelerometers.

### Tie-back to issue #89 (Pi cameras)

- 120 fps modules (Camera Module 3, OV9281 full-res): QC tier only. Contact timing is ±8 ms and travel is 46 mm/frame — no kinematics.
- Global Shutter Camera cropped to ~500 fps: reaches the descent-kinematics tier, and its 30 µs shutter fixes the blur problem — but the fps-vs-crop tradeoff fights the field of view (at 500 fps you get ~100–200 sensor rows; framed on an 80–105 mm specimen that's ~1 mm/px, usable only if you frame tightly on the impact zone, not the descent).
- The ≥5000 fps deformation tier is **beyond any Pi CSI camera** — that's standalone high-speed territory (e.g., Chronos 2.1-HD: 1000 fps at 1080p, ~24 kfps cropped), with the Pi as trigger.

### Why I didn't download from Box

I searched the repo, PR #86's full thread, and all issues — **there is no Box link anywhere**, so I had nothing to download. It also wouldn't change the answer: the camera-native files share the exact 959.04 fps time base stated in the committed [XML sidecars](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/data/drop-tests/prc1kn-60in-5felt/video/prc1kn_video1.XML), so the frames-per-pulse arithmetic is identical; raw files would only remove the pulldown-duplicate cleanup step. I did verify the four committed videos directly with OpenCV (720×1280 / 677 & 830 frames, 1080×1920 / 791 & 962 frames, 30 fps containers) — exactly matching the committed [video analysis](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/docs/drop-test-prc1kn-video-analysis.md) and [metrics](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/data/drop-tests/60in-5felts-validation/video/figures/video_metrics.json), so I reused those measured pulse/kinematics numbers rather than re-deriving them. If there *is* a Box folder with the camera-original 1920×1080/23.98p clips, drop the link in a comment and I'll rerun the pipeline on them — expected benefit is cleaner tracking (full horizontal FOV, no re-compression), not a different fps conclusion.

### Recommendation

If the goal is to replace the borrowed RX100 with a Pi-hosted camera for the *routine* PR #86 workflows: you need **~1000 fps**, which no Pi camera reaches at a useful field of view — keep a 960 fps-class consumer HFR camera (RX100/smartphone slow-mo) for kinematics, optionally add a $50 GS Camera framed tight on the felt for a ~400–500 fps impact-zone view. If the goal is the deformation measurement the current setup can't do, budget for a ≥5000 fps camera + strobe lighting, per the Edison synthesis.

### What the specimen actually does after impact (measured, drop 1 @ 959 fps)

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/6b60ab2/analysis/issue-89-postimpact-minfps/figures/01_postimpact_traces.png?raw=true)

### Why the fps requirement collapses

The camera only needs to follow motion it can *see*. Converting the DAQ top-vertex post-pulse spectrum (n=25 drops) to displacement:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/6b60ab2/analysis/issue-89-postimpact-minfps/figures/02_spectra.png?raw=true)

- 20–50 Hz: **~1 mm RMS** — several pixels, easily visible
- 50–100 Hz: 0.19 mm — ~0.7 px, marginal
- 100–200 Hz: 0.07 mm — subpixel-DIC-only
- above 200 Hz (incl. the ~550 Hz ringdown mode): **<20 µm — invisible to any camera at this framing; that content belongs to the accelerometers**

The video confirms it: the deformation trace's spectrum has 95 % of its variance below **52 Hz**, with measurable content petering out near ~190 Hz. Nyquist for the visible band (≤100 Hz) is 200 fps; waveform fidelity on the dominant ≤50 Hz content needs ~5 samples/period ≈ 250 fps.

Two caveats that survive the reframing:

- **Exposure still matters more than fps early on.** The top vertex snaps back at ~3.8 m/s in the first ~10 ms, so you still want ≤ ~200 µs shutter (bright LED lighting) to avoid blur — at *any* frame rate. Blur, not frame rate, is what inflates the first ~20 ms of the height trace here.
- These are elastic PETG-class specimens that recover in ~100 ms. If a future design (e.g. TPU-heavy) creeps back over seconds, that's *slower* — the fps requirement only drops further; capture *duration* becomes the spec instead.

I analyzed all 25 committed DAQ captures (session "prc1kn 60in – 4 felt 1 cardboard": CH2–4 top-vertex tri-axis, CH5 base plate). The key structural fact: the record length is **not** set by the impact — it's set by the **brake catch at +104.2 ± 0.7 ms**, which re-excites the specimen with a 470–990 g event, after which the deformation-band motion decays exponentially with **τ ≈ 34 ms**. "Enough data" therefore means: past the brake catch plus a few decay constants.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a4cada6/analysis/issue-89-accel-window/figures/01_capture_residual_motion.png?raw=true)

### Measured: time for residual deformation-band motion to die out (n = 25 drops)

Converting the 10–100 Hz top-vertex envelope to displacement-equivalent amplitude (x = a/(2πf)² at the dominant ~30 Hz — it matches the video-tracked ±4–6 mm snap-back and ~1 mm mid-record levels):

| residual-motion threshold | median | p95 | how measured |
|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 0.5 mm (camera-visible) | 166 ms | 171 ms | direct, in-record |
| 0.2 mm | 185 ms | 203 ms | mostly decay-extrapolated |
| 0.1 mm | 207 ms | 237 ms | extrapolated |
| 0.05 mm | 231 ms | 271 ms | extrapolated |
| 0.02 mm | 263 ms | 316 ms | extrapolated |
| 0.01 mm ("truly done") | 287 ms | 351 ms | extrapolated |

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a4cada6/analysis/issue-89-accel-window/figures/02_record_length_vs_threshold.png?raw=true)

Each factor of e in "how still" costs one decay constant, ~34 ms — which is why the answer is a curve, not one number. Extrapolations are needed because **every one of the 25 captures is still measurably decaying when the 200 ms window ends** (the current setting truncates the last ~1–2 decay constants below ~0.2 mm).

### Recommended DAQ setting

- **Post-trigger: 350–400 ms.** 350 ms covers the 0.01 mm p95 (351 ms); 400 ms adds margin for brake-timing drift between configurations (this set catches at +104 ms; the video-analyzed set showed the catch nearer +79 ms — it moves with rig setup).
- **Pre-trigger: ~50 ms** instead of the current **4 ms**. Four ms is too short to baseline anything below ~250 Hz; ~50 ms gives a usable free-fall reference and, critically, quiet padding for double-integrating acceleration → displacement. (If you want the pre-release 1 g reference and the full free fall in-record too, that's +560 ms more — a 1 s total record and still trivial.)
- Cost is negligible: 450 ms × 125 kHz × 4 channels ≈ 225k samples (~2 MB binary, ~10 MB as TP4 CSV) per drop.

Consistency check: the video analysis said the specimen is static to within ±0.6 mm tracking noise by ~150 ms — the DAQ agrees (0.5 mm is crossed at 166–171 ms); the accelerometer simply resolves the tail ~50× deeper than the camera can.

Two caveats: the mm-equivalent conversion is an order-of-magnitude scaling (in-band content at 100 Hz displaces 11× less than at 30 Hz), and if a future softer specimen (e.g. TPU-heavy) creeps back over seconds, capture *duration* scales with that creep — the threshold-vs-length curve would need remeasuring.

### Short answer: the TP4's documentation doesn't publish a hard ceiling — the only rig-specific number on record is Jeff's "~10 more seconds" remark, which at 125 kHz is ~1.25 M samples/channel. Everything your workflows need (≈0.45 s) is far below any plausible limit, and the exact ceiling is a 2-minute check in the Recording Setup dialog at the lab computer.

- [x] Identify the DAQ hardware/software from the committed data and docs
- [x] Read both TP4 manuals attached to issue #36 (User's Guide + Quick Start, every spec page) for a record-length limit
- [x] Check Lansmont's public TP4 (and TP3) datasheets for a memory/record spec
- [x] Derive what the specs *do* pin down + the arithmetic at 125 kHz

### What the equipment actually is

The drop tower's DAQ is a **Lansmont Test Partner 4 (TP4)**, 8-channel chassis, running TP4 software v4.6 (`C:\TP4_46\DataStore\EventDatabase.TP4_db` in every CSV export header). Current settings, identical across all ~1,800 committed drops ([e.g. vertex-acrylic README](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/data/drop-tests/vertex-acrylic/README.md)): **125 kHz (8 µs) sample rate, 25,000 samples → 200 ms window, 2 % (4 ms) pre-trigger**, 4 active channels.

### What the specs pin down — and what they don't

Per the [TP4 User's Guide (W20000-98-14 Rev A)](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28125775/TP4_User.s.Guide_W20000-98-14_Rev.A.PDF) "Record Time" section (p. 22): **Record Time = Sample Size ÷ Samples/Sec**, one window applied to all active channels, with pre-trigger defined as a *percentage* of that window. The 125 kHz rate selection has a valid passband of 0–18.75 kHz (Table 2, p. 15) — plenty for the ≤1.1 kHz structural content.

I went through every page of both attached manuals ([Quick Start](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28125774/TP4_Quick.Start.Guide_W20000-98-15_Rev.A.PDF) included, and the Recording Setup dialog figures) plus Lansmont's public [TP4 datasheet](https://www.rycobel.com/assets/uploads/downloads/testpartner/Lansmont_Test_Partner_4.pdf) and [product page](https://www.lansmont.com/products/test-partners/test-partner-4): **none of them state a maximum Sample Size, record time, or per-channel memory depth.** (The TP3 datasheet doesn't either — Lansmont just doesn't publish this number.) What the docs do establish is that record depth is a buffer/software cap, not an acquisition-bandwidth cap: the sigma-delta ADCs stream continuously, events land in the unit's non-volatile flash, and 125 kHz × 4 ch ≈ 2 MB/s is trivial against the Gigabit Ethernet link.

The one rig-specific data point we have: in the training video, Jeff described capturing **"an additional 10 seconds"** of accelerometer data beyond the shock window ([your issue #36 comment](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/36#issuecomment-4509305026), [video @ 12:06](https://youtu.be/RNjpAmWWmkQ?t=726)). Taking that at face value, the working assumption is **≥ ~10 s at 125 kHz ≈ 1.25 M samples/channel** — 50× the current window.

### The arithmetic at 125 kHz

| Record time | Samples/ch | TP4 CSV export per drop (4 ch) | Per 100-drop campaign |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 200 ms (current) | 25,000 | ~1.9 MB | ~190 MB |
| 450 ms (recommended full-deformation window) | 56,250 | ~4.3 MB | ~430 MB |
| 1 s | 125,000 | ~9.6 MB | ~1 GB |
| 10 s (ringdown target, Jeff's number) | 1,250,000 | ~96 MB | ~9.6 GB |

Even at 10 s the DAQ-side data rate is negligible; the practical constraints become lab-PC disk space, event-database bloat, and re-arm dead time during auto-drop campaigns (a 10 s record occupies ~¼ of the ~42 s/drop cycle). Note two knock-ons if you lengthen the window: (1) pre-trigger is percentage-based, so re-set it (50 ms of a 450 ms window ≈ 11 %, vs the current 2 %); (2) if the cap turns out to be a *total*-memory limit, running 4 channels instead of 8 doubles your per-channel budget — another reason to check with your actual channel config active.

### How to get the exact number (2 minutes at the lab computer)

In TP4: **Setup → Recording Setup**, keep Samples/Sec = 125 kHz, then either click the "…" Quick Pick and choose **Keep Rate / Adjust Size** (the largest window offered *is* the ceiling), or type an absurdly large Sample Size and let the software clamp it — the Record Time field reads back the true maximum. Worth doing once with your real channel setup and posting a screenshot here for the record.

### Bottom line for the workflows

The [record-length analysis from the previous question](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a4cada6/analysis/issue-89-accel-window/README.md) needs only **400–450 ms** — comfortably inside any plausible cap, so you can adopt it today without knowing the exact ceiling. The only long-record use case is the [protocol's full ~10 s ringdown capture](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/docs/drop-test-protocol.md), which sits right at Jeff's quoted figure — if the dialog clamps below 10 s at 125 kHz, the standard workaround is a second recording session at a lower rate (e.g. 25 kHz still gives a 3.75 kHz passband, 5× the record time for the same sample budget, and fully resolves the ~550 Hz ringdown).
