### Short answer

**Barely — and the little they do is in the helpful direction. Buy the Orem one.** Just pick an orientation and keep it constant across all pads and drops.

### What the dots are

Per [Tractor Supply's description](https://www.tractorsupply.com/tsc/product/4-ft-x-6-ft-x-3-4-in-thick-rubber-stall-mat), this is a **dual-surface mat**: molded raised buttons (~2–3 mm tall) on one face — that's your photo — and shallow multi-directional drainage grooves on the other. Neither face is dead flat, but both patterns are uniform and molded, not random. The mat body is ¾ in (19 mm) of solid vulcanized recycled rubber.

### Why it barely affects the pulse

- **The buttons are ~10–15 % of the thickness and flatten almost immediately.** In a ~450 G, ~1.6 ms event, the force needed to squash 2–3 mm buttons flat is a tiny fraction of peak load — within the first fraction of a millisecond the carriage is riding on effectively full-area solid rubber. The bulk 19 mm dominates the stack stiffness; the pulse peak and width come from that, not the surface texture.
- **What effect remains is progressive-rate entry** — reduced initial contact area gives a slightly softer first engagement that *rounds the onset* of the pulse. That's the helpful direction for the actual failure mode this replacement is fixing (high-frequency spike content eating the raw CH5 head-room). Commercial drop-tower programmers are sometimes deliberately shaped (conical/dimpled faces) for exactly this reason.
- **Expected magnitude: a few percent on peak G at most** — smaller than the drift already tolerated on felt (446 → 463 G over 100 drops), and the mini-sweep in [`docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md) measures the real stack anyway — the dots just get characterized along with everything else.

### The one thing that does matter: consistency

- **Fixed orientation** — I'd put **dots down (against the base), grooved side up** toward the carriage, since the grooved face is the flatter contact surface. But dots-up is fine too; what matters is *every pad, every drop, same way up*.
- **Registration doesn't matter** — the dot pattern repeats at a scale far smaller than the ~9 × 12 in / 12 × 12 in pad footprint (per the [anvil measurement](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/88#issuecomment-5076453325)), so lateral placement can't meaningfully change the engaged area.
- **Long-term:** the buttons may take compression set a bit faster than the bulk over hundreds of drops, but they only carry load at the very start of the stroke — and the 25-drop stability check plus `T = TOP/CH5` monitoring catch/cancel any slow drift regardless.

### If you ever want it dead flat (you won't need to)

Stack two pads dot-face-to-dot-face, sand the buttons off, or buy the flat [Boomerang tire-cord reinforced ¾ in mat](https://www.tractorsupply.com/tsc/product/boomerang-rubber-inc-4-ft-x-6-ft-x-3-4-in-rubber-horse-stable-stall-gym-garage-workshop-mat) instead. None of that is worth doing before the mini-sweep says otherwise.

Practical note on the Orem pickup: these mats weigh ~90 lb — bring a truck bed and a second pair of hands, and a utility knife + straightedge is all it takes to cut the 12 × 12 in pads (score-and-flex, several passes).

### Honest answer

**Confident in the ranges and the total stack scale; the specific ½ in + ¼ in split is a defensible starting point, not a calculated optimum — and it can't be calculated, because the carriage + plate mass still isn't recorded anywhere.** That's exactly why [`docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md) §3 says "tune empirically with a mini-sweep rather than by durometer math," and why the source doc gives ranges (PU "~½–¾ in," Sorbothane "~¼–⅜ in") that my condensed shopping table collapsed to single values. So: don't read ½ + ¼ as engineering-calculated — read it as "buy the cheapest point inside the right range, then let the 2–3-combo mini-sweep pick."

### The check that *can* be done without the mass

The measured campaign pins the kinematics regardless of mass: 60 in drop → **5.47 m/s** impact (DAQ Δv 5.5–5.7 m/s corroborates), **~1.6 ms** half-sine at **~450–475 G** CFC-180, 1.9–2.4 m/s rebound ([60 in validation](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/docs/drop-test-60in-5felts-analysis.md)). Integrating that pulse gives the absorber's required dynamic crush: roughly **3–5 mm** (linear-spring estimate v·τ/π ≈ 2.8 mm; energy estimate v²/2ā ≈ 5.2 mm; truth between).

On the proposed **19 mm total** stack (12.7 mm PU + 6.4 mm Sorbothane), 3–5 mm of crush is **~16–28 % peak strain** — squarely in the range where elastomers stay on the usable part of their stress–strain curve. The bounds fail in both directions, which is what makes the *total thickness* the trustworthy part:

- **Much thinner** (e.g. ¼ in total): 3–5 mm crush = 50–80 % strain → the pad runs into its hyperelastic stiffening knee → short, spiky pulse — regenerating exactly the raw-CH5-spike failure mode this replacement exists to kill.
- **Much thicker/softer** (e.g. 1 in+ of soft material): pulse width scales roughly with √thickness, pushing past the **1–2.5 ms acceptance window** in the qualification protocol, cutting trigger margin and drifting the input away from the felt-era anchor.

Reassuring convergence: the ¾ in stall mat — sized by an entirely different industry for repeated impact — lands at the same 19 mm.

### What I'm sure of vs. not

| claim | confidence |
|---|---|
| Total stack ~¾ in (19 mm) scale | **High** — mass-independent kinematic check above |
| Sorbothane **70 duro** (their firmest; 30/50 would bottom out at 450 G) | **High** |
| Sorbothane **¼ in** | **Medium** — it's a floor, not an optimum. Being much softer than the 60A base, it takes most of the early crush and partially bottoms out; that's acceptable by design (it's a spike-smoothing entry layer, the PU carries the pulse), but if the mini-sweep still shows raw CH5 spike content, thickening to ⅜–½ in is the first move (½ in is [$101.50 vs $53.90 at Isolate It!](https://www.isolateit.com/products/sorbothane-vibration-damping-sheet-stock-12-x12in)) |
| PU **60A** durometer | **Lowest** — durometer is the knob most sensitive to the unknown carriage mass and contact pressure. 60A is the center of drop-tower programmer practice for this pulse regime, but 40A–80A are all plausible until the mass is known or the sweep says |
| PU **½ in** specifically | **Medium** — right range; the exact PU/Sorbothane split within the 19 mm total is tunable |

### Practical upshot (ordering plan unchanged)

The ~$105 plan already hedges this: the stall mat gives a ¾ in single-material baseline *and* cuttable base layers, the ¼ in Sorbothane adds the damping layer, and the mini-sweep (2–3 stack combos × 5 drops, acceptance: CH5 raw ≤ 3.1 kG, input within ±20 % of 450–475 G, pulse 1–2.5 ms, TOP CV ≤ 2 %) is what actually picks the winner. Sweep outcomes → adjustments: pulse too short / peak too high → softer durometer or thicker stack; too long / weak trigger → thinner stack or smaller pad area; residual raw spike → more Sorbothane. And the 30-second fix stands: **weigh the carriage + plate once** and all of this becomes calculable instead of judged.

### Answer: 25 kHz is the minimum for the analysis exactly as implemented; 5 kHz with three tiny metric-extraction tweaks; 2.5 kHz is the hard floor. 125 kHz is 5–25× more than the analysis uses.

- [x] Locate DAQ data (`prc1kn - set 1 - 1.zip`, 25 captures, 200 ms @ 125 kHz) and identify what "the current analysis" computes — the PR #86 pipeline ([`drop_test_60in_5felts_analysis.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/scripts/analysis/drop_test_60in_5felts_analysis.py)): CFC-180 peaks, T = TOP/CH5, pulse width, Δv, ringdown frequency, raw-peak saturation/trigger audits
- [x] Re-run that exact pipeline on synthetically downsampled captures at every selectable TP4 rate (two anti-alias flavors bracketing the real instrument)
- [x] Quantify metric errors vs the 125 kHz reference; add rate-robust metric variants to separate information loss from sample-granularity effects
- [x] Commit reproducible analysis + figures
- [x] Report minimum sampling frequency recommendation

### How the check was done

Each of the 25 committed prc1kn captures was re-recorded "as if" the TP4 had been set to a lower rate, using the instrument's actual rate ladder from the [User's Guide Table 2](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28125775/TP4_User.s.Guide_W20000-98-14_Rev.A.PDF) (50k / 25k / 20k / 10k / 5k / 2.5k / 1.25 kHz — each with a flat passband of 0.15·fs, exactly matching the 18.75 kHz @ 125 kHz spec). Two simulation flavors bracket the real acquisition chain: a conservative low-pass at the 0.15·fs passband ("TP4-style") and an ideal near-Nyquist anti-alias. Then the campaign pipeline's metric-extraction functions — vendored **unchanged** from the PR #86 script — were re-run at each rate. Reference values reproduce the established numbers exactly (CH5 CFC-180 467 g, TOP 469 g, T = 1.005, width 1.56 ms, Δv 5.73 m/s, brake catch +104.2 ms, τ 34.3 ms), so the vendoring is faithful.

The key structural fact: the campaign quantities are all **CFC-180 filtered (300 Hz cutoff)**. The raw 4,300–6,000 g contact spike carries energy to ~8 kHz, but everything the analysis reports lives below 300 Hz — the smooth 467 g / 1.56 ms pulse *is* the CFC-180 rendering of that spike:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/538c936/analysis/issue-89-min-sample-rate/figures/02_pulse_vs_rate.png?raw=true)

The 10 kHz and 5 kHz curves sit *on* the 125 kHz curve; 2.5 kHz wobbles; 1.25 kHz smears (its 187.5 Hz passband cuts into the CFC band).

### Error sweep (median over 25 drops, TP4-style flavor)

| TP4 setting | T = TOP/CH5 | CFC-180 peaks | Δv | pulse width | ringdown freq | 300 g trigger fires |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 25 kHz | 0.02 % | 0.05 % | 1.6 % | 2.6 % | 0.05 Hz | 25/25 |
| 10 kHz | 0.21 % | 0.5 % | **6.9 %** | **10.3 %** | 0.18 Hz | 25/25 |
| 5 kHz | 1.0 % | 1.9 % | **7.2 %** → 0.5 %* | **10.3 %** → 4.0 %* | 0.18 Hz | 25/25 |
| 2.5 kHz | 0.9 % | **12.9 %** | 3.5 % | 2.6 % | 0.18 Hz | 25/25 |
| 1.25 kHz | — | **37 %** | — | — | **61 Hz** | **0/25** |

\* with the rate-robust variants (see below). Full 9-panel sweep, both flavors, both metric families:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/538c936/analysis/issue-89-min-sample-rate/figures/03_metric_errors_vs_rate.png?raw=true)

### The three tiers

1. **Pipeline as-is → 25 kHz.** What fails below 25 kHz isn't information — it's sample granularity in the code: `windowed_peak` integrates Δv only over the half-max window, so moving one edge sample swings Δv by ≈ (half-peak accel)·dt ≈ 3 %/sample at 10 kHz, and the width walk quantizes to whole samples.
2. **With three ~5-line tweaks → 5 kHz.** Parabolic peak interpolation, Δv over a fixed −2/+6 ms window, interpolated half-max crossings. At 5 kHz all metrics are then within 0.2–4 % (T: 0.2 %), and CV of T across the 25 drops is unchanged (0.33–0.49 % vs 0.46 % reference) — campaign statistics unaffected. 5 kHz also keeps the specimens' ~549 Hz ringdown mode inside the 750 Hz flat passband (prc1kn's own dominant mode is ~183 Hz).
3. **Hard floor → 2.5 kHz.** Below this the 300 g trigger level stops being reached (raw-peak attenuation crosses the threshold — [trigger-margin figure](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/538c936/analysis/issue-89-min-sample-rate/figures/04_trigger_margin.png?raw=true)), and CFC-180 becomes mathematically undefined at 1.25 kHz. At 2.5 kHz only the CFC-180 peak amplitudes degrade (≈4–13 %); the deformation-band workflow from the earlier issue-89 analyses (brake catch, τ, 10–100 Hz trace) is still intact (trace RMSE ≤ 0.3 mm, brake timing exact).

Two caveats: `ch5_1000_g` (CFC-1000) is the one pipeline metric that genuinely needs 25 kHz (0.4 % error there, ~41 % at 5 kHz); and the raw-peak saturation audit is inherently bandwidth-dependent (the spike reads ~1,900 g at 25 kHz vs ~6,000 g at 125 kHz), so headroom margins across rates aren't comparable — clipping still happens at the analog front end regardless.

### Practical upshot

Dropping from 125 kHz to **25 kHz costs nothing for the current analysis and stretches the same 25,000-sample buffer from 200 ms to 1 s** — which single-handedly covers the 450 ms full-deformation window recommended in the [record-length analysis](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a4cada6/analysis/issue-89-accel-window/README.md). At 5 kHz (with the metric tweaks) the same buffer records 5 s. This also moots most of the "what's the TP4's max record length" question: lower the rate instead of fighting the sample-size cap.

### Why the bandwidth-dependence of the saturation audit matters: it's the campaign's only guardrail against the one failure mode you've already seen, and it silently stops working if the sample rate drops

- [x] Gather context: saturation audit code, felt-sheet sweep rationale, prior min-sample-rate analysis
- [x] Quantify the raw-peak vs bandwidth effect from the 25 committed prc1kn captures
- [x] Demonstrate the silent-clipping failure mode at low rates
- [x] Commit reproducible analysis + figures, write up implications for the optimization campaign

### 1. What the audit is protecting

The felt-sheet sweep ([docs/drop-test-felt-sheet-analysis.md](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/docs/drop-test-felt-sheet-analysis.md)) found that CH5 (base plate, lowest full scale at 9,442.9 g) **actually clips** at harsh settings — 20 in / 1 felt drove it over full scale on 4 of 5 drops, and the clipping showed up as a fake transmissibility of T = 2.28 (vs ~1.0 real). That is the failure mode: **clipping doesn't just lose the spike, it corrupts the CFC-180 pulse the whole campaign is built on**, because clipping is a nonlinear distortion whose error leaks into the 0–300 Hz analysis band.

The defense adopted for the BO campaign is the raw-peak saturation audit: keep the recorded raw CH5 |peak| ≤ FS/3 (3,148 g), so a design up to ~3× stiffer than the test specimen still fits under full scale. That rule chose the 60 in / 5 felt operating point, and the [PR #86 pipeline](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32b009f/scripts/analysis/drop_test_60in_5felts_analysis.py) re-audits it every campaign (`FULL_SCALE_G`, `frac_fs`, clip-run detection, and the height/felt extrapolation model anchored on the raw peak).

### 2. The problem: the audit's guard quantity is a property of the recording bandwidth, not of the impact

The contact spike is a sub-millisecond metal-on-plate event with energy out to several kHz. Its "raw peak" is therefore the peak of whatever band-limited rendering the DAQ records. I re-read the same 25 prc1kn impacts through the whole bandwidth range ([analysis](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5a426fd/analysis/issue-89-raw-peak-bandwidth/raw_peak_bandwidth.py), [metrics](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5a426fd/analysis/issue-89-raw-peak-bandwidth/figures/raw_peak_bandwidth_metrics.json)):

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5a426fd/analysis/issue-89-raw-peak-bandwidth/figures/01_crest_attenuation.png?raw=true)

| TP4 setting | recorded CH5 raw peak (median) | % of full scale | apparent head-room |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 125 kHz (current) | 6,043 g | **64 %** | ×1.6 |
| 50 kHz | 2,955 g | 31 % | ×3.2 |
| 25 kHz | 1,874 g | 20 % | ×5.0 |
| 5 kHz | 977 g | 10 % | ×9.7 |

Same physical event, and the audit's answer swings from "you have 1.6× margin" to "you have 10× margin." Three consequences:

- **Head-room numbers are only comparable at a fixed rate.** Every committed margin — the sweep's 29.7 % FS, the validation campaigns' worst-case fractions, the "each +10 in → ×1.85" extrapolation model that bounds how hard the BO can push — is denominated in 125 kHz raw peaks. None of it transfers to a lower-rate recording.
- **You can't just rescale the threshold.** FS/3 at 125 kHz nominally maps to ~975 g at 25 kHz, but the attenuation factor spans 0.29–0.40 across 25 *nominally identical* drops, and it depends on the spike's spectral shape — which is exactly what changes with contact materials and specimen stiffness, the variables the campaign varies.
- **Even 125 kHz understates reality.** The 18.75 kHz passband is itself a band-limited view, so the recorded peak is a lower bound on the true analog peak — recorded head-room is an *upper* bound on real head-room. The factor-3 target absorbs this, but only at the bandwidth it was calibrated at.

### 3. The dangerous part: below 125 kHz, clipping becomes invisible while its damage doesn't shrink

Clipping happens at the analog front end, at full analog bandwidth, regardless of the sample-rate setting. To show what that means, I scaled each capture's CH5 ×2 (true peak then exceeds full scale on 24/25 captures), hard-clipped at the ±9,443 g rail, and re-recorded at each rate:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/5a426fd/analysis/issue-89-raw-peak-bandwidth/figures/02_silent_clipping.png?raw=true)

- **At 125 kHz** the audit catches it: 24/25 flagged over-FS, 23/25 with flat-top clip-runs.
- **At every rate ≤ 50 kHz: 0/25 detected.** The decimation filter smooths the flat-top into a clean-looking pulse at 11–57 % FS. The audit reports comfortable head-room while the front end is railing.
- **The corruption is rate-independent**: the CFC-180 peak comes out 4.4 % low (median), inflating T ×1.05 — identically at every rate, because the distortion is baked in before any filtering. For scale: the campaign's drop-to-drop CV of T is ~0.5 %, so even this *mild* clipping (~22 % of the spike chopped) is a ~10σ systematic bias on the exact quantity the optimization compares across designs — and it biases *stiff* designs specifically, the region of the search space the audit exists to protect. The felt sweep's real, harder clipping produced T = 2.28.

### 4. What this means for the optimization campaign

This caveat doesn't overturn the [minimum-sample-rate conclusion](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/538c936/analysis/issue-89-min-sample-rate/README.md) — it splits the rate decision by purpose:

- **Production BO drops at a *qualified* operating point: 25 kHz is fine.** All campaign metrics live below 300 Hz; the 5× longer record (1 s from the same 25 k-sample buffer) covers the full deformation transient.
- **Qualification of any new operating point — new height, felt count, contact material, or a stiffer specimen class than what's been audited — must be done at 125 kHz.** A short 5-drop audit set (like the felt-sheet sweep) before committing a campaign, plus an occasional 125 kHz sentinel drop per session if you want ongoing cover.
- **Never mix rates in a head-room argument.** If a future audit or extrapolation quotes "% FS," it needs the rate attached; comparing a 25 kHz fraction to the FS/3 target would overstate margin by ~3.2×.
- **Watch prc1kn specifically**: the calibration-standard sessions (4 felt + 1 cardboard) already run at **64 % FS at 125 kHz** — only ×1.6 recorded head-room, well past the FS/3 rule that governs specimen campaigns, and true analog margin is smaller still. Fine as-is, but don't raise its drop height or reduce its cushioning without re-auditing at 125 kHz.
- **One thing worth checking at the lab PC**: some DAQs latch a channel-overload flag ahead of the decimation chain. If the TP4 reports overload independent of the selected rate, that restores clipping detection at low rates and relaxes the sentinel requirement — the manuals don't say either way.

Caveats: single session (25 drops, one contact configuration); the ×2 clip demo is a simulation of the analog rail, sized to produce mild clipping — real over-range events can be worse; and the exact attenuation factors are specific to this spike shape.

Ran the full Edison simulation ladder (Level 1 analytic sweep → Level 2 CalculiX contact FEA → Level 3 g-code-driven thermal FEA) end-to-end on the PR #35 tendon cages, and the simulations changed the design: the old cage's **120° ring opening was an escape corridor** — the tendon could wobble clean out of the cage in that direction, which no amount of ring tuning would fix. The cage is now regenerated with sim-tuned parameters (rings every **12 mm**, gap **0.8 mm**, opening **70°**) that bound the tendon's wobble to **~1 mm in every direction** while staying removable (the soft TPU cable squeezes out of the sub-diameter opening after printing). ### The simulation ladder (all committed, all reproducible)

**Level 1 — `sweep_cage_design.py` (`6908f8b`):** exact cross-section contact model of the cage (restraint rose = how far the tendon can translate in each direction before touching cage geometry), plus a growing-cantilever model with nozzle force, self-weight sag of the 19.7°-tilted tendon, and a Newton-cooling hot tip, swept over ring spacing × ring gap × opening angle. Panel A shows the old design's escape corridor; panel C shows the escape transition at ~95° opening and the removability trade-off.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/6908f8b/cad/print-supports/verification/t3-prism-pr35-cage-design-sweep.png?raw=true)

**Level 2 — `fea_tendon_wobble.py` (`73e9467`):** CalculiX growing-tendon FEA (tilted B32 beams, NLGEOM, gravity + 10 mN nozzle force, rings as active-set unilateral contacts). It cross-validates Level 1 (bare tendon 4.2 mm vs 4.75 mm analytic; self-weight buckling SF 30.5 vs Greenhill hand-calc ≈29) and adds what the analytic model can't see: **a ring caps translation but rotation carries past it**, so rings only work when several engage together — the old 18 mm spacing really allowed 1.83 mm wobble, the tuned 12 mm spacing holds 1.15 mm.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/73e9467/cad/print-supports/verification/t3-prism-pr35-fea-tendon-wobble.png?raw=true)

**Level 3 — `gcode_thermal_wobble.py` (`30d3d02`):** sliced the committed mesh on the genuine BambuStudio 02.06.00.51 CLI / H2D 0.4-nozzle profile, integrated per-layer times from the g-code (~30 s/layer across the tendon span), ran Newton cooling + an E(T) map for TPU 85A, and fed the per-element modulus profile back into the contact FEA. Result: only **~1.0 mm** of tendon below the print front is still soft when the nozzle returns (0.2 mm on the slower PLA+TPU schedule), so **thermal softening is second-order — cage clearance is the lever**. Even a worst-case 3 s/layer tendon-only schedule (9.5 mm soft) only moves the caged wobble from 1.03 → 1.10 mm, which quantifies Edison's "print several parts at once" advice as insurance rather than a primary fix here.

### 1. How compaction grows with each drop

The requested graph — CH5 raw |peak| (% of the 9,443 G full scale) vs cumulative drops on the one physical stack: [`01_compaction_timeline.png`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/compaction/figures/01_compaction_timeline.png)

| session | stack drops | raw first 5 → last 5 (% FS) | wear (G/drop) | CFC-180 input |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `7xadt6` 07-20 | 1–100 | 21.8 → 33.5 | 9.2 | 446.2 G |
| `9GMQYQ` 07-20 | 101–201 | 41.6 → 64.3 | 19.7 | 462.7 G |
| `prc1kn` 07-21 | 202–302 | 53.7 → 77.1 | 16.4 | 472.2 G |

| `9GMQYQ` 07-27 | 604–704 | 42.0 → 73.0 | 19.1 | 461.3 G |

Three findings, all in the figure:

- **Within a session compaction is monotonic**, ~9–30 G/drop, multiplying the raw spike 1.2–2.8× per ~100 drops (fastest on a rested stack, flattening as it densifies).
- **Between sessions the growth largely resets — and session-start levels are specimen-reproducible a week apart** (`7xadt6` 22 → 25 % FS, `9GMQYQ` 42 → 42 %). So there is **no cumulative baseline creep** over the observed life. The exception: the `prc1kn` overnight pair (77 % end → 76 % start, 24 h) recovered *nothing*, while the 07-22 → 07-23 gap (22 h) reset fully — unrecorded stack handling likely matters as much as rest time. Also note the raw level is strongly **specimen-dependent** (prc1kn runs ~2–3× hotter than 7xadt6), so %-FS thresholds are per-specimen.
- **The real aging signal is the wear *rate***: at matched fresh start, `7xadt6` compacted **×3.2 faster on 07-27 than on 07-20** ([`02_wear_and_recovery.png`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/compaction/figures/02_wear_and_recovery.png); a modest part may be the 1.25 MHz batch-2 capture resolving spikes better). Meanwhile [`03_severity_invariance.png`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/compaction/figures/03_severity_invariance.png) shows what compaction *doesn't* change: the CFC-180 input and Δv are flat across all 704 drops (the Δv step at drop 403 is the 20 ms export window, not physics). Compaction adds high-frequency spike content, not shock severity.

### 2. When does the stack become unusable?

Not yet, and not soon — with management. The binding constraint is CH5 raw head-room:

- From a specimen-typical fresh start, a 100-drop session tops out at ~70–80 % FS; at the current (accelerated) wear rates, clipping (~95 % FS) needs **≈ 220–260 consecutive drops without a reset**.
- The risk scenarios are: sessions > ~150 drops; **starting above ~50 % FS** (the 07-22 near-clip was exactly this — third near-daily session, started at 76 %); hot specimens like `prc1kn`; and continued rate acceleration — if the ×3.2/week trend holds, fresh-start sessions hit ~95 % within roughly 1–2 more weekly cycles, which is the practical "spent" horizon.
- **Operational rule** (replacing the FS/3-refresh advice the lab can't follow with no spare felt): log the first-5-drop raw %FS at session start; proceed if < ~50 %, rest/re-set the stack if above; stop-and-reset on any drop > 90 % FS. Two 30-second additions: measure the stack's free thickness each session (your issue #88 photo is exactly the right measurement) and note any re-stacking/handling — that separates recovery from handling and turns %FS into a physical compaction curve. The durable-pad replacement ([`drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md)) is still the permanent exit.

### 3. Is T consistent across compaction levels? Yes — distinguishable, with one gap

[`04_transmissibility_vs_compaction.png`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/compaction/figures/04_transmissibility_vs_compaction.png)

- **Within sessions** (mount untouched — the cleanest test): the compaction proxy swings hugely (`9GMQYQ` 44 → 69 % FS, `prc1kn` 60 → 79 %) while T moves ≤ ~1 % end-to-end (CV 0.12–0.57 %). If T tracked compaction strongly, these ~100-drop sessions would show it; they don't.
- **Across sessions, same specimen**: the only computable pair is `prc1kn` 07-21 (~70 % FS) vs 07-22 (~83 % FS): T 1.011 → 1.026 (+1.5 %). That's the **upper bound**, and it's confounded with overnight mount re-seating (the `500drops` pair moved 3.7 % with *no* stack change). Compaction's true effect on T is ≲1.5 % across nearly the full usable range, plausibly much less.
- **The gap**: the ideal check — `7xadt6`/`9GMQYQ` T at fresh vs worn stack — isn't computable because 07-27 recorded CH5 only. This week's re-run with the tri-axis re-enabled closes exactly that; no protocol change needed.

Bottom line: T stays safe for ranking designs on ≥10 % differences at any stack state seen so far; sub-2 % cross-session T comparisons remain unreliable, with mount re-seating (not compaction) as the lead suspect.

### Which sheet goes on top? ✅

- [x] Confirm which sheet is harder (McMaster specs are in the thread)

---

### Short answer

**Put the softer ½ in (60 OO) sheet on top facing the carriage, and the harder ¼ in (70 OO) on the bottom against the base.** But the honest framing: order is a second-order effect — what matters far more is picking one order and keeping it identical for every pad and every drop.

And yes, your hunch is right: per the McMaster specs, the ¼ in sheet ([8514K63](https://www.mcmaster.com/8514K63/)) is Durometer **70 OO** (harder) and the ½ in sheet ([8514K65](https://www.mcmaster.com/8514K65/)) is **60 OO** (softer).

### Why order barely changes the main pulse

The two layers are stacked in series, so during the impact the same force passes through both regardless of which is on top (the layers' own mass is grams against a multi-kg carriage). The combined stress–strain of the stack — and therefore the peak G and the ~1.6 ms pulse width — is essentially identical either way. Nobody will see the difference in the CFC-180 filtered input.

### Why soft-on-top is still the better choice

The difference shows up in exactly the failure mode this replacement exists to fix — the high-frequency spike content in the **raw** CH5 signal that eats full-scale head-room:

1. **Gentler first contact.** The first fraction of a millisecond of the impact is governed by the surface stiffness of whatever the carriage touches first. A softer top face engages more gradually, which rounds the pulse onset and generates less high-frequency content. (Same reasoning as the stall-mat dots discussion — progressive entry is the helpful direction.)
2. **Damping at the source.** The HF transient is born at the contact interface. With the high-damping soft layer right there, it gets attenuated before it propagates down into the base and the instrumentation.
3. **No downside from wear.** Both sheets are rated ultra abrasion-resistant, and the impact is flat-on-flat and normal to the surface, so putting the softer sheet on top doesn't create a durability problem.

The one scenario favoring hard-on-top — using the stiff sheet as a load spreader over the soft one — only applies when the striking face is small or uneven. The [measured strike face](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/88#issuecomment-5076453325) is flat and at least as large as the pad, so it doesn't apply here.

### Practical notes for the swap

- **Trim both sheets to the same footprint**, and don't re-trim mid-campaign — pad area sets the stack stiffness, so a size change is an input change. A sharp utility knife with a straightedge and several scoring passes cuts these cleanly.
- **Record the configuration** (layer order, footprint after trimming, orientation) in the protocol doc — same spirit as the standing request to record the carriage + plate mass.
- **Re-anchor before resuming the campaign**: this replaces the felt input entirely, so run the qualification mini-sweep and the ~25-drop stability check from `docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md` (on the `copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again` branch) first. Expect some softening over the first handful of drops (Mullins effect) before it flattens out — that's normal for fresh elastomer.

### One thing to watch in the first qualification drops

A caveat worth flagging: both ordered sheets are McMaster's Sorbothane-class material on the **Shore OO** scale, which is much softer than the Shore **A**-scale PU base (60A) in the original two-layer recommendation — the scales are not comparable (60 OO is dramatically softer than 60A). So this stack is ¾ in of all-soft, high-damping material. The kinematic estimate from the 60 in campaign puts the dynamic crush at roughly 3–5 mm, which is ~16–28 % strain on this stack — likely workable, but closer to Sorbothane's bottoming region than the original firm-base design. If the qualification drops show a short, spiky pulse or the raw CH5 spike coming back, that's the bottoming signature — the fix is a firmer base under the stack (e.g. a stall-mat pad or a Shore-A PU sheet) rather than reshuffling these two layers. The soft-on-top ordering above stays correct either way.

#### How the constraints were applied

**Constant mass (Route A):** each design's `(R, H, strut_d, cable_d, joint_d)` is uniformly re-scaled — twist and all shape ratios preserved, exactly the projection `sim_bo_hybrid_campaign.py` prescribes — until its as-printed solid mass equals m\* = 30.95 g. Because the sensor housings are absolute-mm physical fixtures that don't scale (~6.76 g PLA for all six), the solve iterates on **rendered STL volumes** (`m(s) = m_housings + m_body·s³`), so the converged mass includes joints, cores, skirts, housings, and boolean overlaps. All nine converged to **30.90–30.97 g**.

**Max envelope volume (Route B):** `envelope = π·R_print²·H_print ≤ 250 cm³` (the `bo_evaluator.cell_geometry_metrics` definition). The uniform scale is consumed by the mass constraint, so a shape whose envelope still exceeds V\* at m\* is **infeasible under both constraints simultaneously** — no scale can fix it. ### Camera identified: Sony Cyber-shot RX100 IV (DSC-RX100M4)

From the photos: "RX100 IV" badge, Vario-Sonnar T* F1.8 lens, HFR position on the mode dial, and the Wi-Fi logo on the side. Here are the remote trigger options — with one important catch for high-speed (HFR) mode.

### ⚠️ Key limitation: Wi-Fi remote does NOT work in HFR mode

The smartphone/Wi-Fi remote (Smart Remote / Imaging Edge Mobile) is unavailable while the mode dial is on HFR — users on [DPReview confirm this](https://www.dpreview.com/forums/thread/3935662) and report that a **wired remote plugged into the Multi/Micro-USB terminal is the workaround**. So the plan depends on which mode you're shooting:

### Option 1 — Wired/RF remote for HFR super-slow-motion (recommended for safety use)

This is the setup that actually works for remotely triggering 250/500/1000 fps clips:

1. Plug a remote into the **Multi/Micro USB terminal** (right side of the camera, under the flap next to the HDMI port visible in your third photo). Compatible remotes: Sony **RM-VPR1** (wired, ~$60–70) or the cheaper **JJC SR-F2W** (RF wireless, gives you distance from the rig without line-of-sight).
2. Set the mode dial to **HFR**, then `MENU → Camera Settings → HFR Settings` and choose frame rate (240/480/960 fps NTSC), Priority Setting, and **REC Timing**.
3. Press the **center button** on the control wheel once, at the camera, to enter the HFR shooting (standby) screen — this step can't be done from the remote.
4. From then on, press the **MOVIE button on the remote** to trigger each clip from a safe distance ([workflow per Sony's HFR help guide](https://helpguide.sony.net/dsc/1530/v1/en/contents/TP0001098432.html) + [DPReview thread](https://www.dpreview.com/forums/thread/3935662)).

**Tip for capturing failures:** set REC Timing to **End Trigger** — the camera continuously buffers and saves the ~2–4 s *before* you press the button, so you can trigger *after* the interesting event (e.g., a tensegrity structure failure) instead of anticipating it. Note that in HFR standby, focus/exposure/zoom are locked and no audio is recorded.

### Option 2 — Wi-Fi smartphone remote (normal photo/video modes only)

Per [Sony's official RX100M4 remote-shooting guide](https://support.d-imaging.sony.co.jp/www/cscs/pmm/page2.php?area=gb&lang=en&mdl=DSC-RX100M4&abil=31100&mode=connect) and the [Imaging Edge Mobile how-to](https://www.sony.co.uk/electronics/support/compact-cameras-dsc-rx-series/dsc-rx100/articles/00048733):

1. Install **Imaging Edge Mobile** on the phone (successor to PlayMemories Mobile — [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id489191124) / Android; note Sony has since moved newer bodies to "Creators' App", but this camera uses Imaging Edge Mobile).
2. On the camera: `MENU → Application → Application List → Smart Remote Embedded` (or `Ctrl w/ Smartphone`). The camera displays a QR code and becomes a Wi-Fi access point.
3. In the app: `Camera Connection/Registration → Scan QR Code` (or enter the SSID/password shown on the camera, or NFC one-touch on Android).
4. You get live view on the phone plus shutter/movie trigger, zoom, and exposure settings — works for stills and normal-speed movies, **but not HFR**.

### Option 3 — Programmatic trigger (for automation integration)

The RX100 IV exposes Sony's **Camera Remote API (beta)** over its Wi-Fi AP while Smart Remote Embedded is running — a JSON-RPC endpoint (`http://<camera-ip>/sony/camera`) that a lab PC can call to start/stop capture, ideal if you want to script triggering alongside the tensegrity experiments. Python wrappers: [pysony on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/pysony/) / [Bloodevil/sony_camera_api](https://github.com/Bloodevil/sony_camera_api), plus [sonypy](https://github.com/storborg/sonypy) and an [example control project](https://github.com/jdesfossez/sony-remote/blob/master/README.md). Same caveat as Option 2: since this rides on the Smart Remote app, it can't trigger HFR mode — for automated HFR triggering you'd wire a relay/microcontroller (e.g., Raspberry Pi GPIO + optocoupler) into an RM-VPR1-style Multi-terminal plug, which is a well-trodden hack.

### Bottom line

For the safety use case with high-speed recording: get a **Multi-terminal remote (Sony RM-VPR1 wired, or JJC SR-F2W RF wireless)**, use **HFR + End Trigger**, arm the camera once at the rig, then fire clips from a distance. Wi-Fi remote is only an option if you drop out of HFR mode.

### TL;DR

**The polyurethane sheets solve the head-room/compaction problem outright (raw spike −71 %, 6× inside the FS/3 target), and transmissibility drops from 1.009 on felt to 0.976 on PU — but that T shift is an input-spectrum effect, not the specimen improving, and the PU stack as tested has one real problem: the input pulse toggles between two stiffness states drop-to-drop (input CV 26 % vs felt's 2.8 %).** Right material, wrong operating point + an unseated stack.

### Head-to-head (5 paired drops each, same specimen, same mount, same morning)

| metric | felt + cardboard | polyurethane | change |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| CH5 raw \|peak\| | 1,293–1,584 G (14–17 % FS) | **371–496 G (4–5 % FS)** | **−71 %**, p = 4.6e-06 |
| CH5 input CFC-180 | 407.6 G (CV 2.8 %) | 186.2 G (CV **25.7 %**) | −54 %, p = 3.1e-04 |
| input pulse width | 1.67 ms | 2.5–4.5 ms | ~×2 longer |
| full-pulse Δv | 6.21 m/s (CV 0.2 %) | 5.55 m/s (CV 4.2 %) | both ≈ free fall from 60 in + rebound |
| TOP output CFC-180 | 411.3 G | 182.1 G | −56 % |
| **T = TOP/CH5** | **1.009 (CV 0.4 %)** | **0.976 (CV 1.3 %)** | −3.3 %, p = 2.4e-03, d = −3.6 |

### The transmissibility comparison, read carefully

The same specimen "attenuates" on rubber and mildly amplifies on felt because the PU pulse is ~2× longer — its energy sits at lower frequencies that excite the structure less ([figure](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/pu-vs-felt/figures/02_transmissibility.png)). Practical consequences:

1. **T values don't transfer across absorber configurations.** The felt-era catalog (0.94–1.22) can't be compared to PU-era numbers; switching stacks re-anchors the objective, exactly what the [bridging step](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md) anticipated. (`bpx68c`'s felt-stack T = 1.009 lands in the familiar near-unity band with `prc1kn`/`9GMQYQ`.)
2. **T remains an excellent objective on PU**: despite the 26 % input swing, T holds CV 1.3 % (and ~0.1 % within the repeatable drops) — the ratio cancels the stack-state noise just as it cancelled felt wear.

### The one real problem: bimodal PU input

The five PU drops split into a "stiff" cluster (S3, S5: ~236 G / 2.5 ms — repeatable to 1 %) and a "soft" cluster (S1, S2, S4: 134–173 G / 3.3–4.5 ms), in order soft-soft-stiff-soft-stiff at a uniform 47 s cadence ([pulse overlay](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/pu-vs-felt/figures/01_input_pulses.png)). Momentum is conserved across all five (Δv CV 4 %), so the pulse *shape* is changing — the stack's effective stiffness differs between drops. Prime suspect: **loose sheets seating differently (air gaps / lateral shift)**; the TP4's own series table shows the same clustering, so it's not an analysis artifact.

### Verdict vs the qualification criteria ([absorber-alternatives §4.1](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md))

| criterion | result |
|---|---|
| CH5 raw ≤ 3.1 kG | ✅ 496 G worst case (6.3× margin) |
| input within ~±20 % of felt era | ❌ −60 % — too soft as stacked |
| pulse width ~1–2.5 ms | ⚠️ 2.5–4.5 ms |
| TOP CV ≤ 2 % | ❌ 27 % (input-driven; T CV 1.3 % ✅) |

**Recommended next steps, in order:** (1) stiffen the operating point — fewer/thinner/firmer sheets until the input is back near ~350–450 G and ~1.5–2 ms (2–3 conditions × 5 drops); (2) seat the sheets flat and restrain them laterally (tape/frame/pins), then confirm input CV < ~3 % over 5 drops; (3) run the ~25-drop stability check (stabilized-OLS slope ≈ 0 — the scripts do this out of the box); (4) **check the CH5 trigger level** — PU raw peaks are only 371–496 G, so a felt-era 300–500 G trigger has as little as 1.2× margin (with the HF spike gone, ~150–200 G is safe); (5) then the bridging run (a characterized specimen, n ≥ 25) to anchor PU-era T against the felt catalog.

Logging stack composition in the TP4 session ID (as the felt sessions now do) would cover this going forward.

### Quick take on the sticky PU sheets ✅

**Expected behavior, and your fix is legitimate — it's the field-expedient version of what industry does.** McMaster's "Super-Cushioning" PU is Sorbothane-class material, and surface tack is a known property of it (Sorbothane sells most products with a fabric or PSA facing partly for this reason). The standard anti-tack fix is dusting with talc; a coating of felt debris is functionally the same thing. Three brief notes:

1. **The tack mattered more than it looks.** Adhesion at separation adds a tensile pull on the carriage during rebound — that distorts rebound velocity (and anything derived from it) and can add a low-frequency artifact right after the pulse. The compressive peak and ~1.6 ms width are essentially unaffected. So de-tacking was the right call before qualification drops, not just a convenience.
2. **Keep the surface state consistent, and expect it to evolve.** The felt-dust layer will redistribute and thin over drops, slightly changing first-contact behavior. Cheap insurance: re-dust (felt rub or a puff of talc/baby powder) on a fixed schedule — e.g. before each session — rather than only when sticking recurs, and note it in the log. The 25-drop stability check plus `T = TOP/CH5` will catch any residual drift either way.
3. **If it becomes a nuisance, make the barrier deliberate:** a single dedicated felt sheet laid loose on top of the stack (thin enough not to reintroduce the compaction problem, and replaceable for pennies), or a talc dusting. Avoid slick films (PTFE etc.) — a low-friction top face lets the carriage skate laterally at impact.

Worth one line in the protocol doc alongside layer order/footprint: "top surface de-tacked with felt dust; refreshed each session."

### The headline number: print-to-print scatter in T is **CV 0.72 %** (1.95 % spread)

This is the first direct measurement of the thing the sample-size writeup flagged as uncharacterized, and it comes with an uncomfortable comparison:

| | spread in T |
|---|--:|
| **five copies of the *same* geometry (this study)** | **1.95 %** |
| the three-structure 60 in "different geometries" ranking (`prc1kn`/`9GMQYQ`/`7xadt6`) | 2.3 % |
| the 13 in input-output four-geometry set (`yqpmx1`…`n0jdwk`) | 24 % |

So that 2.3 % three-structure ranking is barely above the noise floor of *identical prints*. Repeat drops on one article are only 1.4× tighter than the print-to-print scatter — meaning **replicate prints, not more drops, are what buy precision** for comparing designs: ~3 prints per geometry to resolve a 2 % difference at 80 % power, 1 print for ≥3 %. I've folded this into [`drop-test-sample-size-analysis.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-sample-size-analysis.md), which had this as an open caveat.

### On the actual question — do the defects show up? This design can't tell

T does rank with defect grade (ρ = −0.90, p = 0.04, and in the physically sensible direction). But three rival explanations each reproduce that ranking:

1. **Defect grade *is* test order.** They were graded 1–5 in the sequence tested. And T declines monotonically *within each day* too (07-28: 1.0432 → 1.0374 → 1.0315; 07-29: 1.0336 → 1.0231), i.e. across the felt adjustment and across the defect-group boundary — a progressive sequence effect fits as well as defects do.
2. **The felt adjustment sits exactly on the group boundary.** CH5 raw drops 60 % (6,193 → 2,471 G) and the filtered input 4.9 % across it. The −5.7 % output-peak difference between defect groups is essentially just that input change.
3. **Mount re-seating, and this is the strongest one.** Within a *single* session with the mount untouched, the 5-drop rolling mean of T moves by up to **2.34 %** (`cruela`) — **more than the entire 1.95 % between-specimen spread**. These are step-like plateau shifts (e.g. `57vqhx` around drop 25), the signature of a coupling re-seat, not the specimen changing.

At the honest unit of replication — the specimen, 3 vs 2 — the high-vs-low-defect contrast isn't significant for T (p = 0.29) or output peak (p = 0.12). The drop-level p-values are pseudo-replication and shouldn't be quoted as evidence about prints. ([variance + confound figure](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/print-defects/figures/03_variance_and_confound.png) · [full series](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/data/drop-tests/print-defects/figures/01_full_series.png))

**The cheap fix:** re-drop 2–3 of these same specimens in *reverse* order, in one session, on one stack state — ~15 min of drops each. If the ranking holds it's the prints; if it re-orders with sequence it's the rig. Also worth randomizing specimen order and grading defects blind to test order next time.

### What replaced the felt criteria

- *"input within ±20 % of the felt era"* → **deleted**. It scored arrangements on resemblance to a stack being retired, and it was the only criterion B/C/D failed on severity. Replaced by a measurability criterion (output clear of the sensor noise floor) that all four pass — the PU stacks aren't remotely signal-starved, which is the fact the felt criterion was obscuring.
- *"pulse width 1–2.5 ms"* → **kept, re-derived from the specimens**. That band was chosen to bracket felt's 1.67 ms. The replacement anchors on the first mode at **519–549 Hz** (from this repo's own ringdown analyses): an SDOF at 550 Hz driven by a half-sine stays near its maximax plateau while f·τ ≲ 1.5, giving τ ≤ 2.7 ms. ### The new criterion is the one that decides it

`T` is a ratio of **CFC-180** peaks — and CFC-180 is 3 dB down at 300 Hz, so it attenuates the 550 Hz structural mode by roughly **12×**. The metric in use removes most of the structural response it's supposed to be sensitive to, which is a large part of why every specimen ever measured sits within a few percent of T = 1. Recomputing the same 40 drops under CFC-1000 (keeps the band):

### Verdict: **do not select B. "None of these — the sweep cannot decide."**

Of the four grounds I gave for B: **grounds 2 and 3 fail outright**, **ground 1 does not survive as stated**, and **ground 4 partly survives** as a descriptive warning against A.

### The finding that does it — and I verified it myself

**The 20 ms exports contain ~0.39 ms of real pre-trigger data.** Raw CH5 first crosses its trigger at 0.348–0.390 ms and is only 0.09–2.6 % of peak at `t = 0`. My script's docstring asserts the opposite — *"the record starts on the trigger, so there is no clean pre-trigger window"* — and on that false premise uses a **full-record median** as the baseline, a window that includes the impact and the entire ringdown.

The "CFC-180 CH5 already reads 22–53 % of its peak at t=0" caveat I wrote is **acausal pre-ringing from zero-phase `filtfilt`**, not truncation. It is not a truncation estimator at all.

Re-baselining on the pre-trigger window:

| CFC-180 T | A (1/4) | B (1/2) | C | D |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| published (full-record median) | 1.022 | 0.996 | 0.986 | 0.989 |
| **pre-trigger baseline** | **1.037** | **1.063** | **1.050** | **1.094** |
| published T CV | 0.43 % | **0.34 %** | 0.95 % | 0.49 % |
| **pre-trigger T CV** | **0.54 %** | 1.18 % | 1.22 % | 2.48 % |

I re-derived this independently in-repo on one drop per arrangement (Signals 1/11/22/32 → T = 1.026 / 1.076 / 1.037 / 1.139) and it matches Edison's per-drop table exactly. The mechanism: the full-record median is displaced by the post-impact ringdown by up to ~15 G on individual tri-axis channels — several percent of these 155–265 G peaks — and it biases the input and the vector-magnitude output differently.

Three consequences: **no arrangement attenuates** (every T > 1); **A, not B, is the most repeatable CFC-180 arrangement**; and the "T falls monotonically with pulse duration" law in §4 disappears (Spearman ρ = 0.40, **p = 0.60**).

### The rest of the teardown

- **The 450–800 Hz band criterion is an estimator artifact.** My Welch estimate has 305 Hz bin spacing — *one bin in band* — and takes the spectrum of the nonlinear vector magnitude. Under signed-axis linear energy the ordering **reverses**: A 30.7 %, B 7.0 %, C 1.4 %, D 1.5 %; absolute band energy favors A ~20×; input-normalized gives yet another order (D > A ≈ C > B). Ground 3 collapses. Note this is the *second* time this criterion flipped — I used it last round to overturn the spectral-centroid claim, and it was no better founded.
- **`f·τ ≤ 1.5` is wrong**, and in the direction I guessed. A 5 %-damped SDOF under a half-sine gives maximax/input = 1.64 / 1.54 / **1.28** at `f·τ` = 0.91 / 1.23 / **1.84** — C/D are not quasi-static. Worse for the logic: the SRS peak has near-zero frequency slope, so targeting it maximizes *response* but can *minimize* frequency discrimination — the criterion was pointed at the wrong quantity.
- **The 519–549 Hz "mode" is unidentified.** CH3 does carry the largest 400–900 Hz output energy in all 40 drops (A 517 ± 6, B 533 ± 3, C 511 ± 37, D 477 ± 54 Hz) — but **CH5, the base, has arrangement-dependent content in the same region**, so forced response, rocking and mount motion aren't excluded. Cheapest resolution: weigh the sensor/wax/specimen, tap-test suspended, repeat with a known added mass at the vertex. Also: the correct mounting standard is **ISO 5348:2021**, not the ISO 5347 our docs have been citing.
- **Every arrangement-level p-value is invalid.** One fixed-order block per arrangement, lag-1 autocorrelation up to 0.98, several n=10 sequences collapsing toward *one* effective observation. After detrending, T CVs are A/B/C/D = 0.45/0.25/0.70/0.36 % (CFC-180) and 2.03/0.89/0.89/0.84 % (CFC-1000) — A stays worse broadband, but with zero arrangement-level d.o.f. And "C vs D is a null" has 80 % power only for ≳1.1 % in T, so it was never equivalence evidence.
- **On my own biggest worry — the minimum-variance trap — it agrees and goes further:** no single-specimen statistic can bound an unobserved geometry effect. A has ~20× more absolute structural-band signal; B has lower broadband drift. "That is a trade-off, not a winner."
- **Peak-ratio T is not an energy-absorption objective.** Ranked replacements: input-conditioned output SRS → band-limited transfer function with coherence → output peak at fixed *measured* incident velocity → ringdown damping → incident/rebound KE loss (the direct metric; needs a photogate/encoder and the moving mass, which still isn't recorded anywhere). Also: **Δv is a processing-dependent descriptor** — agreement with 5.47 m/s free-fall is not validation, and it is not a lower bound as our docs claim.

### What to actually do next

**A 20-drop randomized crossover:** two existing distinct geometries × arrangements A and B, 5 drops per cell, **interleaved in randomized order**, one common trigger level, **≥ 2 ms pre-trigger and 50–100 ms post-impact capture**, with input-conditioned SRS / band-transfer outcomes prespecified before collecting. That directly tests whether B's lower noise pays for its much lower structural-band excitation. It's a screen, not qualification — it can't estimate print variance.

The two capture-setting changes are worth making regardless: the 20 ms window and the ~0.39 ms pre-trigger are what forced every questionable processing choice here.

Short version: **the HFR (super-slow-mo) clips can never leave this camera over Wi-Fi** — HFR records to XAVC S HD, and Sony's own help guide for the RX100M4 says *"You cannot send XAVC S or AVCHD format movies"* ([Send to Smartphone](https://helpguide.sony.net/dsc/1530/v1/en/contents/TP0001087159.html)). So the programmatic story splits cleanly: **stills → lots of options; HFR video → USB/card only.**

---

### Programmatic data-out options, best → worst for this use case

**1. USB Mass Storage + a filesystem watcher — the one that actually works for HFR**

`MENU → Setup → USB Connection → Mass Storage` ([RX100M4 manual p.225](https://www.manualslib.com/manual/1265437/Sony-Dsc-Rx100m4.html?page=225)). Camera mounts as a plain block device; ingest with `rsync`, or a Python `watchdog` observer on the mount point. Works for every file type — XAVC S HFR, AVCHD, MP4, JPEG, RAW. Fully scriptable, zero Sony software.

Caveat: while USB is in Mass Storage/MTP the camera **cannot shoot**. So it's a *between-runs* ingest, not a live stream. Same is true of a plain SD card reader (faster, and the card reader route means you never touch the camera).

**2. USB "PC Remote" tethering → gphoto2 (scriptable capture + download)**

The RX100M4 does expose `USB Connection → PC Remote`, and it's on [Sony's Imaging Edge Desktop supported-device list](https://support.d-imaging.sony.co.jp/app/imagingedge/en/devices/) for Remote (tethered) shooting. More usefully for automation, `RX100M4` is in the [libgphoto2 supported-camera list](http://gphoto.org/proj/libgphoto2/support.php), so:

```bash
gphoto2 --auto-detect
gphoto2 --capture-image-and-download --filename 'run_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S.%C'
gphoto2 --wait-event-and-download          # ingest whatever the camera shoots, as it shoots
```

…and the same thing from Python via [`python-gphoto2`](https://github.com/jim-easterbrook/python-gphoto2). This is the cleanest "capture → file on lab PC, no human" loop — **for stills**. PC Remote is stills-oriented; I could not confirm HFR movie trigger/transfer works through it, and PC Remote definitely isn't available while the dial is on HFR.

**3. Wi-Fi Camera Remote API (JSON-RPC) — stills arrive over the network for free**

Beyond triggering (Option 3 in my earlier comment), the API also *returns data*: `actTakePicture` responds with a **postview URL** you can just `GET` — the JPEG lands on your PC over Wi-Fi with no extra step. There's also an MJPEG **liveview** stream endpoint for monitoring. Both usable from [pysony](https://pypi.org/project/pysony/) / [sony_camera_api](https://github.com/Bloodevil/sony_camera_api).

Whether *your* body also exposes the `avContent` service (`getContentList` / `getContentCount` — i.e. browse and pull *previously recorded* files off the card) is model- and firmware-dependent; the RX100M4's API comes from the Smart Remote Embedded app and is on the limited side. Don't design around it blind — enumerate first:

```python
# with Smart Remote Embedded running and you joined the camera's AP
POST http://<camera-ip>:10000/sony/camera  {"method":"getAvailableApiList","params":[],"id":1,"version":"1.0"}
POST http://<camera-ip>:10000/sony/avContent {"method":"getMethodTypes","params":[""],"id":1,"version":"1.0"}
```

Same hard limit as before: none of this works in HFR mode.

**4. Wi-Fi push: Send to Smartphone / Send to Computer — mostly a dead end here**

- [Send to Smartphone](https://helpguide.sony.net/dsc/1530/v1/en/contents/TP0001087159.html): no XAVC S, no AVCHD, RAW→JPEG on the way out. Kills it for HFR.
- [Send to Computer](https://helpguide.sony.net/dsc/1530/v1/en/contents/TP0001087161.html): pushes over your LAN to a PC — but requires **PlayMemories Home**, which Sony discontinued and never replaced with an equivalent Wi-Fi-import tool. If you happen to have it installed, the destination folder is watchable by a script, so it's "programmatic by proxy." Not something I'd build on in 2026.

**5. Wi-Fi SD card (FlashAir) — cute hack, effectively unobtainable**

Toshiba FlashAir cards run a web server with a [documented CGI/HTTP API](https://petrst.github.io/flashair-developers-site/en/discover/app/index.htm) (`GET /command.cgi?op=100&DIR=/DCIM` to list, then plain HTTP GET to fetch), which would give you card-level pull over Wi-Fi independent of Sony's software. But the line is [discontinued with no successor](https://www.flashairapp.com/flashair-products.html) — used market only, and HFR needs a fast UHS-I card, which FlashAir is not. Mentioning for completeness.

**6. HDMI capture** — clean-ish output to a capture card gives you a live feed for normal modes, but HFR is buffered internally and does not stream out. Not a path to the slow-mo files.

### Practical pipeline I'd recommend

1. RF remote + `HFR → REC Timing: End Trigger` to fire clips from behind the barrier (fire *after* the failure; the camera keeps the preceding 2–4 s).
2. Between runs, pull the card into a reader (or flip the camera to Mass Storage) and run a `watchdog`/`rsync` ingest script that timestamps and files clips against the run ID.
3. If you also want an auto-captured still record of each run, that's where gphoto2 PC Remote earns its keep — it can run unattended in parallel with the manual HFR workflow.

Worth being blunt about the ceiling: this body physically can't shoot and stream simultaneously, and HFR is a 2–4 s buffered burst with several seconds of post-processing. If the goal is hands-off automated capture *and* ingest of failure events, a machine-vision camera (USB3/GigE global shutter, or a dedicated high-speed body) is the architecture that supports it — the RX100 IV will always have a human in the loop for the card.

### Your question first: why CFC-180 → CFC-1000?

Short version: **the recommendation was decided by a criterion I invented mid-analysis, and its stated justification was a number produced by a bug in our own filter.**

The chain was:

1. Removing the felt-continuity criterion (per your instruction on #86) left A and B tied at 7/8.
2. I added a new criterion — *"T computed under CFC-1000 must be as repeatable as T under CFC-180"* — which broke the tie for B (A's CV 6.12 % vs B's 1.36 %).
3. The justification I gave for looking at a wider band at all was, verbatim in §3.2: *"SAE J211's CFC-180 is 3 dB down at 300 Hz, so at the specimens' 550 Hz mode it attenuates by roughly **12×**."*

**That 12× is wrong, and it's wrong because our CFC filter is wrong.**

### The bug

```python
def cfc_filter(x, fs, cfc):
    cutoff = {1000: 1650.0, 600: 1000.0, 180: 300.0, 60: 100.0}[cfc]
    b, a = signal.butter(2, cutoff / (fs / 2.0), btype="low")
    return signal.filtfilt(b, a, x)
```
[`drop_test_60in_5felts_analysis.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/b6a296e/scripts/analysis/drop_test_60in_5felts_analysis.py) — imported unchanged by ~30 analysis scripts.

J211's CFC filter is a 2-pole Butterworth run **forward and backward**. The coefficients carry a factor **2.0775**, which is the *single-pass* corner; the familiar `1.65 × CFC` ("CFC-180 → 300 Hz") is the corner of the **pair** — it's smaller precisely because `filtfilt` squares the response. Our code hands the two-pass number `1.65 × CFC` to scipy's `Wn`, which is a single-pass argument, and then squares it anyway.

Net effect: **every channel class is ~20 % narrow.**

| labelled | spec −3 dB | ours actually | effective class |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| CFC-60 | 99 Hz | 80 Hz | CFC-49 |
| **CFC-180** | **297 Hz** | **241 Hz** | **CFC-146** |
| CFC-600 | 990 Hz | 802 Hz | CFC-486 |
| CFC-1000 | 1650 Hz | 1324 Hz | CFC-802 |

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/da16fba/notebooks/figures/cfc_filter_bode.png?raw=true)

At 550 Hz: a correct CFC-180 passes 0.176 amplitude → **5.7× attenuation**. Ours passes 0.081 → **12.3×**. The "roughly 12×" in the doc is exactly our filter's number, reported as a property of the standard.

Standalone check, no data download: [`scripts/analysis/cfc_verification.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/da16fba/scripts/analysis/cfc_verification.py). The whole claim reduces to one checkable fact — whether 2.0775 is per-pass and 1.65 is per-pair — so it's easy to overturn if I have it backwards.

**How much does it change the published numbers?** Honestly: not much, because both channels get the same wrong filter and it largely cancels in a ratio. Under 1 % on T(CFC-180); up to **+9 %** on T(CFC-1000). The CV ordering that decided A vs B survives. It should be fixed repo-wide and figures regenerated, but on its own it doesn't overturn a conclusion — it just means the *reason* I gave for adding the decisive criterion was inflated ~2× and misattributed to J211.

### The bigger problem, which I think should change how you read all of it

The Edison review found our baseline was wrong (full-record median, on a false "no pre-trigger exists" premise). I confirmed the pre-trigger data is there — ~0.35 ms of it:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/da16fba/notebooks/figures/pre_trigger_window.png?raw=true)

But going further than the review did: **0.35 ms isn't enough to fix it either.** Same 40 drops, same everything, varying only how much of that pre-trigger you average:

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/da16fba/notebooks/figures/baseline_sensitivity.png?raw=true)

| mean T (CFC-180) [CV %] | median | pre 0.05 ms | pre 0.10 ms | pre 0.20 ms | pre 0.30 ms |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| A (1/4) | 1.022 [0.43] | 1.020 [5.05] | 1.140 [2.65] | 1.127 [1.18] | 1.098 [0.71] |
| B (1/2) | 0.996 [0.34] | 1.286 [7.13] | 1.189 [4.77] | 1.153 [3.26] | 1.120 [2.59] |
| C | 0.986 [0.95] | 1.240 [3.94] | 1.332 [2.83] | 1.295 [6.03] | 1.216 [3.96] |
| D | 0.989 [0.49] | 1.365 [5.26] | 1.317 [3.51] | 1.228 [1.71] | 1.194 [0.98] |

The between-arrangement differences the document argues about are **1–3 %**. Changing nothing but the baseline window length moves T by up to **38 %** and reorders the arrangements. The repeatability verdict flips too: under the published baseline all four pass CV ≤ 2 %; at a 0.05 ms pre-trigger baseline all four fail.

So the right conclusion is stronger than "the published baseline was wrong" — it's that **with 0.35 ms of pre-trigger, no baseline estimator is defensible at the 1 % level this comparison needs.** The review's verdict ("none of these — the sweep cannot decide") holds, but its *replacement* numbers are window-dependent in the same way and shouldn't be treated as the corrected truth either. I'd flagged the review's pre-trigger table as independently reproduced; that was too strong — the direction reproduces, the magnitudes depend on the window.

Why so sensitive when peaks are hundreds of G? The numerator is √(x²+y²+z²). Per-axis DC errors don't cancel in a magnitude — they rectify, and they bias numerator and denominator differently.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/da16fba/notebooks/figures/error_magnitude.png?raw=true)

### Is the issue repeatability?

**Short answer: repeatability is what I *ranked* on, and it was the wrong thing to rank on. That's the core of what Edison overturned.**

Your reading of my original recommendation is correct — that *was* the argument I made, and it's why the conclusion didn't hold up.

---

### 1. The physical claim you're describing is real

Mat configuration does change measurement consistency, and that part survives:

- **Arrangement A (1/4 in alone)** drifts hard within its block — raw CH5 input climbs +4.6 %/drop (raw input CV 14.5 % across the 10 drops), and its broadband `T` (CFC-1000) rises monotonically 1.01 → 1.25, Spearman ρ = 1.00. That's a real, deterministic trend, not scatter.
- **Arrangement B (1/2 in alone)** is much flatter broadband (CFC-1000 `T` CV 1.1 % vs A's 6.4 %).
- The **two-sheet interface** is the one clear mechanical repeatability lesson: seated badly it gave input CV 25.7 % in the 5-drop A/B run; seated properly (C/D blocks) 1.7 %. Fewer interfaces = fewer ways to seat wrong.
- All four PU configs fix the felt compaction / near-saturation problem outright. That's a head-room result, and it's solid.

So yes: mats affect consistency, measurably.

### 2. But consistency is a *constraint*, not the objective — and that's the actual finding

Three separate problems with using it to pick a configuration:

**(a) The minimum-variance trap.** If the stack is soft enough that the top vertex essentially rides the base, `T` collapses to a stable near-constant with excellent CV — a perfectly repeatable measurement of nothing. Low variance is exactly what you'd see from the *least* informative configuration. Edison's phrasing: *"No single-specimen statistic can estimate between-geometry sensitivity."* I ranked B first largely on its CVs, and those CVs are compatible with either "clean measurement" or "measuring rigid-body transmission."

**(b) The repeatability ranking itself moved.** My `T` CVs came out of a pipeline that used a full-record median as baseline — a window containing the impact and the whole ringdown. With a proper pre-trigger baseline (the exports *do* carry ~0.39 ms of it):

| CFC-180 `T` CV | A | B | C | D |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| as I published | 0.54 % | **0.34 %** | 0.95 % | 0.49 % |
| pre-trigger baseline | **0.54 %** | 1.18 % | 1.22 % | 2.48 % |

B is no longer the most repeatable — A is. Only the broadband A-vs-B gap survives, and that's A's *drift*, not its noise.

**(c) The design can't attribute the CVs to the mats anyway.** One sequential block per arrangement, fixed order, lag-1 autocorrelation up to 0.98 → **zero arrangement-level degrees of freedom**. Elapsed time, warm-up, sheet history and the 80-minute break between B and C are all confounded with arrangement. So even the differences that do survive can't be pinned on the configuration.

### 3. What the issue actually is

**Discrimination relative to noise** — whether a configuration lets geometry differences show up above print-to-print and drop-to-drop scatter. Roughly `D = (spread between geometries) / sqrt(print variance + drop variance)`.

Scale check on why this is binding: print-to-print scatter in `T` across five copies of the *same* geometry was ~0.72 % CV / 1.95 % spread, and the recent three-structure "different geometries" ranking spanned only 2.3 %. Shrinking drop-to-drop CV from 1.2 % to 0.3 % buys almost nothing against that. (Caveat: that 0.72 % came from a sibling script with the same baseline bug and needs re-running — say the word and I'll do it.)

A has ~20× more absolute structural-band signal; B has lower broadband drift. **Trade-off, not a winner** — and neither has been shown to separate two geometries, because the sweep used one specimen.

### 4. What would settle it

The 20-drop randomized crossover: 2 existing distinct geometries × arrangements A and B, 5 drops per cell, **interleaved in randomized order**, one common trigger level, and capture changed to **≥2 ms pre-trigger + 50–100 ms post-impact**. Prespecify input-conditioned SRS / band-transfer as the outcome. That asks the question directly: does B's lower noise pay for its lower structural-band excitation?

The two capture-setting changes are worth making regardless — the 20 ms window and the ~0.39 ms pre-trigger buffer are what forced every questionable processing choice in that analysis.

### 5. One thing that's a *different* issue, worth separating

If the goal is **energy absorption**, peak-ratio `T` isn't measuring it under any mat configuration. It divides non-simultaneous peaks of a single-axis base channel and a nonlinear tri-axis magnitude, and CFC-180 suppresses ~550 Hz by ~12× — which is a large part of why every specimen ever measured sits within a few percent of 1.0. Fixing repeatability doesn't fix that; changing the metric does (input-conditioned output SRS is the cheapest step, incident/rebound KE loss is the honest one but needs a photogate + the moving mass).

**So: repeatability is necessary, already good enough on every PU config, and not the thing to choose on.** The open question is discrimination, and the sweep as run cannot answer it.

**The rule I've committed** (full version in the doc): primary discriminant is **input pulse width**, because it's a *shape* metric — invariant to overall level, so bedding-in, session drift and trigger changes can't move it. ### The confusion is my fault — they're two independent knobs, not two names for the same thing

- **Arrangement** = the rubber under the carriage. **A = 1/4 in sheet alone**, **B = 1/2 in sheet alone**. A property of the **rig** — it sets how hard and how long the input pulse is.
- **Geometry / specimen** = the printed article being dropped (your two, one bigger). A property of the **article** — it sets how the top vertex responds to that pulse.

Any specimen can be dropped on any arrangement, so they cross:

| | arrangement A (1/4 in) | arrangement B (1/2 in) |
|---|---|---|
| **specimen 1** | 5 drops | 5 drops |
| **specimen 2** | 5 drops | 5 drops |

That's the 20 drops. Nothing extra — just *which specimen is on the tower* is randomized alongside *which sheet is under it*.

**Why it matters:** the whole open question is whether arrangement A or B lets a geometry difference show above the noise. You can't answer that with one specimen, and you can't answer it if the specimen always changes at the same time as the sheet — then the two are perfectly confounded and neither can be blamed for anything. Two specimens crossed with two arrangements is the smallest design that answers it, and it costs you the same 20 drops.

**So the one thing I need to know about your `ABBBBAABA…`:** does `A`/`B` label the **sheet**, the **specimen**, or both-changing-together? All three are runnable, but only the crossed version (sheet and specimen randomized *independently*) answers the question. If it's easiest to think of it as four labels, use `A1, A2, B1, B2` — 5 drops of each, all 20 shuffled together.

### Your settings — all good, and two of my earlier notes were wrong

| setting | verdict |
|---|---|
| 100 ms record | ✅ the biggest single gain here — see below |
| 1.25 MHz / 125,000 samples | ✅ arithmetic checks out exactly; **my "fixed 25,000-sample buffer" guess was wrong** — rate and length are independent |
| 2 % = 2 ms pre-trigger | ✅ consistent, and **better than the 10 % I suggested** — with the record fixed at 100 ms, less pre-trigger buys more ringdown. 2 ms = 2,500 samples is an ample baseline. Withdrawing that suggestion |
| 150 G throughout | ✅ exactly right. Margins on July's *minimum* raw peaks: **10.8× on A, 3.3× on B** |
| 20 fully randomized drops | ✅ **better than my blocks-of-5**, see below |

**Per-drop randomization is a real upgrade, not a variation.** Blocks of 5 leave arrangement confounded with elapsed time and sheet history — the exact defect that gave the July sweep zero arrangement-level degrees of freedom. Randomizing every drop breaks that, gives each drop an independent re-seating of the stack, and drops the guess-alone pass rate from 1-in-6 to ~1-in-10⁶. Generate the key with an RNG and write it down before drop 1.

**One dependency:** if you also want me to call the *specimen* blind, set 1 has to cover all four cells (5 labeled drops each = 20), not just 10 A + 10 B on one specimen — otherwise there's no labeled data to fit a specimen threshold from. ### TL;DR

**C and D aren't "unnecessary" — nothing has been ruled out, because the July sweep had zero arrangement-level degrees of freedom. But C-vs-D specifically is the one contrast in this whole design I can show is undecidable from the input channel, so 20 of your 80 drops would be prepaid abstentions.** Collapse them into one two-sheet arrangement and spend the freed 20 drops on a **second print of the same geometry** — same budget, and the blind test stops being a formality.
