### 1. Why C vs D is the weak link

Pairwise separation on the primary discriminant (CH5 input pulse FWHM), from the adversarial review's independently recomputed per-drop metrics:

| pair | Δ (ms) | separation | ranges overlap? |
|---|--:|--:|:--:|
| A vs B | 0.498 | 22.8 σ | no |
| A vs C | 1.634 | 35.1 σ | no |
| A vs D | 1.501 | 36.9 σ | no |
| B vs C | 1.136 | 25.0 σ | no |
| B vs D | 1.004 | 25.5 σ | no |
| **C vs D** | **0.132** | **2.3 σ** | **yes** |

Every other input feature is worse, not better: input CFC-180 peak **167.29 vs 167.33 G — 0.01 σ**, input CFC-1000 0.45 σ, hardness ratio 1.21 σ, raw peak 2.40 σ. All overlap. There is no input-side feature that sees stacking order.

**Under the rule I already committed, that means every C and D drop gets reported *uncertain*** — the abstention threshold is 3 σ and no July C/D drop reaches 2.9 σ of margin. A midpoint threshold misclassifies 2 of 20 outright.

**And the 2.3 σ that does exist isn't attributable to stacking order anyway.** The C and D blocks ran back-to-back (signals 22–31, 32–41) and drift in *opposite* directions within themselves — C **+0.0124 ms/drop**, D **−0.0120 ms/drop**. Over ten drops that's ±0.12 ms, essentially the entire 0.132 ms difference between the block means. The implied "effect" also depends on which drops you compare: first-3 means differ by 0.053 ms, last-3 by 0.207 ms — a 4× swing from the same data. One block per arrangement, so there's no way to tell stacking order from elapsed time.

So the honest status: **the two-sheet stack is worth keeping; the two *orders* of it are not worth 20 drops.** Keep **1/4 in on top** (your C) — it was the more repeatable of the pair in July (input CFC-180 CV 1.6 % vs 3.8 %, `T` CV 1.2 % vs 2.5 %), which makes sense with the harder sheet as the contact surface.

### 2. Why keep one two-sheet config at all

Three arrangements give input pulses of ≈ **1.64 / 2.14 / 3.2 ms** — a real dose–response axis rather than an A-or-B toggle. If discrimination turns out to be monotone toward the harder end, that tells you to try a *thinner* sheet next; two points can't show you that. Ten drops of C plus ten of D buys you one point on that axis measured twice; ten of C alone buys the same point.

### 3. The freed 20 drops — the highest-value use by a distance

The thing that limits every discrimination claim here isn't the arrangement, it's that **print-to-print scatter is the same size as the between-geometry differences**: five copies of one geometry spanned 1.95 % in `T` (print-defect study), and the three-structure "different geometries" ranking spanned 2.3 %. With one article per geometry, no arrangement can be shown to discriminate geometry, because there's no noise floor to compare against.

Adding a **replicate print of specimen 1** as a third specimen level fixes that inside your existing 80:

| | A (1/4) | B (1/2) | E (1/4 over 1/2) |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| specimen 1 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| **specimen 1b** *(replicate print of 1)* | 5 | 5 | — |
| specimen 2 *(different geometry)* | 5 | 5 | 5 |

8 cells × 5 drops × 2 sets = **80 drops, 8 blind labels — identical budget and identical blind-test structure.** Two of the print-defect articles already exist and serve: `cruela` and `bpx68c`, the two lowest-defect copies.

What it buys: discrimination becomes a *measured ratio* — between-geometry difference ÷ between-print difference, per arrangement. And the blind test becomes informative instead of confirmatory:

> **Failing to separate 1 from 1b while separating 1 from 2 is the success case.** It would show the measurement responds to geometry, not print noise. Separating 1 from 1b as easily as 1 from 2 would show the opposite — and that outcome would invalidate single-print design ranking in the BO campaign, which is exactly the thing worth knowing before committing to it.

### 4. On going back to blocks of 5 — you're right, and I'd withdraw part of what I said earlier

I pushed per-drop randomization last time. That's correct for **arrangement** (a sheet swap) but wrong for **specimen**: changing specimen re-seats the top-vertex accelerometer, and mount re-seating has produced ~2.3 % shifts in `T` — larger than the specimen differences under test. Per-drop specimen randomization would inject that into every single drop. **Blocks of 5 are the right unit here.**

Two things to keep from the randomization argument:

- **Randomize the block order with an RNG and write the key down before drop 1** — which is what you're proposing. Each cell then gets one labeled block and one blind block, separated in time, giving the mount and the stack an independent re-seating per cell. That's the block-level replication every absorber dataset in this repo has lacked, and it's the main reason this design is better than the July sweep regardless of anything else.
- **Set 1's fixed order confounds specimen with time-half.** That's tolerable since set 1 only fits thresholds, but it means the set-2 randomization is doing all the protective work — don't shorten it.

One prediction worth recording now: if the **specimen** call fails while the **arrangement** call succeeds, the lead suspect is mount re-seating, not the pipeline. That would be a first-order result in its own right — it would mean specimens can only be compared within a single mount seating, which constrains how the BO batches have to be sequenced. Log every re-seat so those two explanations stay separable.

### 5. Practical notes

- **~80 × 9 MB ≈ 720 MB** at 1.25 MHz / 125,000 samples. Zip per block and put it on Box.
- **~56 min of dropping** at 42 s/drop, plus 16 block changeovers (sheet swaps + mount re-seats) — realistically a 2–3 h session. Splitting set 1 and set 2 across two sittings is fine and arguably better, as long as the mount isn't disturbed between them beyond the logged block changes.
- Trigger stays at **150 G throughout** — with three arrangements the July minimum raw peaks give 10.8× margin on A, 3.3× on B, 1.6× on the two-sheet stack. That last one is thin; if the two-sheet block trips a missed trigger, note it rather than changing the level mid-run (changing it would confound arrangement with trigger, which is what happened in July).
- Prediction of record, now committed in §7: A and B called with > 5 σ; the two-sheet blocks separated from A and B by > 20 σ; C vs D *not* resolved if you run both.

### 6. Short answer to your two questions

**"Or is arrangement C and D already determined to be unnecessary?"** — No. The two-sheet stack is a useful third point. The two *orders* of it are what I'd drop, and that's a measured claim, not a preference: 0.01 σ on the input peak, 2.3 σ on pulse width entirely accounted for by opposite-sign within-block drift.

**"80 drops, 8 cells, blind order matching?"** — Yes, run 80, and yes to blocks of 5 in RNG-randomized order. Just make the 8th cell a replicate print rather than a second stacking order.

The decidability analysis and the recommended layout are committed as §7 of [`drop-test-ab-blind-protocol.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-ab-blind-protocol.md) — written before any data exists, so the "C/D will come back uncertain" prediction is on the record either way. If you'd rather run all four arrangements anyway, that's entirely reasonable as a belt-and-braces check; I'll run the committed rule as written and report the abstentions.

### First, the thing in your own photo

Zooming your console shot:

> **"DO NOT OPERATE (safety non-functional)"** — taped across the HMI bezel.

Someone already diagnosed this and tagged the machine. It has been operated since. That, plus the fact that the box in your second photo is **unbolted from the machine, sitting on the bench, with its mounting bracket loose and no cable attached**, is the whole answer to "why does it work without the pins": the interlock is not in the circuit. It isn't a tolerance in the design.

### What that box is

Two rubber-grommeted, stepped bores, one per pin, each with a switch behind it. It's the **pin park (stow) station**, and the intended logic is a two-place trapped-key argument:

> A pin can only be in one of two places — in a guide rod, or in the park station. The machine grants the arm/drop permissive **only when both pins are sensed parked**, which is proof neither is in a rod.

Lansmont advertises "programmable safety interlocks" on the [TouchTest Shock 2 controller](https://www.lansmont.com/tts) — note *programmable*, meaning configurable, and therefore also disableable.

### Your question directly

"Removed" splits two ways and the answers are opposite:

| State | Should the machine fire? |
|---|---|
| Both pins out of the rods, **parked in the box** | **Yes** — this is the only state in which it should fire |
| Either pin **not in the box** (in a rod, broken, lost, on the bench) | **No.** It should refuse to arm. One pin missing is as disqualifying as two |

So: **no, the tower should not be functional with either one or both pins missing.** Today it has one pin in existence and an unmounted park station, and it fires. The interlock is defeated.

The pin is a **secondary mechanical hold protecting a person**, not a part the machine is ever meant to load. Shearing one is a near-miss, not a consumable being consumed — and you've now had two.

### Two more things from the photos

**The broken "pin" was a screwdriver shaft.** [The first #92 photo](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/92) is a Klein screwdriver snapped into two pieces. A screwdriver blade is hardened, notch-sensitive tool steel sized for a driver, not for the rod cross-hole — it fails brittle and throws fragments. That's a substitution to stop, not one to reorder. Get the OEM pin part number from Lansmont (a matched pair) before the [MEOrders replacement](https://meorders.byu.edu/order/13142) becomes the standing practice.

**The guide rods are also the brake surfaces.** Lansmont's own description: the brake pistons clamp against the guide rods after impact to prevent secondary impact. So a burr or ovalisation at the cross-hole from the shear event degrades bearing alignment *and* braking. The rods, bushings and brake contact surfaces need inspecting from both breakages before more drops.

### What applies

- **OSHA 1910.147 (LOTO)** — a raised carriage is stored gravitational energy; swapping mats under it is servicing.
- **OSHA 1910.212(a)(1)** — general machine guarding.
- **ISO 14119 / ANSI B11.19** — interlocks must be designed to minimise *reasonably foreseeable defeat*. Unbolting the device is the textbook case.
- **ISO 14119 Annex J, fault masking** — a two-position park station is normally two NC contacts in series; one jumpered or failed-closed contact silently masks the other. Matters if this gets rewired in-house rather than by Lansmont.

### What I'd do

1. **Honour the tag.** Nothing that puts a hand in the impact zone until the interlock is restored and verified.
2. **Inspect the rods** at the cross-holes, plus bushings and brake surfaces, for damage from both events.
3. **Call [Lansmont service](https://www.lansmont.com/contact/service)** with the serial number and ask for four things: the Model 23 / TTS II O&M manual, the safety-pin part number, the park-station wiring/PLC diagram, and a determination of *how* the interlock became inoperative — disabled in PLC config, jumpered in hardware, or never commissioned. Have them verify the permissive on recommissioning rather than trial-and-error in the lab.
4. **Interim procedure for mat changes:** raise → both pins in → **key off and LOTO the console** → change mats → both pins out → both parked → confirm permissive → clear zone → fire. Two-person pin count before every drop. The pin was left in during a repetitive fixed-order swap series, which is the highest-risk task shape for omission errors; a checklist is the standard control.

### One data question worth answering

A drop that struck and sheared a pin isn't a valid data point, and drops after it on a possibly-burred rod carry altered friction and alignment. **Which signal files correspond to the two breakage events?** If the *first* breakage falls inside the 40-drop PU-configuration series, it's a confound for the arrangement comparison in [#86](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/86) / [#94](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/94) — which is already on shaky ground for unrelated reasons. If you can tell me the dates or drop numbers I'll check whether they land in that block.

### Confidence

Lansmont doesn't publish machine manuals. The machine ID, the guide-rod/brake description and the "programmable safety interlocks" feature are sourced. **The specific interlock logic is inferred** from the park-station hardware plus standard practice — the alternative implementation (sensor at the rod rather than at the park station) gives the same answer to your question, but the wiring differs. Confirm against the manual before anyone rewires anything.

**Short answer: yes, but not from the current toolchain — it would require swapping the geometry kernel, and there's a trap where you get a `.step` file that's technically valid and practically useless.**

---

### Why the current pipeline can't do it

Everything I generate comes out of OpenSCAD ([`cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32addaf/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad)). OpenSCAD is a **mesh** kernel (CGAL/Manifold) — internally there is no such thing as "a sphere" or "a cylinder," only triangles. `$fn = 48` on line 59 is exactly that: my "spheres" are 48-sided polyhedra. There is no B-rep to write out, so OpenSCAD has no STEP exporter and structurally can't have one. Same for the `.3mf`/`.stl` artifacts downstream — all tessellated.

### Three ways to actually get STEP, in increasing order of effort and usefulness

**A. Tessellated STEP (mesh → B-rep conversion, e.g. FreeCAD `makeShapeFromMesh`).** ~an hour of work, and I'd advise against it. `t3-prism-struts.stl` is **49,846 facets** — you'd get a STEP with ~50k planar triangular faces. It opens in Onshape/SolidWorks, it's a solid, and it is *worse* to edit than the STL: no cylindrical face to grab, no sphere to change the radius of, no edge to fillet. This is the trap — it satisfies "give me a STEP" while satisfying none of the reason you asked.

**B. Port the model to an OCCT-backed parametric kernel (CadQuery or build123d, both Python).** This is the real answer, ~1–2 days. `export_step()` then emits **true analytic geometry**: a sphere is a spherical face with a radius you can type a new number into, a strut is a cylindrical face, fillets are real fillets. Feasibility on our specific model is good — the SCAD uses only 36 `sphere`, 8 `cylinder`, 7 `cube`, and the booleans, all of which map 1:1 onto OCCT and come out *better* than the mesh version. The one genuinely awkward spot is the 10 `hull()` calls (the teardrop joint blend, the accel-mount skirt, the scaffold pillars) — OCCT has no convex-hull operation, so those would need re-expressing as lofts or revolved tangent profiles. Doable, and arguably cleaner geometry than the hulls, but it's the part that makes this a port rather than a translation.

**C. Drive Onshape directly via FeatureScript / the API** so you get a live **feature tree** (sketches, extrudes, parameters) rather than an imported dumb solid. Heaviest by a wide margin. Worth mentioning only because it's the one option that gives you rollback and named dimensions — a STEP import, no matter how clean, arrives in *any* CAD package with no history, so you'd be direct-editing (move face / offset face / delete face / fillet). Much better than mesh, still not the same as parametric.

### Uploading STEP to Onshape

Essentially free — the plumbing already exists. [`cad/t3-prism/onshape_upload_t3prism.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32addaf/cad/t3-prism/onshape_upload_t3prism.py) uploads via `/api/v6/blobelements/...` with `translate=true` and polls `/api/v6/translations/{id}`. That same endpoint accepts `.step`/`.stp` with no code change beyond the filename list — and it imports as a **solid Part Studio part** rather than a mesh part, which is the good outcome. The existing mm bounding-box readback check would keep working as-is.

### Three caveats worth having on record

1. **STEP can't replace the `.3mf`.** The `.3mf` files aren't geometry containers — they carry the plate layout, per-part extruder routing (PLA→ext 1, TPU→ext 2), filament profiles, and support settings. STEP is geometry only. It would be an *additional* artifact next to the STL/3MF, not a substitute.
2. **The genuinely editable source today is the `.scad`,** not the mesh — 780 lines, fully parametric, diffable in git. For a change like "make the accel pocket 0.2 mm deeper," editing one parameter and re-rendering is strictly easier than hand-editing a STEP. STEP wins for the different case: someone wants to nudge a face in Onshape/SolidWorks without touching code.
3. **Round-tripping is the thing to decide up front.** If anyone hand-edits a STEP, the SCAD immediately goes stale and my next regeneration silently overwrites their change. Whichever way you'd go, we'd need to pick one source of truth.

**If you ever do pull the trigger:** route B (build123d) plus the existing Onshape uploader, emitting `.step` alongside the current STLs. That keeps generation parametric on my side while giving you real B-rep on yours. Not doing anything now, per your note.

### The `hull()` problem — better than I predicted for half of it

I said in the earlier comment that the 10 `hull()` calls were "the part that makes this a port rather than a translation". That was right, but they split into two kinds and one of them turned out to be free:

- **`hull(sphere, sphere)` — the teardrop joint blend.** This has an *exact* closed form: the convex hull of two spheres is the two spheres plus the truncated cone tangent to both, and the tangent circles are analytic. Route B implements exactly that. Not an approximation — the same solid, minus the faceting.
- **`hull(slab, sphere)` — the igloo skirt and bottom key-seat skirt.** No closed form. Both routes use union + fillet instead, which is smoother and lower-stress than a hull but is genuinely a different solid.

Route C's fillet runs on Parasolid and works. Route B's is **off by default**: the exact teardrop meets the shell sphere along a *tangent* circle, and asking OCCT to fillet a tangent edge aborts the process with SIGABRT — not a catchable exception, so `try` doesn't save you.

| | SCAD → STL | route B (OCCT) | route C (Parasolid) |
|---|---|---|---|
| PLA bounding box | 81.19 × 78.65 × 103.81 mm | 81.19 × 78.66 × 103.83 mm | 81.19 × 78.66 × 103.83 mm |
| PLA volume | 18886.3 mm³ | 17146.9 mm³ (−9.2%) | 16675.1 mm³ (−11.7%) |
| TPU volume | 6222.3 mm³ | 6245.5 mm³ (+0.37%) | 6245.3 mm³ (+0.37%) |
| PLA representation | 49,846 triangles | 132 faces | 195 faces |
| TPU representation | 15,324 triangles | 15 faces | 15 faces |

The number I'd point at: **the two independent kernels agree on the TPU volume to 0.003%** (6245.5 vs 6245.3 mm³) and both sit **+0.37% above the mesh**. That sign is the whole check — a `$fn = 48` polyhedron is *inscribed* in the sphere it approximates, so the mesh must under-report, and it does, by about the right amount.

The PLA deltas are the `hull()` substitution, not a bug: route B keeps the exact teardrop and only substitutes the two skirts (−9.2%); route C substitutes the teardrop too (−11.7%). The 2.8% between them is the teardrop bumps.

### Five Onshape API traps, now documented in [`README-parametric.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/README-parametric.md)

1. **`BLEND_BOUNDS` is already exported by `onshape/std/fillet.fs`.** Redeclaring it kills the entire Feature Studio compile and the API reports it as `featureSpecs: []` with **no error message of any kind**. All bounds in the file are `T3_`-prefixed for this reason.
2. **`fSphere` takes its centre as a `Query`, not a `Vector`** — `opSphere` is the one for generated geometry. `fCylinder` and `fCuboid` *do* take vectors, so the inconsistency is easy to trip over.
3. **Operation ids must be contiguous per parent**, which rules out the obvious "solids under `pla`, cutters under `cut`" structure when their creation interleaves.
4. **`POST .../features` needs the flattened `btType` serialization** — the older `{"type": 134, "typeName": ..., "message": {...}}` envelope is rejected with a bare `"Feature has invalid type"`.
5. **`BTMParameterEnum` needs the custom feature's namespace.** Empty is accepted by the API (200 OK) and then fails at regeneration with a bare `featureStatus: ERROR`. Quantity and boolean don't need it.

Debugging note, since this cost the most time: Feature Studio compile failures are *silent*, but the Part Studio's `POST .../featurescript` eval endpoint gives real line-numbered errors. It only accepts a single anonymous function — no `FeatureScript NNNN;` header, no `import` — so to lint the file you rewrite each top-level `function foo(...)` as `const foo = function(...)`, inline them with the feature body, and submit that. Every error above was found that way.

- **`t3_prism_scaffold()` is in neither route.** The 7-per-cable breakaway pillars are print-support geometry, not the specimen. They'd port trivially (truncated cones, no hull problem) if a STEP of the as-printed body is ever wanted.
- **`cables_z_anchor()` dropped** — it only exists to pin a separately-exported STL's bounding box for Bambu's per-part bed placement. Inside one Part Studio both halves already share coordinates. That's why the TPU bbox is 88.84 mm tall here vs 103.83 in the STL.
- **STEP still can't replace the `.3mf`** — plate layout, extruder routing and filament profiles aren't geometry. Unchanged from my earlier answer.
- **`cad/t3-prism/` isn't on `main`** — it lives on `copilot/get-bambu-sliced-print-t3-prism`. These files are standalone ports (they don't read the `.scad` at runtime), but the directory is only complete once that branch lands too.

**Yes — the geometry is still two materials, in both routes. What is *not* multi-material is the print job: no extruder assignment, no filament profiles, and no colour distinction survive into STEP. That data only ever lived in the `.3mf`.**

### The split is real in both routes

Route C builds the two halves as disjoint body lists — [`plaBodies` / `tpuBodies`, `t3-prism.fs:343-345`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs#L343-L345) — and names them at the end via [`setProperty(PropertyType.NAME)`, lines 539-556](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs#L539-L556). Those names make it all the way into the exported STEP, which is the part I actually checked rather than assumed:

```
#3620=MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('t3-prism-struts (PLA)',#3587);
#3621=MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('t3-prism-struts (PLA)',#3588);
#3622=MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('t3-prism-struts (PLA)',#3589);
#3623=MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('t3-prism-cables (TPU)',#3590);
```
— [`step/t3-prism-onshape-featurescript.step`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/step/t3-prism-onshape-featurescript.step), with matching `PRODUCT` entries. One file, four solids, each labelled with its material.

Route B keeps the split as [`build_pla()`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3_prism_b123d.py#L225) / [`build_tpu()`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3_prism_b123d.py#L307) written to [separate files](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3_prism_b123d.py#L400-L403) — but **carried by filename only**: each is a bare `PRODUCT('COMPOUND')` with no per-solid names. Same convention as the STLs.

Solid counts cross-check between the two kernels: **PLA = 3 disconnected solids, TPU = 1 connected net.** That's the tensegrity — the struts don't touch each other — and it's why this can't be printed as two parts and assembled.

| | route B (OCCT) | route C (Parasolid) |
|---|---|---|
| PLA solids | 3 (`t3-prism-struts.step`) | 3, named `t3-prism-struts (PLA)` |
| TPU solids | 1 (`t3-prism-cables.step`) | 1, named `t3-prism-cables (TPU)` |
| material carried by | filename | solid name inside the file |

The `part` enum is also still there and still first-class — [`Both (PLA struts + TPU cables)` / `Struts only (PLA)` / `Cables only (TPU)`, lines 80-88](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs#L80-L88), and `part=STRUTS` was one of the three parameter kinds driven through the live API in the earlier run.

And the reason multi-material matters at all is intact: [`useCaptiveCore`, line 251](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs#L251) — TPU core bonded to the inner PLA shell wall at [zero clearance by design, line 327](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs#L327). Interlocked, so it has to be co-printed.

### Three things that do *not* survive

1. **No colour distinction.** All four solids in the route-C STEP route through four `STYLED_ITEM`s to a *single* `COLOUR_RGB` — `#3619`, Onshape's default light blue. The FeatureScript sets only `PropertyType.NAME`, never `APPEARANCE`. Slicers key off object identity rather than colour so nothing breaks, but you don't get the visual PLA/TPU split you get from the `.3mf`.
2. **No material entity.** Zero `MATERIAL_DESIGNATION` / `PRODUCT_MATERIAL` in any of the three STEPs. Neither Parasolid nor OCCT writes one here, so there's no density → no mass properties, and nothing a slicer could auto-map to an extruder.
3. **No extruder routing or filament profiles.** Unchanged from my first answer, and this is the substantive one. That lives in `Metadata/model_settings.config` + `project_settings.config` *inside* the `.3mf`, written by [`patch_mm_extruder.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32addaf/cad/t3-prism/patch_mm_extruder.py) — which exists precisely because Bambu's CLI puts every part on extruder 1 and ignores `--load-filament-ids`. STEP has no equivalent field.

### What that means in practice

Import the route-C STEP into Bambu Studio and you get four correctly-named parts, all on one extruder — you'd reassign PLA→1 / TPU→2 yourself, exactly as the `.3mf` patch does programmatically. The names make that assignment unambiguous, which is more than the mesh path gave you (there, the only signal is which file it came from). The `.3mf` remains the print artifact; STEP remains a geometry artifact alongside it.

### Two cheap fixes if you want them (not done — say the word)

- Add `PropertyType.APPEARANCE` per half in `t3-prism.fs` so the STEP carries two distinct colours, plus `PropertyType.MATERIAL` for real mass properties in Onshape. ~10 lines, no geometry change.
- Give route B's export per-solid labels so its STEPs are self-describing like route C's, and commit the combined `t3-prism.step` — [line 403](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/ffcfae9/cad/t3-prism/t3_prism_b123d.py#L403) writes it but only the two halves were committed.

### What's actually happening

`accel_mount_local()` springs the igloo crown straight off the housing body's **top rim** (`bz1 = pocket_z`). The pocket mouth is flush with the body's front face (`bx1 == accel_pocket_x()`), so the pocket's top-front edge *is* the body's top-front edge — and any convex cap hulled from that rim has **zero** thickness there by construction. Not tolerance, not faceting; it falls straight out of the geometry.

Ray-casting down through the pocket footprint on the rendered `part="struts"` STL:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| roof at the open (cable-exit) mouth | **0.085 mm** | 2.085 mm |
| roof at the crown | 2.99 mm | 4.99 mm |
| roof area under 1.0 mm | 12% | 0% |
| roof area under 0.4 mm (= 2 × 0.2 mm layers) | 4% | 0% |

**Your read on the bottom vertices is right, and it's the same root cause seen from the other side.** The bottom key-seats skip the dome entirely — `accel_mount_local(domed = false)` caps them with a plain `accel_flat = 2.0 mm` slab, uniform everywhere. No taper, nothing to feather out. That's exactly why they look fine.

### The fix

A new `accel_roof` (default **2.0 mm**, deliberately = `accel_flat`) carries the straight-walled body that far past the pocket ceiling *before* the crown starts — on the **domed top mounts only**. The flat bottom key-seats keep `bz1 == pocket_z` and are geometrically unchanged. So the top mounts now get the same guaranteed minimum cap as the bottom seats you signed off on, with the igloo still on top of it.

Ported identically to all three:

| file | parameter | kernel |
|---|---|---|
| [`t3-prism.scad`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/0f3300c/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad) | `accel_roof` | CGAL |
| [`t3-prism.fs`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/0f3300c/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.fs) | `accelRoof` — a real field in the feature dialog | Parasolid |
| [`t3_prism_b123d.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/0f3300c/cad/t3-prism/t3_prism_b123d.py) | `ACCEL_ROOF` | OCCT |

One thing that made this land cleanly: the body top *and* the crown-sphere centre both rise by `accel_roof`, so the crown/box intersection circle is unchanged (r = 3.95 mm, still comfortably inside the 8.2 × 10.2 mm top face). No new tangency for Parasolid's fillet or OCCT's union to choke on — which is the trap the earlier `hull()` substitutions kept hitting.

| block | signals | **call** | | block | signals | **call** |

Arrangements `B A C B C A A B C`, specimens `2 1 1 1 3 3 2 3 2`. All nine cells used exactly once — and that bijection was *not* enforced; arrangement and specimen were called independently and it came out consistent, which is itself a check.

**Confidence, honestly split:** the **arrangement** row is as close to certain as this gets (no drop within 0.17 ms of a threshold, blocks group 3/3/3). The **specimen** row is solid for A and C. **If one thing is wrong it's blocks 1 and 4 swapped** (B1 ↔ B2) — the two nominally identical prints, on the one arrangement whose blocks straddle a session break. Two routes say block 1 = B2, one says B1.

**Also: Signal 12 is not a valid drop.** Base-plate raw peak 108.6 G — *below* the 150 G trigger — impact at 9.9 ms with a 10 ms pulse. Excluded, so block 3 has 4 drops. Worth knowing whether that was an aborted drop or a spurious trigger.

### ⚠️ Set 2 is two sessions, at different drop energy

Not a complaint — it changed how the analysis had to work, and you'll want it in the log:

| | signals | when | input Δv |
|---|---|---|--:|
| set 1 | 1–50 | 08-04 00:15 → 03:02 | 5.47 ± 0.26 m/s |
| set 2 **block 1** | 1–5 | 08-04 03:12 (10 min after set 1) | 5.35 ± 0.03 m/s |
| set 2 blocks 2–9 | 7–46 | 08-05 23:42 → 08-06 00:40 | **4.22 ± 0.64 m/s** |

That's ~22 % lower impact velocity two days later (≈ 43 in equivalent vs 60 in). Absolute G levels don't transfer across it — set-2 arrangement A reads 292–303 G where set-1 A read 354–369 G. The pre-registration's choice of a *shape* discriminant (pulse width) is untouched by this, which is the one thing that went exactly to plan. **Please log drop height per session** — it's the single missing piece of metadata that cost the most here.

### The unexpected finding: a big secondary event at 17–35 ms

Only visible because you went to 100 ms. Every record has a second burst on the top vertex, 17–35 ms after impact — the band-limited envelope rises **9–15 dB above** its post-impact level on arrangement C, raw CH4 hitting 400–870 G. It's **not** the carriage (the base plate reads 11–51 G at the same instant, 2–5 % of its primary) and **not** the brake catch (video put that at +76–89 ms). My first ringdown fit ran straight across it and returned *negative damping*, which is how I found it.

Its delay scales in proportion to impact velocity — the 22 % energy drop shortens it 13–19 % — so it's ballistic: the top vertex separates at ~0.1–0.17 m/s and lands back. Which makes

**`e_rebound = g·t_second / (2·Δv)` ≈ 0.019 (spec 2) · 0.022–0.024 (spec 1) · 0.028–0.030 (spec 3)**

a dimensionless specimen constant that holds across all three arrangements *and* across the session/energy change — the first quantity in this program that transfers between sessions.

### Repeatable? Yes — that's not the constraint

Within-cell CV over 5 drops (set 1): `T` is **0.12–0.48 %** in 8 of 9 cells; input ~1 %. The two worse cells have causes, not noise: **A3** carries a bedding-in transient (its first drop reads 1.863 ms FWHM vs 1.66–1.72 for the rest, after a 7-min pause) and **C1/C2** drift upward through the block. Both argue for the 2-drop discarded warm-up already in the SOP.

Between-specimen SNR, and the hard contrast (**specimen 1 vs 2 — same model, differing only in print defects**):

| feature | | A (1/4) | **B (1/2)** | C (two-sheet) |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **secondary-event time** | SNR | 11.9 | **29.8** | 13.8 |
| | \|d\| 1v2 | 10.1 | **18.6** | 7.8 |
| `e_rebound` | \|d\| 1v2 | 3.0 | **11.9** | 7.1 |
| `f_n` (ringdown) | \|d\| 1v2 | 1.7 | 2.9 | 2.1 |

| | \|d\| 1v2 | 0.75 | 1.50 | 3.02 |

**Arrangement B (1/2 in alone) is the more informative one** — best on every feature that carries specimen information, and among the most repeatable. A is a close second; C is weakest and least settled.

Note this is the same recommendation I made in July that Edison overturned — but the review's objection is now answered rather than repeated. July ranked B on **repeatability**, which was the minimum-variance trap. This ranks B on **measured discrimination across three specimens**, which is the quantity that matters and which the single-specimen sweep couldn't estimate. Same answer; only this one is evidence.

**And the uncomfortable part:** `T` is the *weakest* discriminator in the dataset. It spans 0.88–3.50 % across the three specimens — the same order as the ~1.95 % print-to-print scatter the defect study measured — while the secondary-event timing spans 40–53 %. Two readings I can't separate: either `t_second` is genuinely more geometry-sensitive, or it's tracking something correlated with the specimen swap. The replicate-print cell settles it.

**Print defects are detectable.** Specimens 1 and 2 separate at \|d\| = 3.0–18.6, and the blind set reproduced the 1-vs-2 ordering independently on A and C. That's a warning rather than a reassurance: it means a single print carries noise the same size as the design effects you'd be optimizing over.

### Ringdown decay — fitted, with an honest caveat

300–900 Hz band, Hilbert envelope, log-linear fit, `f_n` from the analytic phase slope (sub-bin resolution):

| cell | f_n (Hz) | ζ (%) | r² | | cell | f_n (Hz) | ζ (%) | r² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| A1 | 528 ± 9 | 6.01 ± 1.07 | 0.85 | | B3 | 518 ± 1 | 7.19 ± 0.61 | 0.91 |
| A2 | 552 ± 2 | 5.66 ± 0.49 | 0.89 | | C3 | 504 ± 6 | 7.84 ± 0.77 | 0.91 |
| A3 | 450 ± 22 | 11.40 ± 1.66 | 0.90 | | B1 | 383 ± 39 | 7.20 ± 0.53 | **0.48** |
| C2 | 510 ± 26 | 6.18 ± 1.51 | 0.75 | | B2 | 317 ± 2 | 11.25 ± 0.59 | **0.66** |
| C1 | 406 ± 84 | 6.95 ± 9.70 | 0.73 | | | | | |

Where r² ≥ 0.85, **ζ = 5.7–11.4 % and repeats to 0.5–1.7 % absolute** — usable damping numbers, the first in this program. Where it's poor (B1, B2, C1) the ζ is not a damping ratio; C1's 140 % CV is the estimator telling you the envelope isn't one decaying mode. `f_n` isn't trustworthy yet either — it ranges 317–552 Hz and its specimen ordering flips between arrangements, so it's partly tracking the input spectrum.

**The blocker isn't record length — it's the hop.** 98 ms was meant to buy ~50 cycles at 550 Hz; it buys 5–13 ms (3–7 cycles) because the secondary event re-excites the structure. A longer record won't help. **Restraining the specimen to the plate would** — and that's the highest-value fixture change on the table. Though it's in genuine tension with the fact that the hop is currently the best discriminator you have, so it's worth doing on 2 blocks and comparing rather than deciding by default.

§2 step 4 says abstain within 3 σ of the threshold with σ "pooled". Arrangement C's *class* σ is 0.233 ms — 4× A's — because specimen 3 shortens the C pulse to 2.70 ms while 1 and 2 sit at 3.15 ms. ### It's not a fillet failing — it falls out of the `hull()` substitution

The crown radius is `min(pocketX + wall, pocketY + 2·wall) / 2` = **4.1 mm**, and the crown sphere's centre sits at `roof + accelDome − rcrown`. At `accelDome = 10` its underside is **1.8 mm above** the housing roof. Exact, not a tolerance.

The reason it looks like a bug rather than an obvious input error: **OpenSCAD cannot show it.** The `.scad` builds the crown as `hull(top rim, sphere)`, which stays connected for *any* dome height — you'd get an ugly spire, not a floating ball. Parasolid and OCCT have no convex hull, so both ports use a plain union, and the sphere just leaves.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/493e206/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism-constraint-dome.png?raw=true)

*OCCT at `ACCEL_DOME = 10 mm` with the new check bypassed — a second, independent kernel reproducing your Parasolid screenshot.*

### Two layers, because enumerating the failures is a losing game

**Closed-form guards**, each naming its own limit. In the dialog these are `regenError`s that highlight the offending field; `ValueError` in build123d; `assert()` in the SCAD where the failure is representation-independent, `echo("WARNING: …")` where the SCAD is genuinely fine and only the ports break.

| check | limit at S0 | what goes wrong past it |
|---|---|---|
| `accelDome < 2 · rcrown` | **8.2 mm** | the crown floats free — your screenshot |
| `accelHover < r(1 + √(1−0.4²))` | 11.28 mm | key-seat + skirt lift clear of the joint sphere |
| `2 · jointOuterR < R√3` | 49.96 mm | the three struts fuse — it stops being a tensegrity |
| bore length `< R√3 − jointOuterR` | 44.08 mm | a cable bore tunnels into the **next** vertex |

The bore one is the find. The default bores already run **41.94 mm against a 44.08 mm limit** — a `Radial gap` of 2.1 mm instead of 1.0 silently drills a hole clean through a neighbouring joint shell, and the model still looks right. That was 2.14 mm of margin nobody knew was there.

Warnings (non-fatal, geometry still builds) cover the near-tangent crown seat, `accelRoof` under two 0.2 mm layers, and any wall under two 0.4 mm extrusions.

**A topological invariant** behind all of them, which is the part that catches what I didn't think of: whatever you type, the PLA half is exactly **3 solids** and the TPU net exactly **1**. That isn't a heuristic — *"three mutually disconnected compression members"* is the definition of a tensegrity, so a model failing it is not the structure. Pushing `ACCEL_DOME = 10 mm` past the closed-form check returns **6** (3 struts + 3 orphaned crowns), which is exactly how the picture above was made.

### A sixth Onshape API trap for the list

The REST layer **does not return regen message text.** `POST .../features` gives you `featureState: {featureStatus: ERROR}` and nothing else; `GET .../features` drops `featureMessages` entirely. Those strings only ever reach the browser client. So a script can prove a guard *fired* but not *what it said* — to check the wording you evaluate the formatting through `POST .../partstudios/.../featurescript`, which does return strings. That's how I confirmed the messages render as `8.2 mm` and not `8.199999999`.

### On your other point, @me-madsen

You're right that this isn't sketches-and-extrudes. It's one custom feature, so you get named parameters, rollback and history but not a tree you can step through operation by operation. Getting that would mean emitting `newSketch`/`opExtrude` calls per operation instead of `opSphere`/`fCylinder` — the parameters would then be sketch dimensions you could grab in the graphics area. Real work, and it'd trade away the closed-form guards above for constraint solving. Happy to scope it if that's the direction you want.

Flagging rather than guessing.
- `accelSink` has **no hard guard**. I chased one and it doesn't exist: the housing box is wider than the joint sphere in plan, so it stays connected at any sink depth. The topological check covers it if I'm wrong.

| Public share link that allows uploads? | Not with a regular shared link. Box has no upload-enabled shared link — use a **File Request link** instead, which is exactly this. |
| Separate account needed? | Not for the people uploading. Someone with a Box Business+ account (BYU Box qualifies) must own the folder and create the File Request; uploaders need nothing. |
| Tied to an email? | No, unless you add an email field to the form or your Box admin enforces "require login." Uploaders are anonymous by default. |

### Why a plain shared link won't work

Box shared-link permissions top out at view/download. Upload rights come only from being a **collaborator** on the folder (the `Viewer Uploader` role is the upload-capable one), and collaborators must be signed-in Box users. Box support states plainly that there are no upload-only shared links — [Folder and Account Sharing Settings](https://support.box.com/hc/en-us/articles/360043696814-Folder-and-Account-Sharing-Settings), [Want to send a link out for upload only](https://support.box.com/hc/en-us/community/posts/360049226233-Want-to-send-a-link-out-for-upload-only).

### What does work: Box File Request

[File Request](https://support.box.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045304813-Using-File-Request-to-get-Content-from-Anyone) generates a public URL pointing at a drag-and-drop upload form bound to one folder:

- **No Box account, no login** for whoever uploads — they open the link and drop files in.
- Uploads land directly in the target folder; uploaders **cannot see** what else is in it (one-way drop box, which is the behavior you want on a shared lab machine).
- Large files supported (5 GB+, plan-dependent) — fine for drop-tower video.
- Optional metadata fields (e.g. "run ID", "operator", "specimen"), each toggleable required/optional. This is where an email field *would* come from if you wanted one; it isn't there by default.
- Link can be disabled or given an expiration date.

Two caveats worth checking on the BYU side before committing:

1. **Creator must be folder owner/co-owner** on a Business plan or higher. BYU Box is enterprise, so this should be fine, but external collaborators can't create File Requests — the form has to be made by the BYU account that owns the folder.
2. **Admins can force login org-wide.** If BYU OIT has that toggle on, every File Request form requires a Box login and Box captures/validates the uploader's email — which would defeat the anonymous-upload goal and put you back to needing an account. Worth a quick test at [box.byu.edu](https://box.byu.edu) before wiring anything up.

### On "dedicated/separate account/login"

Given File Request, the drop-tower computer in CB 152A doesn't need a Box login at all — no credentials stored on a shared lab machine, nothing to rotate when a student graduates. That's a meaningful security win over installing Box Drive with someone's NetID signed in.

If you *do* want a persistent login (e.g. Box Drive mapped as a drive letter so uploads are pure file-copy with no browser), don't tie it to a personal NetID: [BYU deactivates Box accounts 14 days after you leave the university](https://box.byu.edu) and explicitly recommends moving shared/research data to a **service account**. A service account, not a second Windows account, is the right unit here — Windows accounts don't affect Box ownership.

### One thing to flag about the read-back path

The plan was to hand me a public share link so I can pull the files. That part is less clean than the upload part:

- A **folder** share link renders as a JavaScript app. `curl`/`WebFetch` on it returns the login/preview HTML, not a file listing — so I can't enumerate a folder from a public link alone. Programmatic folder access needs the Box API with a developer token plus a `BoxApi: shared_link=...` header.
- A **file** share link can be turned into a direct-download URL (`https://byu.app.box.com/shared/static/<hash>.<ext>`), which `curl` fetches fine. Direct links only exist for individual files, and only when access is "People with the link."

So the workable pattern is: uploads via one File Request link → you (or a script) grab per-file direct links for the runs you want analyzed → paste those into the issue. If this becomes routine, a Box service account + API token stored as a repo secret would let me list the folder myself, which is the version that actually scales.

### 1. The filter bug: confirmed, and my correction was itself slightly wrong

The audit **confirms** the stage error. `2.0775` is the −3 dB corner of *each* 2-pole pass; the familiar "CFC-180 → 300 Hz" is the corner of the forward-backward *pair*. Our code hands the pair number to scipy's single-pass `Wn` and then squares it anyway.

But it corrects the arithmetic I used. The exact pair corner is not `1.65 × CFC` — it's

$$f_{-3\,\mathrm{dB,pair}} = (\sqrt{2}-1)^{1/4} \times 2.0775 \times \mathrm{CFC} = 1.6666604 \times \mathrm{CFC}$$

which gives exactly 100.0 and 300.0 Hz for CFC-60/180, matching ISO 6487:2015 Table 2's $F_N$. The 1.65 I divided by is a tabulated corridor value, not the Appendix C ratio. So my equivalent-class labels were off by a couple of counts:

| labelled | J211 pair −3 dB | ours | error | equivalent class (I said) | **(actual)** |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| CFC-60 | 100.00 Hz | 80.22 Hz | −19.78 % | CFC-49 | **CFC-48** |
| **CFC-180** | **300.00 Hz** | **240.67 Hz** | **−19.78 %** | CFC-146 | **CFC-144** |
| CFC-600 | 1000.00 Hz | 802.24 Hz | −19.78 % | CFC-486 | **CFC-481** |
| CFC-1000 | 1666.67 Hz | 1323.70 Hz | −20.58 % | CFC-802 | **CFC-794** |

And the number that started this whole thread — the "roughly 12× at 550 Hz" that justified adding the CFC-1000 criterion in §3.2 — is **5.68×** under a correct J211 CFC-180, against 12.3× from our filter. Confirmed verbatim.

I re-derived all of it independently ([`verify_report_numbers.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/6445221/edison-trajectories/j211-audit/verify_report_numbers.py), runs in a second, no data needed) — every digit in both of the report's tables reproduces:

```
(sqrt(2)-1)**0.25 * 2.0775 = 1.6666604   (report: 1.6666604)
butter(2, 2.0775*CFC) == Appendix C recurrence: True
 550 Hz | J211 CFC-180 0.1761 (5.68x) | repo CFC-180 0.0813 (12.3x)
```

One thing I hadn't noticed: **J211 §9.4.1 mandates Appendix C only for CFC-60 and CFC-180.** CFC-600 and CFC-1000 are defined by a *response corridor*, so applying the same shape there is a defensible choice but needs a numerical corridor check rather than being asserted from the function name.

### 2. Two things I asserted that the audit refutes

**"Standards require a baseline window."** — **REFUTED.** Neither SAE J211-1:1995 nor ISO 6487:2015 specifies a baseline window or a minimum quiet pre-event duration anywhere. §9.4.2 only says software *should* determine zero levels rather than assume no drift, and warns that per-axis offset errors corrupt resultants in ways that are hard to detect. Appendix C's 10 ms is **endpoint-padding** guidance, not a zero-estimation rule — I had been conflating the two. A full-record median isn't prohibited by any clause; it's just indefensible on a record containing the impact.

**"Transmissibility."** — **REFUTED.** The ratio of two non-concurrent CFC-filtered peaks, one of them a tri-axial norm, isn't defined as transmissibility in J211, ISO 6487, ISO 18431-2/-4, ASTM D3332, ASTM D7136, or MIL-STD-810 Method 516. The recommended label is *CFC-filtered output/input peak-acceleration ratio*. Using "transmissibility" implies a frequency-response function we haven't estimated, which is exactly the overreach the #86 review flagged.

ISO 5348:2021 as the mounting standard (not ISO 5347, now withdrawn in favour of ISO 16063) is **confirmed**.

### 3. It raised my own recommendation on me

I told you **≥ 2 ms pre-trigger**. That's under-specified and the audit says so: 2 ms is 1.1 cycles at 550 Hz, and a numerical impulse-response check puts correct CFC-180 above 1 % of peak out to **~3.3 ms** and above 0.1 % to ~4.8 ms. The filter's own settling is longer than the window I proposed.

> **≥ 10 ms of verified quiet pre-trigger, preferably 20 ms**, plus 50–100 ms post-impact or enough to show complete decay.

Related: scipy's default `filtfilt` padlen is **9 samples — 7.2 µs at 1.25 MHz**, against Appendix C's "copy at least 10 ms at each end." For an impact starting 0.35 ms into the record that is not adequate, and padding can't manufacture data that wasn't captured.

### 4. What this means for the published numbers

The audit's verdict on the ratio-cancellation argument is harsher than mine. I said the wrong filter "largely cancels in a ratio." It says that holds only if numerator and denominator have proportionally identical spectra, waveforms and filter-induced peak shifts — not true when the peaks occur at different times with different modal content. My "<1 % on T(CFC-180)" stands as an *empirical result on those 40 files*, not a general guarantee. (It could not check that: the audit was scoped to standards, so the waveforms weren't attached — flagged in the report itself.)

Flagged for recompute after the filter fix: every CFC-filtered peak G, every pulse width, every band-energy fraction, every Δv, every CFC-1000 ratio.

**Bottom line, in the auditor's words:** *correct the filter code, but do not use the existing 0.35 ms pre-trigger records to defend 1–3 % absorber or geometry rankings.* That is the same conclusion the #86 adversarial review and my notebook reached by two other routes, now with a third independent one — and none of the three is the original analysis.

Three independent passes now agree the switch shouldn't be trusted, each killing a different link:

### Prior art

- **The HMS code** ([0300-0900-0002-0001](https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/h2/troubleshooting/hmscode/0300_0900_0002_0001)) is "extrusion motor overloaded — extruder clogged or filament stuck in toolhead." Bambu's [extruder motor overload guide](https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/h2/troubleshooting/extruder-motor-overload) lists exactly your suspects: clog remnants, external feed-path resistance (tangles, spool tension, sharp bends), and volumetric speed set too high for the hotend.
- **Jams during AMS runout switches are a known failure mode.** The retract/splice cycle can leave a ground or broken segment in the PTFE path; Bambu has a dedicated guide for [removing broken filament from AMS 2 Pro / H2D tubes](https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/h2d/troubleshooting/remove-broken-filament-in-ams-2-pro-and-h2d-tubes). Worn PTFE tubes and loosened/worn feeder gears causing feed resistance and grinding are also well documented ([AMS troubleshooting guide](https://www.adpindustries.com/blog/bambu-lab-ams-troubleshooting-guide/)).
- **White PLA is notoriously the most clog- and under-extrusion-prone color.** Titanium-dioxide pigment (~200 nm particles, ~20× larger than carbon black, at high loading) raises melt viscosity, so white needs more temperature/pressure to flow at the same rate ([Simplify3D forum: White PLA problems](https://forum.simplify3d.com/viewtopic.php?t=2527), [Hackaday: watch out for white filament](https://hackaday.com/2022/12/06/psa-watch-out-for-white-filament/)). A marginal restriction (partial clog, feed drag) that black tolerates will show as under-extrusion with white.

### Likely sources of error, ranked

1. **The white PLA roll itself** — moisture (white is worst for hiding it; wet PLA gives exactly the rough, porous strut surfaces in your photos) and/or a ground/damaged section left over from the jam event.
2. **Residual partial clog in the left nozzle/heatbreak** from the original jam. Pulling filament out doesn't clear charred residue; higher-viscosity white reveals the restriction, lower-viscosity black doesn't.
3. **AMS slot 2 feed resistance** — worn PTFE, debris in the feeder from the runout switch, or spool drag adding back-pressure. Your slot-swap experiment is the right single-variable test to separate this from (1).

On the directional gaps: with black printing fine, belts/motion are unlikely culprits. Marginal flow tends to fail first on walls where seams/overhangs align and where flow demand spikes after direction changes — so axis-correlated gaps are consistent with borderline under-extrusion, not a kinematics fault.

### Applicable solutions

- **Dry the white PLA** (55–60 °C, 8–12 h) before drawing conclusions from the swap test — otherwise a wet roll fails in every slot and mimics an AMS fault.
- **Cold-pull / hot-clean the left nozzle** and inspect the heatbreak for charred residue per the [overload guide](https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/h2/troubleshooting/extruder-motor-overload).
- **Give white its own filament profile**: +5–10 °C nozzle temp, reduced max volumetric speed, and rerun flow-dynamics calibration for that roll specifically.
- **Inspect the slot-2 path**: cut out any gouged filament, check the AMS-to-printer PTFE for wear/kinks, and look for bite marks on filament exiting the feeder (gear slippage).
- Prevention: Bambu suggests periodic PTFE replacement for heavy AMS use, and trimming/inspecting filament ends after any runout-splice jam.

If the black-in-slot-2 print comes out clean and white-in-slot-3 reproduces the defects, dry the white roll and retest before condemning it — that final test discriminates "bad roll" from "wet roll."

### How well can per-specimen energy absorption be measured with this setup? Honest answer: it can't — but two good proxies can, and here's the full map ✅

- [x] Re-read the ABC×123 setup/data, the blind-analysis doc, and both Edison audits
- [x] Review what the rig can and cannot determine about per-specimen energy absorption
- [x] Explain every metric in use (`T`, `f_n`, ringdown ζ, `e_rebound`, Δv, SRS, …) with equations and validity conditions
- [x] Verify and link source papers/textbooks/standards
- [x] Commit the full write-up: [`docs/drop-tower-energy-absorption-review.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/3ea494c/docs/drop-tower-energy-absorption-review.md) (`3ea494c`)

Everything below is the condensed version; the doc carries the same content with full equations, validity checklists, and the complete reading list.

---

### 1. What the rig physically is — and why that bounds the question

Follow the energy of one drop. The plate + specimen falls 60 in and arrives at Δv ≈ 5.47 m/s, so `E_in = ½MΔv² ≈ 15·M` joules — and **M, the falling mass, is not logged anywhere**, so nothing in this program is currently expressible in joules. That energy then goes: overwhelmingly into **PU-mat hysteresis** (that's what turns a 5.5 m/s arrest into a 2–3 ms, few-hundred-G pulse); some into the **tower** (normally small — but the #92 pin break showed a damaged tower silently eating 26–38 %, more than everything specimen-related combined); and only a small slice into the **specimen**, which rings elastically at ~500–550 Hz for 5–13 ms and hops off the plate at 2–3 % of impact speed.

The specimen never enters large deformation. So this rig is a **shock-transmission screen** — the geometry of ASTM D1596 cushion testing, with the T3 prism riding as the "product" — not an energy-absorption test. That's the right instrument for what it's been doing (repeatability, discrimination, the 18/18 blind key), but it means:

- **Not measurable from this data, by any reprocessing:** joules absorbed by the specimen, and *crashworthiness-sense* energy absorption — work done through strut buckling / snap-through / densification, which is what a T3 prism designed as an absorber is actually *for*. The current test never loads that regime.
- **Measurable per specimen, now demonstrated repeatable:** two genuine energy-*dissipation* proxies (ζ and `e_rebound`), a modal readout (`f_n`), and a transmission level (`T`). These are defensible optimization signals for "attenuate/dissipate shock," but they probe the small-strain linear regime only.

### 2. The metrics, one by one

**Δv (input)** — `∫a_base dt` over the pulse = the plate's arrest velocity. Free rig-health gauge (5.4–5.5 m/s healthy from 60 in). Ties to energy only through the unlogged M; also processing-dependent (per the J211 audit), so a monitor, not a calibration.

**Pulse width τ (FWHM)** — duration of the base pulse at half peak. A *shape* metric, invariant to level — which is why it survived an unlogged 22 % energy change and carried the blind classification. `f_n·τ ≈ 0.9–1.7` here puts the specimen near the SRS peak: it neither isolates nor strongly amplifies; it rides the pulse and rings after.

**`T` ("transmissibility" — a misnomer)** — ratio of CFC-filtered peak output (tri-axis magnitude, top vertex) to peak input (base). The two peaks aren't simultaneous and the ratio matches no standard's definition of transmissibility (J211, ISO 6487, ISO 18431, ASTM D3332/D7136, MIL-STD-810 all checked in the Edison audit) — call it a *filtered peak-acceleration ratio*. It's also filter- and baseline-sensitive, and empirically the **weakest** discriminator in the dataset. True transmissibility is a frequency-response function `|H(f)|` with coherence — it needs averaged/broadband excitation (shaker or tap test), which one transient drop can't provide.

**SRS** — the standard language for "what does this shock do to hardware": an array of imagined single-DOF oscillators rides the measured pulse; plot each one's peak response vs its natural frequency. [Irvine's free tutorial](https://www.vibrationdata.com/tutorials2/srs_intr.pdf) is the best entry point; ISO 18431-4 / MIL-STD-810 M516 define it. An input-conditioned output SRS remains the recommended successor to `T`.

**`f_n` (ringdown frequency)** — after the pulse the specimen vibrates freely at `f_n ≈ (1/2π)√(k_eff/m_eff)`, estimated from the Hilbert-phase slope of the band-passed ringdown. The tensegrity-specific payoff: **`f_n` is a prestress gauge** — natural frequencies of tensegrities shift measurably with member self-stress ([Ashwear & Eriksson 2014](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260156059_Natural_frequencies_describe_the_pre-stress_in_tensegrity_structures)), demonstrated by modal-hammer tests on a tensegrity *simplex*, i.e. the T3 topology ([Appl. Sci. 10:8733, 2020, open access](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/10/23/8733)). So per-specimen `f_n` drift reads out print tension / mount health, and possibly a design variable. Current caveat: our fits ranged 317–552 Hz with orderings that flip across arrangements — still contaminated by input spectrum and multiple modes. Fixing arrangement B helps; a bench tap test (specimen suspended, no tower) would give the clean reference.

**ζ (ringdown decay fit)** — model the decay as `x(t) ≈ A·e^(−ζω_n t)·cos(ω_d t+φ)`; fit a line to the log of the Hilbert envelope; slope = −ζω_n. Classical equivalents: log decrement `δ = 2πζ/√(1−ζ²)`, quality factor `Q = 1/(2ζ)`, and the energy statement that makes it *the* per-specimen dissipation metric in our data — **fraction of vibrational energy dissipated per cycle = 1−e^(−2δ) ≈ 4πζ**. At our ζ ≈ 6–8 % and f_n ≈ 520 Hz that's ~50–60 % of the vibrational energy gone *every cycle*, envelope time-constant ≈ 4–5 ms — exactly why the usable ringdown is only 5–13 ms. Validity rules: single-mode band, window ending before the secondary event, and **a ζ with poor r² is not a damping ratio** — it's the estimator telling you the envelope isn't one decaying mode (B1/B2/C1 in the current data). ![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/95b7b07/data/drop-tests/abc123-blind/figures/04_ringdown.png?raw=true)

**`t_second` and `e_rebound` (the hop)** — the top vertex separates and lands back 17–35 ms after impact; ballistic flight gives separation velocity `g·t_second/2`, and `e_rebound = g·t_second/(2Δv)` is mathematically identical to measuring a coefficient of restitution from time-between-bounces — a classic technique ([Bernstein, *Am. J. Phys.* 45:41 (1977), free PDF](https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-pdf/45/1/41/11809656/41_1_online.pdf)). Energy view: the hop returns only `e² ≈ 0.04–0.09 %` of the corresponding KE scale — the vertex–plate interaction is almost totally dissipative, and `e_rebound` measures the *partition*: a dimensionless specimen constant (0.019 / 0.022–0.024 / 0.028–0.030 for specimens 2/1/3) that survived both the session change and the tower damage. The scheduled restrained-vs-unrestrained check decides whether it's structure or fixture.

**The vocabulary the campaign objective actually lives in** (none computable from current captures): absorbed energy `E_abs = ∮F dx` (area of the force–displacement hysteresis loop), **SEA** = E_abs/mass, plateau stress, densification strain, crush-force efficiency = mean/peak force, cushion curves (ASTM D1596), damage boundary (ASTM D3332). All defined in Lu & Yu, [*Energy Absorption of Structures and Materials*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9781855736887/energy-absorption-of-structures-and-materials).

### 3. If the objective is literally energy absorption: three upgrade paths

1. **Quasi-static compression (recommended first).** Load frame, F–d loop per specimen → E_abs, SEA, CFE. This is exactly the protocol of the closest published analogue to this campaign — [Pajunen, Johanns, Pal, Rimoli & Daraio, *Mater. Des.* 182:107966 (2019)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127519304046) ([open access](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/96998)) — 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired cells under quasi-static compression *plus* drop-weight impact, showing the two agree on mechanism. Caveat: printed PU is rate-dependent, so this complements rather than replaces dynamic testing.
2. **Instrumented direct impact.** Drop a *known mass* carrying the existing accelerometer straight onto the specimen: `F = M·a`, integrate twice → F–d loop → **joules absorbed per impact**, plus a restitution coefficient from rebound velocity (the bookkeeping of ASTM D7136's instrumented impactor). Minimal hardware, but a real protocol change that loads specimens much harder — sacrifice articles first.
3. **Slo-mo velocimetry on the current test.** So far the video has been used for event *timing* (brake catch at +76–89 ms). Its higher use is *velocity*: marker + calibrated length scale + known frame rate → incident and rebound velocity → stack-level absorbed energy `½M(v_in²−v_out²)` per drop, once M is logged. Per-*specimen* differencing will drown in mat/rig variability, so treat this as a rig/stack energy audit and Δv cross-check, not a specimen metric. A photogate does the same with less analysis.

**Zero-cost metadata to start logging now:** falling mass, specimen mass per print, mat mass/batch, drop height per session (already agreed), first-block Δv (already adopted).

### 4. Reading list (all links verified; full annotated list in the doc)

**Tensegrity impact & EA:** [Pajunen et al. 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127519304046) (+ her free [PhD thesis](https://thesis.caltech.edu/13754/9/Thesis_Kirsti_Pajunen_6-2-2020_Full.pdf) on tensegrity-metamaterial dynamics) · [Rimoli, AIAA 2016-1511](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/abs/10.2514/6.2016-1511) on tensegrity-lander impact tolerance · [NASA SUPERball (free NTRS PDF)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20140011157/downloads/20140011157.pdf) · [Ashwear & Eriksson 2014](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260156059_Natural_frequencies_describe_the_pre-stress_in_tensegrity_structures) · [tensegrity-simplex modal hammer study, open access](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/10/23/8733).
**Fundamentals:** [Irvine's SRS tutorial (free)](https://www.vibrationdata.com/tutorials2/srs_intr.pdf) and [vibrationdata.com](https://www.vibrationdata.com) generally · Lalanne *Mechanical Shock* (Vol. 2) · *Harris' Shock and Vibration Handbook* · Inman *Engineering Vibration* (log decrement) · Ewins *Modal Testing* (FRF/coherence) · Feldman *Hilbert Transform Applications in Mechanical Vibration* (our envelope method) · [Lu & Yu](https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9781855736887/energy-absorption-of-structures-and-materials).
**Standards:** SAE J211-1 (see our audited notes in [`edison-trajectories/j211-audit/`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/tree/claude/issue-94-20260806-0326/edison-trajectories/j211-audit)) · ISO 18431-4 · MIL-STD-810 M516 (free via EverySpec) · [ASTM D1596](https://www.astm.org/Standards/D1596.htm), D3332, D7136 · ISO 5348.
**COR from timing:** [Bernstein 1977](https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-pdf/45/1/41/11809656/41_1_online.pdf) · [Aguiar & Laudares 2003](https://www.if.ufrj.br/~carlos/artigos/AJP2003_listening.pdf).

### Bottom line

The drop tower is doing what a transmission screen does well — repeatable, discriminating, blind-validated — and it now yields two honest per-specimen *dissipation* proxies: **ζ** (fraction of vibrational energy lost per cycle, ≈50–60 % here) and **`e_rebound`** (the one session-invariant constant in the program). But it cannot produce "energy absorbed per specimen" in joules, and no metric computed from these captures should be labeled that. If energy absorption is the optimization objective, the objective function has to come from §3's direct measurements — quasi-static F–d first, per the Pajunen et al. precedent — with the tower retained as the dynamic screen and `f_n` doubling as a per-print prestress gauge.

### A lesson: what a drop tower actually measures, and how to read our four numbers

- [x] Read the review doc on this PR
- [x] Build teaching figures (committed in [`a189fb3`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/commit/a189fb3), generated by [`scripts/teaching/make_drop_tower_primer_figures.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/scripts/teaching/make_drop_tower_primer_figures.py) — synthetic illustrations, not measured data)
- [x] Write the lesson below

This is the classroom version of [`docs/drop-tower-energy-absorption-review.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/docs/drop-tower-energy-absorption-review.md): same physics, taught from intuition up, with worked examples using our real numbers and a short quiz at the end.

---

### 1. The one idea everything hangs on

An accelerometer measures **acceleration versus time**. That's it. Every quantity we report is a shape extracted from that curve. To get to **energy** you need two more ingredients: a **mass** (to turn acceleration into force, `F = Ma`) and a **displacement** (to turn force into work, `E = ∫F dx`). Our setup logs neither the falling mass nor any displacement of the specimen — which is *the* reason no result in this program can currently be stated in joules. Not a software limitation; an information-theoretic one. Keep that in mind and everything else in the review doc follows.

### 2. The mental model: a mass on a spring, riding a moving floor

Picture the specimen as a single mass `m` on a spring `k` with a little damper, bolted to a floor (the plate) that suddenly decelerates. This "single-degree-of-freedom oscillator" is the workhorse model of all shock analysis, and each of our metrics is just this model asked a different question:

| question you ask the oscillator | metric that answers it |
|---|---|
| How hard was the floor hit, integrated? | `Δv` |
| How long did the hit last? | `τ` (pulse width) |
| How hard did the mass shake relative to the floor? | `T`, or properly the SRS |
| What note does it ring at afterwards? | `f_n` |
| How fast does the ringing die out? | `ζ` |
| How bouncy is the mass–floor contact? | `e_rebound` |

### 3. Reading one drop record, left to right

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/docs/figures/primer_fig1_drop_anatomy.png?raw=true)

**The pulse and Δv.** The base channel sees a ~300 G half-sine lasting a couple of milliseconds. The *area* under it is the velocity change: `Δv = ∫a dt`. Worked check: a 60 in (1.524 m) free fall arrives at `v = √(2gh) = √(2·9.81·1.524) ≈ 5.47 m/s` — exactly the Δv we measure on a healthy tower. That's why Δv is our free rig-health gauge: it should equal free-fall speed, every drop. During the pin-break sessions it read ~4.6 m/s. Energy scales with `v²`, so the tower was silently eating `1 − (4.6/5.47)² ≈ 29%` of the drop energy — issue #92's 26–38% range, recovered from one number.

**The ride-through and T.** During the pulse the specimen is too stiff-and-fast (see §4) to do anything but move with the plate, so the top vertex peak ≈ base peak and `T ≈ 1`. This is why T is our weakest discriminator: everything rides the pulse, so everything scores ~1.

**The ringdown: f_n and ζ.** After the pulse, the specimen is a struck tuning fork: free vibration at its natural frequency `f_n ≈ (1/2π)√(k/m) ≈ 520 Hz`, decaying. Two things to internalize:

- *f_n is a prestress gauge for tensegrity.* A tensegrity gets its stiffness largely from member pre-tension — like a guitar string, tighter means a higher note. So f_n drift between prints or sessions is a tension-health readout, not just a stiffness number ([Ashwear & Eriksson 2014](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260156059_Natural_frequencies_describe_the_pre-stress_in_tensegrity_structures)).
- *ζ is the energy metric hiding in plain sight.* The envelope of the ringdown is `e^(−ζωₙt)`. Energy goes as amplitude², so the fraction of vibrational energy lost per cycle is `1 − e^(−2δ) ≈ 4πζ` (with log decrement `δ = 2πζ/√(1−ζ²)`). At our ζ ≈ 0.07 that's **~58% of the vibrational energy dissipated every single cycle**, and the envelope time constant is `1/(ζωₙ) = 1/(0.07·2π·520) ≈ 4.4 ms` — which is precisely why our usable ringdowns are only 5–13 ms long. The signal doesn't end because the record does; it ends because the specimen destroys its own vibration that fast.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/docs/figures/primer_fig2_damping.png?raw=true)

The log-scale panel is the whole fitting method: a clean single-mode decay is a *straight line* in log-amplitude, and its slope is `−ζωₙ`. That's also why the r² gate matters — if the log-envelope isn't straight (r² < 0.85), two modes or a secondary event are superposed, and the "ζ" the fit returns describes nothing physical.

**The hop and e_rebound.** The vertex separates and lands back `t_second` later. Ballistics does the rest: something that flies for `t` under gravity left with `v_sep = g·t/2`. Worked example with `t_second = 25 ms`: `v_sep = 9.81·0.025/2 = 0.123 m/s`, and `e_rebound = 0.123/5.47 ≈ 0.022` — specimen 1's actual value. It's a coefficient of restitution measured by timing between bounces (a classic classroom technique — [Bernstein 1977](https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-pdf/45/1/41/11809656/41_1_online.pdf)). Energy view: the returned fraction is `e² ≈ 0.05%`, i.e. the vertex–plate interaction is ~99.95% dissipative, and what `e_rebound` measures is the *partition* — a dimensionless constant of the specimen that survived both the session change and the tower damage. That robustness is exactly what you want in an optimization objective.

### 4. Why "how fast is your structure vs. how fast is the hit" decides everything

Shock severity isn't about G's alone — it's about the ratio of the structure's period to the pulse duration, captured by the dimensionless product `f_n·τ`. The shock response spectrum (SRS) makes this quantitative: sweep an imaginary family of oscillators across frequency, ride each on the measured pulse, plot peak response.

![](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/docs/figures/primer_fig3_srs.png?raw=true)

Three regimes: soft structures (`f·τ ≪ 1`) can't follow the pulse and are **isolated**; structures near `f·τ ≈ 0.5` get **amplified** (the pulse pumps them near resonance); stiff structures (`f·τ ≫ 1`) follow the pulse **quasi-statically**, response ≈ input. Our specimens (`f·τ ≈ 0.9–1.7`) sit just past the peak — they neither isolate nor strongly amplify, they ride and then ring. If you wanted the drop tower to *load the specimen harder*, this figure tells you how: soften the specimen or shorten the pulse (less mat) until `f·τ` slides left toward the amplification peak.

### 5. Two vocabulary traps, so we all say the right words

- **"Transmissibility."** Real transmissibility is a frequency-response function `|H(f)|` measured with repeated or broadband excitation plus a coherence check. Our `T` is a ratio of two peaks that don't even occur at the same instant, filtered, one of them a nonlinear tri-axis magnitude. Call it a *filtered peak-acceleration ratio* and nobody can audit-flag it (this repo's J211/Edison audits already did).
- **"Energy absorption."** In the crashworthiness literature this means `E_abs = ∮F dx`, area of the force–displacement hysteresis loop through *large deformation* — strut buckling, snap-through, densification. Our specimens never leave the elastic regime in this test, so ζ and e_rebound are **dissipation proxies on the small vibrational energy slice**, not measurements of absorbed drop energy. Legitimate optimization signals for "attenuate and dissipate shock"; not joules. Getting joules is §4 of the review doc: a quasi-static F–d loop on a load frame (path A, recommended — it's the Pajunen/Daraio protocol), an instrumented direct impact (path B), or slo-mo velocimetry as a rig-level audit (path C). And the zero-cost move available today: **start logging the masses.**

<summary>Answers</summary>

### Would several hundred ms of accelerometer data give us this info?

Your instinct is partly right — and we've already cashed it in. The current records are **100 ms @ 1.25 MHz** (abc123) and **200 ms @ 125 kHz** (earlier campaigns), so the hop and the brake catch are *inside* the record: the hop was found in the DAQ data before video confirmed it, and `e_rebound = g·t_second/(2Δv)` is precisely the trick of extracting hundreds-of-ms flight information from an accelerometer via bounce **timing** (the Bernstein method). Timing at long timescales: yes, the accelerometer delivers.

Deformation at long timescales: no, for three reasons that longer records don't fix.

1. **There is no deformation out there to measure.** Both video passes at ~960 fps and the DAQ agree the deformation event spans 1–3 ms; after snap-back the specimen translates as a rigid body. The [abc123 analysis](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/b309ed8/docs/drop-test-abc123-blind-analysis.md) reached the same conclusion from the DAQ side: *"the blocker is the secondary event, not the record length"* — 98 ms of post-impact record buys only 5–13 ms of usable ringdown because ζ ≈ 7 % destroys the vibration itself (and the hop interrupts what's left). By +30 ms the specimen's vibration amplitude is down ~1000× — under the noise floor no matter how long you record.
2. **The channels are AC-coupled ICP accelerometers** (per the [DAQ setup](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/b309ed8/data/drop-tests/burn-in-wax/README.md)). Piezo/ICP sensors physically cannot see quasi-static acceleration: the −1 g free-fall shift during the bounce flight and the ~2–4 g brake deceleration spread over tens of ms are at or below the coupling corner. Longer records would faithfully capture more *nothing* between the sharp contact events.
3. **"Deformation" means displacement, and acceleration→displacement is double integration.** With the measured baseline offsets (sd 0.6–48 G in the abc123 records), even a 1 G residual bias produces `½bt² ≈ 0.4 m` of spurious displacement at t = 300 ms — versus the ~mm of real specimen deformation. Over milliseconds double integration is workable; over hundreds of ms it's noise-cubed.

**What a longer record *would* cheaply add:** bounce-count and settle timing, plus confirmation the post-catch tail is quiet. It's nearly free — keeping the same 125k-sample memory and dropping the rate to 250 kHz gives a 500 ms record — and worth doing once as a check. But it won't change any metric, and it won't yield deformation-vs-time.

**If deformation info is the goal**, the two instruments split cleanly by timescale: for the slow, large-amplitude part (flight, rebound, settle) the *video* is already the right sensor — and becomes quantitative with the plate-mounted scale recommended in [§4 of the prc1kn video analysis](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/b309ed8/docs/drop-test-prc1kn-video-analysis.md). For the fast part where the deformation actually lives (the 1–3 ms crush), the fix is faster frames (≥5000 fps DIC) or the instrumented-impact / load-frame paths in [§4 of the review doc](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/a189fb3/docs/drop-tower-energy-absorption-review.md) — not longer records.

|---|--:|--:|
| prc1kn drop 1 | 1 frame ≈ **1.0 ms** | 1.57 ms |
| prc1kn drop 2 | ≤2 frames ≈ **2.1 ms** | 1.57 ms |
